t.tarentum@40.5,17.2:
Taranto is a city between two seas. The old town sits on a small island between the Mar Grande, an open bay of the Gulf of Taranto, and the Mar Piccolo, an inner lagoon, connected to the mainland by bridges, including a swing bridge that opens to let warships pass into the naval base. Founded by Spartan colonists in the eighth century BC as Taras, it became one of the richest and most powerful cities of Magna Graecia, the Greek world in southern Italy, before falling to Rome.

The National Archaeological Museum of Taranto, the MArTA, is one of the finest in Italy, with a collection of gold jewellery, the Gold of Taranto, as well as sculptures, vases and mosaics from the Greek and Roman city. Allow a good two hours. The old town, Taranto Vecchia, is atmospheric but partly run down, with narrow alleys, a cathedral and the Castello Aragonese, a fortress built by the Aragonese kings of Naples in the fifteenth century, which can be visited with guides from the navy. The remains of a Doric temple stand near the castle.

Taranto's modern history has been dominated by its huge steelworks, one of the largest in Europe, which has brought jobs but also serious pollution problems that remain a subject of controversy. The city is also famous for its mussels, cultivated in the Mar Piccolo for centuries, and its seafood is excellent.

The riding around Taranto is mostly flat, along the coast and across the plain. To the west, the coast road toward Metaponto and the beaches of the Ionian Sea is straight and busy in summer. To the north, the Murgia plateau offers more interesting roads, with gentle curves through olive groves and dry-stone walls, toward Martina Franca, Locorotondo and the trulli of the Itria valley. Matera, about eighty kilometres away, with its cave dwellings, makes a great day ride. City traffic is heavy and chaotic, so park and walk in the centre.

Taranto has every service. Spring and autumn are ideal; summer in Puglia is very hot.
t.vjetrenica cave@42.8,18.0:
The karst country inland from Dubrovnik is a landscape of grey limestone hills, stony fields and long, flat-bottomed valleys called poljes, which flood in winter and dry out in summer. Popovo Polje, on the Bosnian side of the border, is one of the largest, and at its edge, near the village of Zavala, lies Vjetrenica, the most famous cave in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its name means wind cave, from the strong current of air that blows out of its entrance, cool in summer and noticeable from a distance.

Vjetrenica is a long cave system, with several kilometres of passages explored, and it is renowned among biologists as one of the richest caves in the world for cave-dwelling animals, with many species found nowhere else. Among them is the olm, a blind, pale salamander that lives in underground waters in the Dinaric karst. The cave is on the tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage. A section of the cave is open for guided tours, with lighting and walkways, and the temperature inside is cool all year round, so bring a layer.

Zavala is a small village with a monastery, and the area is sparsely populated, with stone houses, dry-stone walls and the occasional vineyard. Trebinje, the main town in the area, is a pleasant place on the Trebišnjica river, with a stone bridge, plane trees and the Tvrdoš monastery, which produces wine. Popovo Polje is known for its wines, both white and red.

The riding in this area is wonderful and quiet. The roads from Dubrovnik climb steeply into the hills and cross the border into Bosnia, then wind across the karst plateau, with long views and almost no traffic. Surfaces vary, and some roads are narrow. The border crossings can involve queues in summer, and you need a green card for insurance. Be aware that some areas in Bosnia still have unexploded mines from the war of the 1990s, so stay on roads and marked paths.

Fuel is limited in the hills; Ljubinje, Trebinje and Dubrovnik, about twenty-five kilometres away, are the nearest options. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.the via appia from mesochorum to scamnum:
The last stretch of the Via Appia ran across this flat, sun-drenched part of Puglia toward Brundisium, the port from which Romans sailed to Greece and the East. The road, begun in 312 BC from Rome, was the queen of roads, and the whole route became a UNESCO site in 2024. The section between the stations the Romans called Mesochorum and Scamnum passes near Oria and Francavilla Fontana, and while little of the original paving survives here, the line of the road still shapes the landscape, with modern roads, field boundaries and farm tracks following its course.

Oria is the place to stop. It is a hilltop town of white houses, narrow alleys and steep steps, crowned by a castle that the emperor Frederick II rebuilt in the thirteenth century, and a baroque cathedral with a colourful tiled dome. It was a major centre of the Messapians, the people who lived here before the Romans, and later had an important Jewish community in the early Middle Ages, which you can trace in the old Jewish quarter. From the top of the town, the plain spreads out in every direction, a sea of olive trees, vineyards and stone farmhouses.

The riding is flat, straight and hot. Roads across the Salento plain are generally good but can be patched and dusty, with farm vehicles and cyclists, and local driving can be adventurous. The scenery is quietly beautiful, especially the masserie, the fortified farmhouses that dot the countryside, and the dry stone walls. Sadly, many olive groves have been devastated by the Xylella bacterium, and you will see whole fields of grey, dead trees, a heartbreaking sight. Spring brings wildflowers and mild temperatures; summer heat can be overwhelming, with the scirocco wind adding to the discomfort.

Oria and Francavilla Fontana both have fuel, cafés and restaurants, and the food is excellent: orecchiette pasta with turnip tops, fava bean purée with chicory, and the local red wine from Primitivo and Negroamaro grapes. In August, Oria hosts a medieval festival with a famous tournament between the town's districts. Brindisi, where the Appia ended at a pair of columns above the harbour, is about thirty kilometres away and a fitting place to finish a ride along Rome's oldest highway.
Radimlja, just outside Stolac in Herzegovina, is the finest of the stećak graveyards, and it lies right beside the main road, which makes it one of the easiest pieces of medieval Europe to stop for. Stećci are massive limestone tombstones, shaped like chests, slabs or little gabled houses, carved between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries across the medieval kingdom of Bosnia and neighbouring lands. Many are decorated with reliefs: spirals, vines, crescents, stars, hunting scenes, dancers holding hands, and knights with swords and shields, and one figure at Radimlja raises an oversized right hand in what may be a greeting or a blessing. In 2016 UNESCO listed a group of these graveyards across four countries together.

Who made them is still debated. They were once linked to the Bosnian Church, a dissident Christian community, but Catholics, Orthodox and others used them too, and they seem to reflect a shared regional culture rather than a single faith. Walking among the stones in the late afternoon, when the low sun brings out the reliefs, is quietly moving.

Stolac itself is worth a stop. The small town sits in the canyon of the Bregava river, with old mills, stone bridges, a fortress on the hill and mosques that were destroyed in the war of the 1990s and later rebuilt. The war's scars are still visible here and there, and the town's mixed history is complex and sensitive, so tread respectfully.

The riding in Herzegovina is excellent: limestone karst, dry hills covered with scrub and pomegranate trees, vineyards and tobacco fields, and roads that twist through canyons and over passes with little traffic. The road from Stolac toward Mostar, about forty kilometres away, follows the Bregava and then the Neretva valley, with the Počitelj fortress village on the way, and the road south toward Neum and the Adriatic coast crosses wild karst plateaus. Summers are scorching, often well over thirty-five degrees; spring and autumn are perfect. Watch for loose gravel and the occasional landmine warning sign in remote areas, and stay on roads and paths.

Stolac has fuel, cafés and simple restaurants, and the local food is hearty: grilled meats, burek and fresh river fish, washed down with Žilavka white wine. Mostar has full services and its famous bridge.
t.lokrum island@42.6,18.1:
From the walls of Dubrovnik you look straight across a short stretch of sea to a low, dark green island covered in pines and holm oaks. That is Lokrum, and it is the closest thing the city has to a back garden. No cars or motorbikes are allowed on it, and nobody may stay overnight. You leave the bike on the mainland, catch one of the regular boats from the old harbour, and in about a quarter of an hour you step onto a quay with peacocks strutting about as if they owned the place, which they more or less do.

The island's story is rich in legends. Benedictine monks founded a monastery here in the Middle Ages, and one tale says Richard the Lionheart was shipwrecked on Lokrum on his way back from the Crusades and promised to build a church in thanks. When the monks were forced out in the early nineteenth century, they supposedly placed a curse on anyone who would own the island, and a string of later owners, including the Habsburg archduke Maximilian, who turned it into a summer retreat and brought the peacocks, met unhappy ends. Maximilian later became Emperor of Mexico and was executed there.

Today Lokrum is a nature reserve with a botanical garden, the ruins of the monastery, a small fort on the hilltop with views over the city, and a little salt lake known as the Dead Sea, linked to the open sea through the rocks and good for a calm swim. The rocky shores are popular with swimmers in summer, and the island has a few cafés.

Getting to Dubrovnik on two wheels is the riding part. The Adriatic coastal road, the D8, runs high above the sea with tight bends and stunning views, crossing the white suspension bridge over the inlet north of the city. Traffic in summer is heavy and the run into the old town can be gridlocked, so arrive early and park outside the walls. The climb up Srđ hill behind the city on a narrow road gives an aerial view of Lokrum and the old town together.

Dubrovnik has fuel and every service, though prices are high in season. Boats to Lokrum run mainly between spring and late autumn. Bring water, a swimsuit and sun protection, and check the time of the last boat back.
t.boljuni@43.0,17.9:
In the stony hills of eastern Herzegovina, a few kilometres from Stolac, a field of grey limestone blocks lies scattered among oak scrub and dry grass. These are stećci, medieval tombstones carved between roughly the twelfth and sixteenth centuries, and Boljuni has a few hundred of them, many decorated with reliefs: rosettes, crescents, spirals, hunters with spears, dancing figures holding hands, a man raising an oversized hand as if in greeting. Nobody fully agrees on who made them or what all the symbols mean, which makes standing among them oddly moving. Together with other cemeteries across Bosnia and Herzegovina and its neighbours, Boljuni is part of the UNESCO site of Stećci Medieval Tombstone Graveyards, inscribed in 2016.

Stolac itself is a small town on the clear green river Bregava, with old mills, stone bridges and a fortress on the hill above. It was badly damaged during the war in the 1990s, and much has been rebuilt since, including its mosques and Ottoman-era houses. Just outside town, the necropolis of Radimlja is the best-known stećci site in the country, right beside the main road and easy to visit.

Herzegovina is hot, bright country. Summers bake the karst, cicadas buzz in the oaks, and pomegranates and figs ripen in village gardens. The local white wine, Žilavka, is crisp and well suited to the heat, and the red Blatina is worth a try too.

The riding is good and often empty. From Mostar you come via Blagaj, where a dervish lodge sits under a cliff at the spring of the Buna, then over the hills to Stolac. Beyond, roads continue south-east through barren karst towards Ljubinje and Trebinje, with long views, fast bends and very little traffic. Surfaces are generally decent on the main roads but rougher on side routes, and livestock, slow trucks and sudden gravel need watching. One serious note: rural parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina still have areas affected by landmines from the war. Stay on roads, marked paths and visited sites, and never wander off into overgrown fields.

Stolac, about nine kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés. Order a coffee Bosnian style, thick and sweet, served in a small copper pot, and some ćevapi with fresh bread, and sit by the river in the shade.
t.the appia traiana along the adriatic coa:
Between Ostuni and Brindisi, along the Adriatic coast of Puglia, ran the Via Appia Traiana, a road built by the emperor Trajan in the early second century as a faster alternative to the old Appian Way, carrying traffic to the port of Brundisium, the gateway to Greece and the East. In 2024, stretches of both roads were inscribed by UNESCO as Via Appia, Regina Viarum. Here the old route followed the coastal plain through olive groves, and traces of it, together with ancient settlements, can be found near the sea.

The best-known site along this stretch is Egnazia, a short ride north, where the ruins of an ancient town lie right beside the sea, with a section of the Roman road running through them, its paving stones still marked by wheel ruts. Near Carovigno, the Torre Guaceto nature reserve protects dunes, wetlands and a marine area, with a watchtower overlooking clear water.

This is a land of ancient olive trees, some of them hundreds of years old, with twisted, hollow trunks like sculptures. In recent years, a bacterial disease has killed vast numbers of olive trees in southern Puglia, and the dead groves are a heartbreaking sight, though efforts are under way to replant and protect the survivors. Ostuni, a few kilometres inland, is a white city on a hill, its houses whitewashed and stacked up around a cathedral, glowing in the sun. Further inland, the Itria valley is dotted with trulli, the round stone houses with conical roofs.

The riding is pleasant, with coastal roads offering sea views and inland roads winding through olive groves, stone walls and farms called masserie, many converted into guest houses. The main coastal highway is fast and busy, so use the smaller roads for enjoyment. Summer brings heat and heavy traffic, especially near the beaches, while spring and autumn are ideal. Watch for potholes, gravel and local drivers.

Carovigno, about six kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Ostuni offers more choice. Try orecchiette, the ear-shaped pasta of Puglia, with turnip tops, or friselle, hard rings of bread softened with water and topped with tomatoes and olive oil, and finish with a pasticciotto, a custard-filled pastry.
t.castel del monte@41.1,16.3:
You see it long before you reach it: a pale stone crown sitting alone on a hilltop above the Murge plateau, visible for miles across the olive groves and wheat fields of northern Puglia. Castel del Monte was built in the 1240s for Emperor Frederick II, the brilliant and restless Hohenstaufen ruler whom contemporaries called the wonder of the world. It is perfectly octagonal, with eight octagonal towers at the corners and an octagonal courtyard in the middle, and nobody really knows what it was for. It has no moat, no stables, no obvious defensive purpose, which has fed centuries of theories about astronomy, geometry and mysticism. UNESCO listed it in 1996, and Italians carry it in their pockets: it is on the back of the one-cent euro coin.

The landscape around it belongs to the Alta Murgia National Park, a limestone plateau of rocky pastures, dry-stone walls, sinkholes and sparse almond trees. It is a stark, open place, especially in high summer when the grass turns blond and the heat shimmers on the road. In spring, wild orchids and poppies brighten the fields, and kestrels hunt overhead.

The ride in is part of the appeal. From Andria or Corato the roads climb gently across the plateau, mostly straight with long bends, and the castle grows on the skyline the whole way. Traffic is light, but tour buses gather in high season, and the wind can be strong and gusty across the exposed tops. The final approach is controlled, and visitors usually leave vehicles in a car park below and walk or take a shuttle up, so be ready for that. Golden hour, when the stone glows honey-coloured, is when the place is at its best.

Fuel and food are found in the nearby towns. Corato, with forty-six thousand people, and Andria, with nearly a hundred thousand, have all services, and Minervino Murge is a smaller hill town with views across the plain. Andria is said to be the home of burrata, the creamy-centred mozzarella, so it would be rude not to try it. Puglia's olive oil is superb, and orecchiette with turnip tops is the local pasta dish to order.
t.old bridge area of the old city of mosta:
The Old Bridge in Mostar is a single stone arch, slender and impossibly high, leaping across the emerald-green Neretva between two fortified towers. The Ottomans built it in the 1560s, designed by an architect named Mimar Hayruddin, and for more than four centuries it stood as a symbol of the city. On 9 November 1993, during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was shelled and collapsed into the river. It was rebuilt with the original techniques and stone recovered from the riverbed and reopened in 2004, and the following year UNESCO listed the Old Bridge Area as a symbol of reconciliation and cultural coexistence.

On summer days, local divers stand on the parapet, wait for the crowd to gather and drop some two dozen metres into the cold river, a tradition that goes back centuries. The old town around the bridge is a maze of cobbled lanes lined with shops selling copperware, carpets and souvenirs, and mosques with slender minarets. A short ride south, the Blagaj Tekke, a Dervish monastery, stands at the foot of a cliff beside the spring of the Buna river, one of the most beautiful places in the country.

The ride to Mostar from Sarajevo is a classic: the road follows the Neretva canyon from Konjic and Jablanica, through deep gorges with turquoise water, tunnels and bridges, with tight curves and stunning views. The road south to the Adriatic coast at Neum or toward Dubrovnik is also scenic, though busier in summer. Mostar is one of the hottest cities in the region, with temperatures often over forty degrees in July and August, so ride early in the morning and take a long siesta. Watch for potholes, slow trucks and impatient overtaking.

Mostar, with over a hundred thousand inhabitants, has plenty of fuel, accommodation and restaurants. The old town is pedestrianised and cobbled, so park outside and walk. Try ćevapi, small grilled sausages served with flatbread and onions, burek, a flaky pastry filled with meat or cheese, and a cup of Bosnian coffee, thick and strong. The local wines, Žilavka white and Blatina red, are excellent and inexpensive.
t.durmitor national park@43.1,19.0:
Durmitor is the kind of mountain range that makes you pull over every few minutes. In the north of Montenegro, a limestone massif rises above a high plateau around Žabljak, with jagged peaks, glacial lakes and deep canyons carved by the Tara, Piva and Sušica rivers. The national park was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1980, and it includes the Tara canyon, one of the deepest gorges in Europe. Glaciers shaped the range, leaving cirques and lakes scattered across the high ground, of which the Black Lake near Žabljak is the best known.

The Durmitor ring road is one of the best rides in the Balkans. From Žabljak, the road climbs over the Sedlo pass at about 1900 metres, through an open, wild landscape of grass, rock and snow patches that linger into summer, and then descends in tight bends toward Plužine and the Piva lake. The road is narrow, sometimes without barriers, with livestock, potholes and rockfalls. Fog can roll in quickly, and snow can close the pass from late autumn to late spring. Ride it in summer or early autumn, carefully and slowly.

The Đurđevića Tara bridge, a concrete arch built just before the Second World War, spans the Tara canyon north-east of Žabljak and was famously blown up and rebuilt during the war. Today you can ride across it, watch rafters below and zipliners above. The village of Umoljani and the shepherds' settlements on the plateau keep the traditions of summer grazing, with katuns, the seasonal huts where families make cheese and kajmak.

Žabljak is the main base, a small town with fuel, accommodation and restaurants, though prices rise in high season. Plužine, at the other end of the ring, also has fuel. Pljevlja, the nearest larger town, is a good hour away. Try the local lamb cooked under a sač, a metal lid covered with embers, and the cheeses from the high pastures. Nights on the plateau are cold even in July, so bring a warm layer and keep an eye on the weather.
t.historic city of trogir@43.5,16.3:
Trogir is an island, though you barely notice it. The old town sits on a tiny islet between the mainland and the larger island of Čiovo, linked to both by short bridges, and inside its walls is one of the best preserved medieval towns on the Adriatic, a UNESCO site of narrow lanes, stone palaces and churches, crammed into an area you can walk across in five minutes.

Greeks from the island of Vis founded a settlement here in antiquity, and later the Romans, Byzantines, Croatian kings, Venetians and Austrians all left their mark. The cathedral of St Lawrence is the jewel, and its west portal, carved by the master Radovan in 1240, is one of the most important Romanesque works in Croatia, with Adam and Eve standing on lions and scenes of the months of the year. Climb the cathedral tower for a view over the red roofs. At the western tip of the islet stands the Kamerlengo fortress, built by Venice in the fifteenth century.

Riding to Trogir is mostly about the Adriatic coast road, the D8, which runs along the shore with the sea on one side and bare limestone mountains on the other. It is a wonderful road in spring and autumn, with constant views of islands and bays, but in summer it gets very busy with traffic and coaches, and the stretch near Split airport, just east of Trogir, can be congested. The road into the hinterland, towards the Dalmatian interior, is quieter and climbs quickly into a stony, dry landscape. Watch for strong winds: the bura, a cold north-easterly, can gust violently on this coast.

Trogir town has fuel and all services, and the waterfront promenade, the Riva, is lined with cafés and restaurants looking across to Čiovo. Seafood is the obvious choice: grilled fish, black risotto with cuttlefish ink, and Dalmatian ham. Parking near the old town can be difficult in summer, but motorcycles have an easier time. Early in the morning, before the tourists arrive, the lanes are cool and quiet, and the stone glows in the low sun. In the evening, when the day trippers leave, the town comes back to life with locals.
t.gastgivars@61.5,16.4:
Gästgivars is a farm in the village of Vallsta, in Hälsingland, in central Sweden, and inside its wooden buildings are some of the finest painted rooms in the country. It is one of the seven decorated farmhouses of Hälsingland inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012, recognized for the extraordinary wealth of folk art that prosperous farmers commissioned in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The name means the innkeeper's farm, and it once served as an inn for travellers along the road through the Ljusnan valley.

The farmers of Hälsingland grew rich from flax and forestry, and they spent their money on large houses with rooms reserved for festive occasions, painted from floor to ceiling by itinerant artists. The paintings at Gästgivars include biblical scenes, flowers and decorative patterns in bright colours, combining rural traditions with styles borrowed from the manor houses of the nobility. The farm is still owned by the same family, and guided tours show the rooms in summer.

The Ljusnan valley is a peaceful landscape of forests, lakes and farms, with the river flowing south towards the Gulf of Bothnia. The roads are well surfaced, with gentle curves following the valley and long straights through the forest. Traffic is light, but watch out for moose and deer, especially at dawn and dusk, and for logging trucks. Summer is the best season, with long days and mild temperatures, and the light at midsummer is magical, with only a short twilight at night. Winters are long and cold, with snow and ice on the roads.

Arbrå, seven kilometres away, is a small village with basic services, and Bollnäs, twenty kilometres south, is a larger town with fuel and shops. Järvsö, to the north, is a popular summer destination with a ski hill used for mountain biking and a wildlife park. Swedish fika, coffee and a cinnamon bun, is a ritual not to be missed. In the evening, the light on the river and the red wooden houses of the valley is beautiful, and the silence of the forest is broken only by birdsong.
t.kucarin in hrancici@43.7,18.8:
Grey limestone slabs lie in the grass at Hrančići like a congregation that sat down six hundred years ago and never got up. These are stećci, the carved medieval tombstones that are found across Bosnia and Herzegovina and its neighbours, and the group at Kučarin is one of the sites included in the UNESCO listing of stećci graveyards in 2016. Some are plain chests, some are gabled like little houses, and a few carry reliefs of spirals, vines, shields or figures with raised hands that still nobody fully agrees how to read.

The place lies in the hills above the upper Drina, in the stretch of valley between Foča, Ustikolina and Goražde. The Drina here is that unreal green you see in photographs, cutting through steep wooded slopes, and the main road along it is a fine ride in its own right: a two-lane route that follows the river closely, with long fast bends, a few tighter sections where the valley pinches, and some uneven patches and gravelly verges. Watch for trucks, slow farm vehicles and drivers who overtake on faith. Side roads up to villages like Hrančići turn narrow and steep, with surfaces that can change from good tarmac to broken asphalt without warning.

History in this valley is heavy and close. Ustikolina has one of the oldest mosques in Bosnia, rebuilt after the war of the 1990s, and Goražde was a besieged enclave during that conflict; a quiet word with locals will tell you more than any guidebook. Foča, upstream, is the base for rafting on the Tara and the Drina, and in summer you will see roof racks full of boats.

For practical stops, Goražde is the biggest town nearby, with petrol stations, shops and plenty of cafés along the river where a strong Bosnian coffee arrives with a glass of water and often a cube of Turkish delight. Foča has the same. Smaller places have bakeries selling burek in the morning, which is all the fuel a rider really needs until lunch.

Spring and early autumn are the sweet spots, when the slopes are green or golden and the heat is manageable. Midsummer in the valley can be scorching, so ride early. Spend a few quiet minutes among the stones, trace a carved spiral with your eyes, and then roll back down to the river with the feeling of having met someone very old.
t.grcka glavica in the village of biskup@4:
The Greek hillock, Grčka glavica, is a misleading name: the medieval tombstones that crown it have nothing to do with Greece. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, folk tradition often credited the stećci, the great carved medieval tombstones of the region, to Greeks, giants or other mysterious ancestors, and the names have stuck. The necropolis near the village of Biskup, in the hills south of Konjic, is a group of these stones, some decorated with reliefs of crosses, rosettes, hunting scenes or figures, and it is one of the sites in the UNESCO listing of stećci medieval tombstone graveyards, listed in 2016.

The stones stand on a ridge with views over the surrounding hills, and the site has a lonely, windswept quality, especially in autumn and winter. Biskup lies in the upper valley of the Neretva, in a landscape of limestone mountains, forests and pastures, where small villages are scattered among the hills and life follows a slow rural rhythm.

Konjic, about twenty kilometres away, is a pleasant town on the Neretva with a restored Ottoman stone bridge and a long tradition of wood carving. Nearby, hidden inside a mountain, is a vast nuclear bunker built for Tito and the Yugoslav leadership during the Cold War, now open to visitors and used for contemporary art exhibitions. Boračko lake, a glacial lake in the mountains, and the canyon of the Rakitnica are beautiful places to explore.

The riding in the upper Neretva valley is excellent. Roads wind along the river and over the hills, with tight curves, steep gradients and spectacular views of the mountains and the turquoise water. Surfaces vary from good to rough, with gravel, potholes and occasional rockfalls, and traffic is light. Watch for livestock, trucks carrying timber and the occasional car taking a corner on the wrong side. Weather can change quickly in the mountains.

Konjic has fuel, shops and restaurants, and smaller villages have a store or bar. Local food includes lamb roasted on a spit, trout from the river, ćevapi, small grilled sausages, served with flatbread and onions, and pita, savoury pastries filled with meat, cheese or spinach. Come in late spring or early autumn. Find the stones on the ridge in the evening light, when the carvings cast long shadows, and enjoy the silence of one of the oldest graveyards in the Balkans.
t.ravanjska vrata@43.9,17.3:
The Kupres plateau is one of the high, open places of Bosnia and Herzegovina, more than a thousand metres up, with wide grasslands, cold winters and a sky that seems close enough to touch. Ravanjska vrata, the gates of Ravno, lies in this landscape, between Kupres and Tomislavgrad, and it is known for a group of stećci, the carved medieval tombstones that are found across Bosnia, Herzegovina and the neighbouring countries. UNESCO listed a selection of these necropolises in 2016. The stones are often decorated with spirals, crosses, hunting scenes and figures with raised hands, and their makers remain a subject of debate.

The plateau is a place of shepherds and wind. Snow lies here for months in winter, and Kupres has a ski centre; in summer, the grasslands are covered with flowers and sheep. The history is harder. The plateau saw fierce fighting during the war of the 1990s, and memorials stand by the roads. Tomislavgrad, to the south, is a market town on the edge of the Duvno field, one of the large karst plains of the region, and the town is named after Tomislav, the first king of Croatia, who according to tradition was crowned nearby.

The riding is wonderful in its open, high-altitude way. The roads across the plateau run over long straights and gentle bends with big views, and then drop down through forests to the karst plains below. The surface is mostly good on the main roads, rougher on minor ones, and there can be livestock on the tarmac. Weather changes fast: thunderstorms in summer, fog in autumn and snow from late autumn to spring. Wind across the plateau can be strong. Respect warnings about mines away from roads and marked paths; they are rare now, but the past is still not entirely buried here.

Kupres and Tomislavgrad both have fuel and food. The local cooking is hearty and meat-based, with lamb roasted on a spit, cheeses and bread baked under a bell. Cafés serve strong coffee in the Bosnian style. If you stop to look at the stećci, walk slowly among them, touch the carvings gently, and enjoy the silence of the plateau. These stones have watched over the high grasslands for centuries, and they will be here long after we have ridden on.
t.grebnice@42.9,18.5:
Grebnice, a name that simply means something like grave-stones, is a field of stećci near Bileća in eastern Herzegovina. These are the massive carved tombstones of medieval Bosnia and its neighbours, cut from local limestone between roughly the twelfth and sixteenth centuries, shaped like chests, slabs or little houses with gabled roofs, and sometimes covered with spirals, rosettes, swords, shields and dancing figures. UNESCO listed a selection of the most important sites together in 2016, and the necropolis here is one of the eastern Herzegovinian groups. Standing among them on a still afternoon, with the grass grown up around the stones, is a strangely moving experience.

Bileća is a town of some thirteen thousand on the edge of a large reservoir, the Bilećko jezero, created when the Trebišnjica river was dammed in the 1960s. The lake is long and blue-green, set in a landscape of bare grey karst and scrubby oak, and in summer people swim from its shores. Further south, the Trebišnjica flows toward Trebinje, a pleasant town with plane trees, a stone bridge from the Ottoman period and a Serbian Orthodox monastery, Tvrdoš, known for its wine cellars. The local wines, from the dark Vranac grape and the white Žilavka, are good and inexpensive.

The riding in eastern Herzegovina is a revelation for those who have only ridden along the Croatian coast. The roads climb from the coast through karst plateaus and across deep valleys, with long open bends, very little traffic and wide views. Surfaces are generally decent on main routes, more uneven on minor ones, and the heat in summer can be fierce, radiating off the white rock. The bora, a cold, gusty wind, blows in winter. Expect livestock, slow trucks and occasional police checks.

Bileća has fuel, shops and cafés; Trebinje, about twenty-five kilometres away, has a larger choice and a lively market. Herzegovinian food includes smoked ham, cheese preserved in a sheepskin, lamb roasted under a metal bell and cevapi, small grilled sausages served with onions and flatbread. If you visit the stećci, walk carefully, as the ground can be uneven and full of thorny plants. Look closely at the decorations, and notice how different each stone is, as if the carvers wanted every grave to tell its own story.
t.mehmed pasa sokolovic bridge in visegrad:
Eleven stone arches cross the Drina at Višegrad, pale against the green water, and the bridge has been doing so since the 1570s. It was commissioned by Mehmed Paša Sokolović, a boy from a nearby village who was taken as a child into Ottoman service and rose to become Grand Vizier, the most powerful man in the empire after the sultan. He had it built by Mimar Sinan, the greatest architect of the Ottoman age, and it remains one of the masterpieces of that era, listed by UNESCO in 2007.

The bridge is famous across the world thanks to Ivo Andrić, whose novel The Bridge on the Drina tells the story of the town and its people across four centuries, using the bridge as the constant thread. Andrić won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1961, and the book remains the best introduction to this region. In the town, the film director Emir Kusturica built Andrićgrad, a small stone town of shops, cafés and a cinema, intended as a tribute to the writer. It divides opinion, but it is worth a look.

The history of Višegrad also includes darker chapters. During the war in the 1990s the town saw terrible violence against its Bosniak population, some of it on the bridge itself. Many visitors find it right to be aware of this, and to treat the place with the respect such memories deserve.

The riding around Višegrad is superb. The road along the Drina is spectacular, with the river in a deep green gorge, tunnels cut through rock, and bends that follow every turn of the water. East towards the Serbian border and Mokra Gora, the road climbs into the mountains, with forests, meadows and views. Mokra Gora has the Šargan Eight, a restored narrow-gauge railway that loops in a figure of eight to climb the mountain. The surfaces are mixed, from smooth to potholed, and trucks and buses use the main roads, so take care in tunnels and on blind bends.

Višegrad has fuel, shops, cafés and restaurants. Try ćevapi or a plate of grilled trout from the river. Border crossings to Serbia are close, so carry your documents and green card. Sit on the bridge for a while, as Andrić's characters did, and watch the river slide past.
t.dolovi in the village of umoljani@43.7,1:
Umoljani clings to the edge of the Bjelašnica massif above the Rakitnica canyon, an hour or so southwest of Sarajevo by road, and it is one of those mountain villages that feel a world away from the cities below. Stone houses with steep roofs, a small mosque and a scattering of shepherds' huts sit on a high green plateau, and nearby, at a spot known as Dolovi, a group of medieval tombstones called stećci lies in the grass. These carved limestone monuments, made between roughly the twelfth and sixteenth centuries, are found across Bosnia and neighbouring countries and were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2016. Their reliefs of hunters, dancers, spirals and crescent moons are a fascinating window onto a culture that left few written records.

The landscape is the real star. Bjelašnica rises behind the village, a broad limestone mountain that hosted Olympic events in 1984, and the Rakitnica canyon cuts a deep, sheer gash through the plateau to the south. In summer the meadows are full of wildflowers and grazing sheep, and shepherds still bring their flocks up to these pastures, living in simple huts. In winter, snow often cuts the village off. Lukomir, the highest permanently inhabited village in Bosnia, lies further along the plateau and is often combined with Umoljani on a mountain loop.

Getting here is half the adventure. From the Sarajevo side, the road climbs past the Bjelašnica ski area and then narrows into a mountain lane with tight hairpins, steep gradients and sections of rough asphalt and gravel. It is entirely doable on a road bike with care, but an adventure or dual-sport machine will feel more at home on the rougher bits, especially after rain. Watch for livestock, deep potholes, and loose stones on the bends, and be aware that landmine warnings still exist in some remote areas of Bosnia, so stick to roads and marked paths.

Nobody sells petrol on the plateau. Fill the tank in Hadžići or the outskirts of Sarajevo before you start the climb, and bring water and snacks. In summer, some families in Umoljani offer simple food, such as pies, cheese and kajmak, but do not count on it. Park near the village, walk to the stećci, and listen to the wind across the high pastures. It is a remarkable place, and the ride back down, with the light falling across the canyon, will stay with you.
t.old city of dubrovnik@42.6,18.1:
Dubrovnik is the place where the Dalmatian coast reaches its theatrical climax: a walled city of pale limestone thrust out into a sea that refuses to be any colour but deep blue. The walls run for nearly two kilometres around the old town, with towers, bastions and the great Minčeta fortress on the landward side, and inside them the marble-paved Stradun runs straight from the Pile Gate to the old port. For centuries this was the Republic of Ragusa, a small, astute maritime state that survived between Venice and the Ottoman Empire through trade, diplomacy and a famously effective tribute system, until Napoleon ended its independence in the early nineteenth century.

The town has seen hard times. The 1667 earthquake destroyed much of it, which is why so much of what you see is Baroque reconstruction, and in 1991 and 1992 it was shelled during the siege by Yugoslav forces. The restoration since then has been remarkable, though you can still find maps at the entrance showing where shells struck. Today the problem is the opposite: crowds, especially when cruise ships are in, and the old town can feel like a stage set by mid-morning in summer.

For riding, Dubrovnik is best seen from above. The Adriatic Highway, the D8, runs along the coast north and south of the city, carved into the cliffs with endless curves, superb views and plenty of traffic in summer, including tour buses and slow camper vans. The road up to Mount Srđ behind the city climbs in tight hairpins to a viewpoint where the whole old town lies beneath you like a model. Southward toward Cavtat and the Konavle valley, the country turns greener and more rural, with vineyards and quieter lanes. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer heat can be brutal.

Practicalities matter here. Parking inside the city walls is impossible, and finding a spot near the Pile Gate can be a challenge, so use the public car parks and expect to pay. Fuel is easy to find in the city's suburbs and along the coast. For food, the old town is pricey and touristy; look a little outside for better value, and try local black risotto, fresh fish or Ston oysters from the peninsula to the north. And when the crowds get too much, ride up to Srđ for sunset.
t.potkuk in bitunja@43.1,18.1:
Grey limestone, thin grass, a scatter of oaks and juniper, and among them heavy blocks of carved stone lying where they were set some six or seven hundred years ago. Potkuk, near the hamlet of Bitunja in eastern Herzegovina, is one of the necropolises of stećci, the medieval tombstones that were added to the World Heritage list in 2016 together with sites across Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia.

Stećci were carved roughly between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries, by communities whose faith historians still argue about: Catholic, Orthodox, members of the independent Bosnian Church, and often all of them in the same region. The stones take the form of slabs, chests and gabled houses, and the best are decorated with spirals, vines, crescents, crosses, shields, swords and lively figures of hunters, horsemen and circle dances. They are among the few things that speak directly for the ordinary people of medieval Bosnia.

The landscape here is high karst, the plateau country between Stolac, Nevesinje and Ljubinje. Water vanishes into the rock, so valleys are dry poljes, flat-floored basins that flood in winter and dry out to pasture in summer. Roads cross the plateaus on narrow strips of asphalt that are sometimes patched, sometimes gravel, often shared with sheep and the occasional slow car. In July and August the heat reflects off the white rock like an oven, while in winter the bura wind can be fierce. Spring, when the meadows bloom, and early autumn are the sweet spots.

Stolac, fourteen kilometres away, is the most rewarding town in the area. It sits in the green gorge of the Bregava river, with old mills, Ottoman houses and the ruins of a hilltop fort. Nearby are Radimlja, the best known stećci necropolis of all, right by the main road, and Daorson, a hilltop town of the Illyrian Daorsi with walls built of huge cut blocks. Vjetrenica, the largest cave in the country, lies to the south in Popovo polje.

One practical point matters more than any other. Bosnia and Herzegovina still has areas contaminated by mines from the 1990s war, so stay on roads, paths and clearly used tracks and respect any red warning signs. Stolac and Nevesinje both have fuel, bakeries and cafés; fill up before heading into the plateaus.
t.kalufi in krekovi@43.3,18.2:
The Nevesinjsko polje is a broad, flat-floored basin high in the karst of eastern Herzegovina, ringed by bare limestone hills, and at Krekovi, near its edge, a group of stećci known as Kalufi stands in the grass. These medieval tombstones, carved between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries, belong to the transnational World Heritage Site inscribed in 2016. At Krekovi you find slabs, chests and gabled forms, some decorated with crosses, rosettes and borders, set in rows facing roughly east to west in the old tradition.

Nevesinje, nine kilometres away, has a famous place in Balkan history. In 1875 the Christian peasants of the area rose against Ottoman rule, an uprising remembered as the Nevesinje rifle, which spread across Herzegovina and Bosnia and set off a chain of events leading to the great Eastern crisis, wars between Russia and the Ottoman Empire and, in 1878, the Congress of Berlin. Few visitors realise that such a quiet place helped redraw the map of Europe.

The polje itself is a typical karst feature: water disappears into sinkholes, and the basin floods in wet winters, becoming a lake for weeks or months. In summer it is a sea of grass and fields, with herds of sheep and cattle and the occasional horse. The surrounding hills are covered with scrub, juniper and stunted oaks, and the light is harsh and bright at midday, soft and golden in the evening.

The main road from Mostar to Nevesinje climbs out of the Neretva valley in a series of curves, past Blagaj, where a dervish monastery stands beneath a cliff at the source of the Buna river, one of the most beautiful spots in the country. Beyond Nevesinje, roads lead across the high plateaus to Gacko and towards Montenegro, with long straights and wide views. The asphalt is mostly fair, but potholes and livestock are common hazards.

Nevesinje has fuel stations, a bakery or two and plenty of cafés. Mostar, with its famous bridge and old town, is about an hour away. As elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina, landmines from the war of the 1990s remain in some areas, so stay on roads and well-used paths. Grilled lamb, cheeses from the high pastures and strong coffee are the local staples.
t.quartiere monti@40.8,17.2:
Alberobello looks like a fairy tale for about the first thirty seconds, and then you start wondering how on earth the trulli stay up. These little round houses of limestone, with conical roofs built of flat stones stacked in rings and no mortar at all, are a building tradition unique to this corner of Puglia, and the Rione Monti quarter on the southern hill of town has the densest concentration of them anywhere, around a thousand packed along a few steep lanes.

The usual explanation for the dry-stone method is a tax story. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the local counts of Conversano are said to have encouraged peasants to build without mortar so the houses could be dismantled quickly if a royal inspector came to count dwellings and levy taxes. Whether every detail is true, it fits the place: the trulli feel like homes built by people who needed to be clever with what they had. Many roofs carry symbols painted in whitewash, crosses, hearts, planets and signs whose meaning is debated, and the pinnacles on top are a stonemason's signature.

Rione Monti is the busy side, lined with souvenir shops, small bars and rooms to rent inside trulli. Walk across the main road to the Aia Piccola district for a quieter version where people still simply live, and visit the Trullo Sovrano, the only two-storey trullo in town. Arrive early or stay into the evening, when the coach groups have gone and the stone glows in the low sun.

The real reason to come on a bike, though, is the Itria Valley that surrounds the town. It is not much of a valley, more a rolling plateau of red earth, olive trees, vineyards and dry-stone walls, but the small roads between Alberobello, Locorotondo, Cisternino and Martina Franca are a delight: narrow, gently curving, dotted with trulli in the fields, and almost empty in the middle of the week. Locorotondo, a white town built in a circle on its hill, makes a lovely coffee stop, and its crisp white wine is worth remembering for the evening.

Alberobello has around nine thousand residents, so fuel, cash machines and workshops are not a problem. Eat bombette, small rolls of pork stuffed with cheese and grilled over coals, a speciality of the Itria butchers, or orecchiette with turnip tops, the classic pasta of Puglia. Summer is hot and crowded; May, June and September are the months to choose for this ride.
t.bare zugica@43.1,19.2:
Near Žabljak, on the high plateau below Durmitor, a group of medieval tombstones lies in a meadow at Bare Žugića. These are stećci, massive carved stones that mark graves from the twelfth to the sixteenth centuries, found across Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro. Some are simple slabs, others shaped like houses or sarcophagi, decorated with carvings of spirals, crosses, vines, hunting scenes, dancers and figures with raised hands. Their makers belonged to various Christian communities of the medieval Balkans, and their meaning is still debated. In 2016 UNESCO listed a selection of the most important sites, including Bare Žugića, as the Stećci Medieval Tombstone Graveyards. Seeing these stones in a high meadow, surrounded by mountains, is quietly moving.

Durmitor is the great mountain massif of northern Montenegro, a national park and UNESCO site of limestone peaks, glacial lakes and forests, with the highest summit, Bobotov Kuk, rising to over two and a half thousand metres. Žabljak, at around fourteen hundred metres, is one of the highest towns in the Balkans, a base for hiking in summer and skiing in winter. The Black Lake, a short walk from town, reflects the peaks in its dark water.

The Tara river canyon, to the north, is one of the deepest in Europe, cutting through the mountains for many kilometres. The Đurđevića Tara bridge, a concrete arch bridge built just before the Second World War, spans the canyon at a dizzying height, and you can ride across it and stop to look down at the river far below.

The riding is spectacular. The Durmitor ring road climbs from Žabljak over the high plateau and the Sedlo pass, nearly two thousand metres up, through a lunar landscape of limestone and grass, with views of jagged peaks, and then descends towards Plužine and the Piva lake. The road is narrow, often without guardrails, with sheep and cows on the road and a surface that varies from good to rough. It is usually closed by snow from late autumn to late spring. The Piva canyon road, to the west, goes through dozens of rough-hewn tunnels carved into the rock.

Žabljak has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try kačamak, a rich porridge of cornmeal, potatoes and cheese, and local lamb cooked under a metal lid buried in embers.
t.brundisium@40.6,17.9:
Brindisi is where the Appian Way ends, and the Romans knew it as Brundisium. The old road ran from Rome across southern Italy to this harbour, the gateway to Greece and the East, and a tall Roman column near the waterfront marks its final stretch; a second column stood beside it until it was taken to Lecce in the seventeenth century. The harbour itself is a long, sheltered inlet, a natural port that has served merchants, crusaders and armies for more than two thousand years.

The poet Virgil died here in 19 BC on his way back from Greece, and the town has never let anyone forget it. Julius Caesar besieged Pompey here in the civil war, and in the Middle Ages the crusaders gathered at the port. Today the old centre has the Swabian castle, built by the emperor Frederick II, and an Aragonese fortress on an island in the harbour, plus a small, tidy historic quarter with churches and narrow streets. The sea breeze, the smell of salt and diesel from the docks, and the sound of the ferries create a feeling of arrival and departure.

Riding in the city is like riding in any busy southern Italian town: traffic is quick, pedestrians cross when they please, and scooters appear from every direction. Outside, the roads of Salento are flat and fast, with long straights through olive groves, vineyards and low stone walls, and pleasant coastal stretches to the north and south. Surfaces are generally good but can be rough on minor roads, and summer heat is intense in July and August. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with light that makes the whitewashed villages glow.

Brindisi has fuel at every turn, and the centre is full of cafés, bars and restaurants serving fresh seafood, orecchiette with turnip tops, and the local taralli, ring-shaped crackers that go well with wine from the Salento. Park near the waterfront and walk the old streets, because the historic centre has limited-traffic zones that catch the unwary. If you are catching a ferry, arrive early, and take a moment at the column, where one of the great roads of the ancient world quietly ends.
Croatian cathedrals are usually built of brick and timber, so the first odd thing about St James in Šibenik is that it is made entirely of stone, vaulted and roofed in carefully shaped slabs that lock together without a scrap of wood or mortar in the structure. It took more than a century to finish, from the 1430s into the 1530s, and the work passed through the hands of Juraj Dalmatinac and later Niccolò Fiorentino, which is why Gothic and Renaissance ideas sit in the same building. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 2000.

Walk round the east end and look up at the frieze. Seventy-one carved heads run along the apse, men, women and children, and the story goes that the sculptor used ordinary townspeople as models. Some are grumpy, some look surprised, one or two look faintly drunk. It is the kind of detail that makes you stand in a side street for ten minutes with a neck ache.

Šibenik itself is a proper working town of about thirty-seven thousand people, so it has fuel, supermarkets, and cafes in the old lanes that climb up from the waterfront. It sits where the Krka river reaches the sea through a long, deep channel, and the fortress of St Nicholas guards the entrance. If you are on the day out from Zadar, the coast road, the old Jadranska magistrala, gives you the sea on one side and bare grey karst on the other, with the island-studded Adriatic changing colour with every kilometre. It is a busy road in summer, so patience pays, and the bura wind can blow hard across exposed sections in winter and early spring.

Upstream from town lies Krka National Park, whose travertine waterfalls are a good reason to extend the day, though swimming in the main falls is no longer allowed. Vodice and Brodarica along the shore have beaches and fish restaurants, a decent lunch option if the old town's tourist menus feel too staged. Go early, before the tour groups, and the cathedral square is nearly empty, the stone pale and the pigeons the only crowd.
t.the appia traiana from beneventum to aeq:
Trajan was an emperor who liked roads, and in about AD 109 he opened a new one to shorten the journey from Rome to Brindisi, the port for Greece and the East. The old Via Appia went the long way round, down through the marshes and the coast, and the Via Traiana cut inland from Benevento through the hills of Irpinia and across the Apulian plain. This section, from Beneventum toward the old stop of Aequum Tuticum near modern Ariano Irpino, crosses a country of rolling grain fields, hill villages and wind turbines turning on the ridges.

Traces survive if you look. Near Buonalbergo a Roman bridge known locally as the Ponte delle Chianche still spans a stream, built from big carefully fitted blocks, and in places the line of the old road can be followed by field tracks. The modern road, the SS90 and its neighbours, follows the same logic as the Romans, taking the easiest line over the watershed, so the ride rolls through long open climbs and descents, with few tight corners and big skies. The surface is variable, and the provincial roads have patches, potholes after winter and the occasional herd of sheep.

This is a quiet, authentic corner of southern Italy, less visited than the coast. Villages like Buonalbergo and Sant'Arcangelo Trimonte are small, with a bar, a bakery and a church, and fuel is scarce, so tank up in Benevento, which has everything. Eat what the farms make: hard cheeses, cured pork, thick bread and strong red wine from Aglianico grapes, which the region is known for. Summers are hot and dry, with the wheat gone gold by June, and winters can be cold and windy, because these hills are exposed to the Apennine weather.

It helps to think of the whole road as a conversation with the past. Benevento's arch of Trajan, dated to the 110s, stood at the start of the route, and Brindisi had the other end, so every legionary, trader and pilgrim passed through this landscape. At a gentle pace, with a stop for a coffee in one of the villages, it is a day that makes more sense than any museum label.
t.grcko groblje@43.3,19.6:
Pljevlja lies in a high basin in the north of Montenegro, an hour or so from the great canyon of the Tara and the peaks of Durmitor, and it is a town that people rarely visit on purpose. It has a coal mine and a power station, and in winter smoke can hang in the valley. But the old centre has two buildings that deserve a stop, the Husein-pasha mosque, a sixteenth-century Ottoman building with a tall slender minaret and painted interior, and the Holy Trinity monastery, with its fine iconostasis, carved by local craftsmen in the nineteenth century. The mix of mosque and church a few minutes apart says a lot about this part of the Balkans.

Grčko groblje, the name of this stop, means Greek cemetery in Serbian and Montenegrin, though the name is a folk one that did not need to mean Greek. In the Balkans such names are used for old burial grounds of unknown origin, and in this region they are often medieval necropolises with stećci, the large carved limestone tombstones of the Middle Ages, which UNESCO listed in 2016 across Bosnia, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia. They are slabs and chests, sometimes decorated with figures of horsemen, crescents and spirals, standing in grass among sheep, and there is a quiet melancholy about them. I cannot describe this particular site, so ask locally for the way and treat any graveyard with respect.

Pljevlja, with about nineteen thousand people, has fuel, a market and a few cafes, and Sokolovo Brdo is a tiny hamlet nearby with little more. Fill up in town, particularly before heading into the mountains, where stations are rare. The riding is excellent on the high roads, with long bends over open grassland and pine forest, wide skies and light traffic, though surfaces can be broken, with frost heave and potholes after winter.

The northern Montenegrin highlands are cold, with snow from November to April, and mist sits in the valleys. Late spring and September are the best seasons, when the meadows are green, the sky is clear and the air smells of hay. Try a plate of kačamak, the local cornmeal and cheese dish, and kajmak, a thick cream, with fresh bread, in one of the roadside restaurants, and expect warm hospitality and strong coffee.
t.mramor in vrbica@43.4,18.9:
The Drina is a river that runs through every story in this part of the Balkans, and Foča sits on one of its finest stretches. The town, with about fourteen thousand people, lies where the Drina meets the Ćehotina, among steep green mountains, and the old Aladža mosque, a painted sixteenth-century building, was one of the most beautiful Ottoman monuments in the region before it was destroyed in the war of the 1990s and then rebuilt. Foča carries that history quietly, and it is a place where you should listen more than talk.

Mramor, in the village of Vrbica, is a medieval necropolis of stećci, the massive carved limestone gravestones that stand in fields all over Bosnia and the neighbouring countries. They date from the twelfth to the sixteenth centuries, are cut as slabs, chests and gabled forms, and sometimes carry carved scenes of hunting, dancing and swords. The UNESCO listing of 2016 includes this site. They were long attributed to the Bogomils, a heretical medieval sect, but that is mostly legend, and most scholars link them to ordinary Christian communities. Stand among them in the grass and the sound is only wind and the odd cowbell.

The riding in this region is superb. The road from Foča toward Montenegro follows the Drina, then the Sutjeska river, through deep gorges and forested valleys into the Sutjeska National Park, which holds Maglić, the highest mountain in Bosnia, and one of the last primeval forests in Europe at Perućica. Bends are long and flowing, with tunnels and narrow sections, and the surface is mixed, from smooth to rough, so keep your speed within sight. Traffic is light, but lorries and local cars take the middle of the road on blind corners.

The other ride in the title heads to Višegrad, where the famous Mehmed Paša Sokolović Bridge crosses the Drina in eleven stone arches, built in the sixteenth century and made famous by Ivo Andrić's novel The Bridge on the Drina. Čajniče, a small town nearby, is quiet and rural. Fuel is available in Foča, but stations are sparse in the mountains, so plan ahead. Late spring and early autumn are best, and roads can be icy and closed by snow in winter.
t.paklenica national park@44.3,15.5:
Paklenica is a place where the Velebit mountains drop in a wall to the Adriatic. The national park, created in 1949, protects two gorges, Mala and Velika Paklenica, which cut into the limestone like a pair of knife wounds, with vertical walls up to four hundred metres high. The big wall of Anića Kuk is a famous climbing area, and on a clear day you can watch climbers as small as ants. Between the walls, the path winds through black pine and beech forest, with the sound of a stream and the smell of resin. Griffon vultures nest on the cliffs and often circle overhead, and the caves in the hills hold bats and old stories.

The park is a hiking place more than a riding one, so leave the bike at the entrance in Starigrad, a seaside village with about a thousand people, and walk up the gorge. The path is easy at first, with a wide track and good signs, and a stone hut about an hour in sells drinks. Ražanac, a little further south, is quiet and has beaches of pebbles.

The riding around the park is excellent. The coast road, the Jadranska magistrala, runs along the foot of the Velebit with the sea and islands on one side and bare grey slopes on the other, with long views, steady bends and sometimes strong wind, the bura, which can gust hard and make bikes lean. Behind the mountains, roads climb over passes to the plateau of Lika, toward Plitvice Lakes, with hairpins and cooler air. Fuel is sparse in the villages, so fill up in Zadar, a short ride south, before going on.

Summer is hot and busy, with crowds on the coast, so spring and autumn are better, when the light is clear and the mountains are still capped with snow. The sea is warm enough for a swim until October. After a walk, eat grilled fish or lamb from the spit in a village konoba, and drink a glass of local red wine while the sun sets behind the islands.
t.fortified city of kotor@42.4,18.8:
Kotor is a walled medieval town squeezed between a vertical limestone mountain and a deep green bay, and the whole arrangement looks almost too neat to be real. The bay is not a fjord, as people like to say, but a drowned river canyon, a ria, whose channels twist inland in several arms so that the mountains seem to close behind you as you ride around it. Black Mountain, Montenegro itself, takes its name from the dark forest on Mount Lovcen, which rises straight above the town to nearly fifteen hundred metres.

The old town has a Venetian look because Venice ruled here from 1420 until 1797, and the lion of St Mark still sits on the gate. The walls climb the hill behind it to a ruined fortress, and the climb on the steps takes a sweaty half hour but rewards you with a view over the red roofs and the bay. The Cathedral of St Tryphon dates from the twelfth century, and the town has a quirky devotion to its cats. In summer, cruise ships dock beside the walls and the narrow lanes fill with tour groups, so go in the early morning or the evening if you can.

The riding is the real treat. The old road up from Kotor to Njegusi, with its twenty-five hairpins, is one of the great motorbike climbs of the Balkans, tight and steep and decorated with views over the bay that get better with every bend. The surface can be rough in places, and in summer there is a lot of tourist traffic, including buses, so patience is needed. At the top you cross to the old royal capital of Cetinje and on toward Podgorica. Back at sea level, the coast road around the bay passes the little baroque town of Perast and the island churches in front of it.

Fuel is available in Kotor and in Dobrota just to the north, and there are plenty of cafes and fish restaurants along the bay front. Rain can be heavy in autumn and winter, since the mountains behind Kotor are among the wettest in Europe, and summer afternoons are hot and slow. Late spring and September are ideal.
t.cerro pelon@19.4,-100.3:
Every winter, something close to a miracle arrives at Cerro Pelon. Monarch butterflies, which have flown from Canada and the northern United States, a journey of some four thousand kilometres, gather in the oyamel fir forests of the high volcanic mountains on the border between Michoacan and the State of Mexico. They cluster in the millions on the trunks and branches, so thick that the boughs bend under their weight, and when the sun hits them they leave the trees in a swirl of orange that sounds like rain. The sanctuaries here are part of the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve.

The butterflies are only present from about November to March, and the best displays come on warm, sunny days in January and February, when the colony wakes up and flies down to drink. Cerro Pelon is one of the quieter sanctuaries, reached by a long and fairly strenuous walk or a horse ride on a steep forest trail, at an altitude of about three thousand metres. The air is thin, cool and smells of fir resin, and it is very quiet if you keep your voice down. Local guides from the nearby communities run the visits, and it matters to go with them, as the forest is also their livelihood, saved from loggers by the butterflies.

The ride up is the other half of the experience. The roads on the approach are mountain roads with tight bends, patchy surfaces and a good deal of loose gravel, and the last stretch is often unpaved. The villages are small, with a few shops and little fuel, so fill the tank in a bigger town such as Zitacuaro before you leave. Rain and mist can arrive quickly, and winter mornings are cold enough to need a proper jacket.

Respect the rules at the sanctuary. You must not touch the butterflies or shout, and flash photography is not welcome. In return, you will get one of the great natural spectacles of the continent, and a very good plate of quesadillas at a roadside stall on the way home.
t.erik anders@61.3,17.0:
The farms of Hälsingland are one of the odder success stories of Swedish history. In the nineteenth century, farmers in this part of the country grew rich on flax and linen, and they spent their wealth not on grand manor houses but on enormous wooden farmhouses with elaborate painted interiors. Rooms were reserved for celebrations, and decorated with biblical scenes, flowers and ornamental borders by travelling artists. Seven of these farms are on the UNESCO list, among them the Erik-Anders farm, near Söderhamn, whose neat red buildings stand in a clearing among fields and forest.

What you see from outside is a cluster of wooden buildings painted in the familiar falu red, in a design that was shared by many farms in the region: a large main house, barns, a bake-house, and often a separate guest hall for festivals. Inside, the best rooms are astonishingly bright, with every surface painted in blue, ochre and rose. Many of the farms can be visited in summer on a guided tour, with opening hours that change from year to year, so it is worth checking before you go. The local style of life was frugal in daily habit and extravagant on feast days, which is one of the more appealing contradictions of the north.

The riding in Hälsingland is quietly lovely. Roads wind through spruce and pine forest, past small lakes, along river valleys, and across open farmland with hay racks in the fields. The surfaces are generally smooth and the corners long and open, with very little traffic away from the E4. Be careful at dawn and dusk, because elk are a real hazard, and do not be tempted to speed on straight stretches. Summer evenings are long and gentle, and autumn brings gold birch against dark spruce.

Söderhamn, on the Baltic coast, is a town of around twelve thousand with fuel, supermarkets and cafes. Bring food for a picnic, though, since the farms are in quiet country, and a thermos of coffee and a cinnamon bun will serve you well. Midsummer is the best time to see the region at its greenest, but September, with fewer mosquitoes, is a close second.
t.quartiere aja piccola@40.8,17.2:
Alberobello is famous for its trulli, the little whitewashed stone houses with grey conical roofs that look as if they belong in a children's book. They stand in thousands across the Itria valley in Puglia, but in the town of Alberobello they come in two dense clusters on opposite hillsides, and the quarter called Aia Piccola is the quieter of the two. It holds around four hundred trulli, climbing a gentle slope, and unlike its showier neighbour across the valley, it is still mostly residential, with washing on lines, geraniums in pots and the occasional shop selling local cheese and wine. UNESCO listed the town in 1996.

The trulli are built entirely of dry stone, without mortar, and the cone is a corbelled vault of flat limestone slabs laid in overlapping rings. The method is ancient, but the buildings in Alberobello mostly date from the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries. A popular story holds that they were built so that they could be quickly dismantled, to fool the tax collectors of the Kingdom of Naples, and whether or not it is true, it is a good story and the guides tell it with relish. Painted symbols on the roofs, some Christian and some older, add to the sense of mystery.

The countryside is the real reward for a rider. The roads of the Itria valley are quiet and gently curving, running between dry stone walls, olive groves, almond trees and vineyards, with whitewashed villages on the hilltops. Locorotondo, a circular town on a ridge, is a short ride away, and its white lanes and views over the valley are lovely. Martina Franca, with its baroque centre, is a bit further. The surfaces are generally good, though some minor roads are patchy and farm vehicles are slow. Midday in summer can be intensely hot, so ride in the morning or evening.

Alberobello has fuel, supermarkets and many restaurants, and in the evenings the old quarter fills with visitors. Eat orecchiette with turnip tops, burrata and the local primitivo wine, and visit a trullo cellar if one is open. Spring, when the fields are full of red poppies, and autumn are the best seasons, and in winter the town is almost empty.
t.plitvice lakes national park@44.9,15.6:
Plitvice is sixteen lakes arranged in a staircase, linked by waterfalls and bordered by beech and fir forest, all coloured an unreal turquoise by the minerals in the water. The lakes form because the water is rich in calcium carbonate, which settles out as travertine, or tufa, on moss and plants, building natural dams that grow slowly over the centuries. It is a living process, which is why the park is protected, and why visitors have to keep to the wooden walkways that wind across the water. UNESCO listed it in 1979, and it is today Croatia's most visited natural site.

The park has a darker history too. In March 1991, a clash at Plitvice between Croatian police and Serb forces is often counted as one of the first incidents of the Croatian War of Independence, and the area was occupied for several years. The old hotels were damaged, and it took time to recover. Nowadays the park is peaceful again, with busy visitor centres, electric boats on the big lake and a small train. Bears, wolves and lynx live in the forests around, though the visitors will mostly see ducks, fish and butterflies. The film series of Winnetou, based on German western novels, was partly shot here in the 1960s.

For riders, the lakes are on the main road between Zagreb and the Dalmatian coast, which makes them a classic stopping place. The roads around are good, with moderate curves through forested hills, and the nearby Lika plateau offers open, empty country with long views and sudden changes in weather. On busy summer days, the car parks and entrances fill early, so arrive at opening time or late in the afternoon. In winter, the lakes freeze and the waterfalls turn to ice, and the park is quiet and beautiful, though some paths close.

The label places the nearest settlement on the Bosnian side, but most visitors approach from Croatia, where Korenica, a small town near the park, has fuel and food. Roadside stalls sell roast lamb and suckling pig, and a plate of cheese and cured ham goes well with a coffee. Bring a rain jacket, because the weather can change quickly, and wear shoes with a good grip for the damp boards.
t.the sanctuary of san michele@41.7,16.0:
Few pilgrimage sites in Europe sit as dramatically as this one, high on the spur of the Gargano peninsula, the spur on Italy's boot. Monte Sant'Angelo is a white town draped along a ridge about eight hundred metres above the sea, and the sanctuary of San Michele is built into a natural cave below the main street. Tradition holds that the Archangel Michael appeared to the local bishop here at the end of the fifth century, and the cave has drawn pilgrims ever since: Lombards who made it their national shrine, Norman knights, crusaders on their way to the Holy Land, and the faithful of every age. You enter down a long flight of steps, eighty-six of them by the usual count, and the air cools as you descend. Inside, the rock itself is part of the church, damp and bare, with a statue of the archangel and centuries of carved and painted additions around it. It was inscribed as part of the Longobards in Italy World Heritage listing in 2011.

Getting there is half the fun. From Mattinata on the coast the road climbs in a long series of bends and hairpins through olive groves and then bare limestone, with the Adriatic spreading blue and wide behind you. From the inland side you cross the Gargano National Park, a high limestone plateau where the Foresta Umbra, the Shady Forest, shelters beech and old pine and cools the air even in August. Roads here are narrow and the surface is variable, so expect patches of broken asphalt and the occasional goat. Early spring and autumn suit it best, and a clear evening on the terraces gives you enormous light over the plain of Puglia.

The town itself is steep and narrow, the old quarter of white stone, with a mix of tight alleys and a few pretty courtyards. It has about twelve thousand people, so fuel, food and a bed are all available. Expect the local specialities of the Gargano, such as orange and lemon from the coast, strong cheeses, and the oval wafers of local bakers. Ask about the Tomb of Rotari, a small Romanesque baptistery beside the sanctuary, which many visitors miss.

Park at the top of town and walk the last stretch. Lugging a helmet down eighty-six steps is no hardship, and the cave is worth the knees.
t.trullo sovrano@40.8,17.2:
Apulia is full of oddities, but nothing in it looks as unlikely as a trullo. These are round or square dry-stone houses topped with conical roofs of grey limestone slabs, laid without any mortar, and the town of Alberobello has well over a thousand of them. The Trullo Sovrano, the Sovereign Trullo, is the biggest and the grandest, a two-storey building on a hillside square at the edge of the old quarter, and it was built in the eighteenth century for a wealthy family. Inside, it houses a small museum of everyday life, rooms divided by curtains and arches, and a dome that rises overhead like an upturned bowl.

The method is ancient and simple. Farmers cleared the stony fields of the Itria valley and used the stones to build walls and shelters. A trullo could be taken apart quickly, and the old story says that was the point, because the local lords used it to dodge taxes on permanent buildings. Whether that is entirely true or not, the town today has two zones of them, the Rione Monti on a hillside and the quieter Aia Piccola, and it is inscribed as a World Heritage site. Painted symbols on the roofs, in white, are believed to be good-luck marks.

Riding around Alberobello is quite gentle. The Itria valley is a landscape of low rolling hills, dry-stone walls, olive groves, almond trees, and small farmhouses, with the roads running straight and then curling softly between fields. It is not a mountain road, but it has charm, and the traffic is light except in summer weekends. Go in May or late September, when the light is good and the crowds are manageable, and avoid midday heat in August.

Locorotondo and Martina Franca lie nearby, the first a circular white town and the second a baroque one, and both make good lunch stops. With nine thousand people, Alberobello has fuel and plenty of places to eat; try orecchiette with turnip tops, burrata or a glass of the local white from Locorotondo. Visit the lanes early in the morning, before the coaches, and you will have the stones almost to yourself.
t.casa d amore@40.8,17.2:
Behind the souvenir shops of Alberobello lies a story about taxes and kings that locals like to tell, and the Casa d'Amore is a handy place to start telling it. The house is one of the older buildings in the Rione Monti, the hillside quarter of conical trullo roofs, and it dates to the closing years of the eighteenth century. It is known as the first of the trulli to be built with mortar, and its interior now serves as a small exhibition with traditional furnishings and, as in many such houses, a tiny shop selling local crafts and wine.

The history behind these houses is a good one. The land here belonged to the counts of Conversano, who ruled their territory like a private kingdom. The tale says that when the Kingdom of Naples demanded a tax on every new settlement, the count ordered his tenants to build without mortar, so that a trullo could be pulled down whenever inspectors came and rebuilt after they left. The truth is probably more mixed, since stone shelters were simply the cheapest answer to a stony land. Either way, in 1797 the town got a royal charter from Ferdinand IV and the lords lost their hold, and after that the builders could use mortar and make houses of a more settled sort.

The roads around Alberobello are the right sort for a slow afternoon. From the Murge plateau, the land falls gently into the Itria valley, with red soil, walls of grey stone and ancient olive trees whose trunks twist like wrung cloth. You can wander along narrow farm roads, past dry-stone huts and small vineyards, with almost no traffic apart from tractors. Spring brings poppies and wild flowers, and the harvest in autumn smells of crushed grapes and smoke. Avoid the heat of July and August afternoons, when the stone reflects the sun and the town fills with coach parties.

Alberobello has about nine thousand people, so fuel, a bank machine and a decent lunch are easy to find. Locorotondo, a little north-east, has the better view and the better wine, and Martina Franca has the baroque squares and the local capocollo.
