If the souvenir shops drain your energy, step into a side alley and look up: the roof stones, the painted symbols and the chimneys make the place work again.
t.piazza del mercato@40.8,17.2:
Every Puglian town has its square where the day's business happens, and in Alberobello the market has long been part of the modern town, the one that grew up on the flat ground below the trulli hillside. Travellers tend to rush straight to the Rione Monti and its sea of grey cones, then rush back out again, which is a pity, because the lower town gives the clearest sense of how people really live here. Old men sit on benches, women carry shopping bags from the stalls, and the bakeries open early for the focaccia and the taralli, the ring-shaped crackers that are a Pugliese staple.

The market days bring the farm country into town. Peasant produce from the Itria valley fills the stalls, including olives and olive oil, almonds, figs, tomatoes, courgettes, cheese, and the wild greens that appear in so much local cooking. Cime di rapa, turnip tops, are cooked with orecchiette, the small ear-shaped pasta that grandmothers still shape with a thumb in some back streets. If you see a cheese called burrata, a soft mozzarella shell filled with cream, it comes from this part of Apulia and tastes best the day it is made.

Riding in the surrounding countryside is relaxed, with lots of small roads between white towns. The landscape is high-lying limestone, rolling and broken by dry-stone walls, and the surface is usually decent but can be patchy on minor roads, with sand and gravel at the edges. The most pleasant hours are the early morning and the last two hours of daylight, when the sun turns the stone a warm honey colour. Midsummer middays are very hot, and shade is scarce.

Locorotondo is a short ride away, a perfectly round white town above a valley of vineyards, and from the terrace below its main church you can see for miles. The coast at Monopoli and Polignano a Mare is less than an hour's ride to the east, with fish restaurants and old harbours. Bari, to the north, is the regional capital, with a busy port, the basilica of San Nicola and fresh orecchiette being made on doorsteps in the old town.

With over nine thousand people, Alberobello has petrol, food and cash machines without trouble. Come here for the ordinary rhythm of a southern town rather than a postcard, and buy something to eat from a stall.
t.jon lars@61.4,16.1:
Farms in Hälsingland look like farms, until you open the door. Jon-Lars, near Alfta in the forested heart of the province, is one of the seven farmsteads inscribed in 2012 as the Decorated Farmhouses of Hälsingland, and from the road it seems a tidy group of dark red timber buildings around a yard. Inside, the festive rooms are covered with painted decoration, with flowers, curtains, biblical scenes and trompe-l'oeil swags painted in the nineteenth century, when the farmers were rich.

The wealth came from flax. In the early and middle 1800s, Hälsingland farmers grew flax, spun and wove it, and sold linen across Sweden, and some of them did extremely well. Rather than build grand manor houses, they put their money into an extra, decorated wing used only for weddings, christenings and other parties, often a little show-off in its taste, with paintwork that was done by travelling artists and carried on in local traditions. That is the key to the Hälsingland house: the plain exterior and the lavish interior, shown off only on special days. The industry collapsed when cotton and later synthetic fibres took over, and the farms were preserved almost by accident.

You ride here through proper northern Swedish country. Forests of spruce and pine close in on both sides of the road, interrupted by lakes, fields and the Voxnan river, and the villages are spread out. The roads are quiet and generally in good shape, with long easy curves, a fair amount of up and down, and plenty of places to pull over. Elk are a real hazard, especially at dawn and dusk, and a collision with one is serious, so keep your speed down in the woods. Speed cameras are common on the main roads, and the limits are firmly observed. Summer is the best time, with long light evenings, and the autumn colours are good in September.

Alfta is a small town, with a couple of thousand people and basic services, and Edsbyn, about twelve kilometres away, is bigger and has the wider choice of fuel and food. Edsbyn is also known as a stronghold of bandy, the Swedish ice hockey on a football-sized pitch, and winter evenings there draw crowds. Swedish cafes serve coffee with a cinnamon bun, and in summer the local farm shops offer berries, cheese and smoked fish.
t.hajducki i rozanski kukovi@44.8,15.0:
The Hajdučki and Rožanski Kukovi are a field of limestone towers in the northern Velebit, a landscape of pale spires, pinnacles and karst pavements that look like a city abandoned by giants. They sit in the Northern Velebit National Park, a long mountain range that parallels the Adriatic coast and shelters the Croatian interior from the sea. The sea is close, and the contrast is part of the appeal: bare white stone and wind above, blue water far below.

You will not ride all the way in. Access is on foot from the road, and the road itself is a long way from anywhere. The nearest places in the data are on the coast and the island of Rab, but the practical bases are Senj, a historic port town of around 5,500 people, and Gospić inland. Senj is also where the Velebit meets the sea, and the main coastal road, the Magistrala, is a famous ride in its own right, with the Adriatic on one side and the Velebit on the other.

Be honest about the surface and the weather. Roads that climb into the range from the coast are steep and narrow, with a lot of hairpins, and some of the upland tracks are unsealed and closed in winter. The bura, a cold, gusty wind that comes down from the mountains onto the Adriatic, can be violent enough to close the coastal road to motorcycles. Check the forecast. In summer the mountains offer relief from the heat, and the best months for the upland roads are generally late spring through early autumn.

The Velebit is a place of rare plants and wildlife. Its limestone supports endemic species, among them the Velebit degenia, a yellow-flowered cabbage relative found nowhere else, and the forests hold bears and lynx, though you are unlikely to see either. In the old days the region was a frontier between Venetian and Ottoman influence, and the hajduks of the name were outlaw bands who lived in these hills and took on the authorities of the day. Carry water and a layer, fill up before leaving the coast, and keep an eye on the sky.
t.maculje@44.1,17.7:
Central Bosnia is a country of green hills folded one behind another, and Maculje sits in the middle of it, a few kilometres from Novi Travnik in the Lašva valley. If you have not heard of it, you are in good company, because what draws people here is quiet and very old. Maculje is a necropolis of stećci, the massive carved limestone tombstones that medieval Bosnians, Croatians and Serbs raised between roughly the twelfth and the sixteenth centuries. They stand in the grass in rows, slabs shaped like chests and gabled roofs, with weathered carvings of crescent moons, spirals, hunters and dancers.

Nobody can say with full confidence what every motif meant, and that is part of the charm. The people who made them belonged to the medieval Bosnian realm, and the stones were left to the weather and the sheep for centuries, which is partly why so many survive. Several necropolises across the region are now on the UNESCO World Heritage list as a group. Standing in a field with the stones around you and a church bell somewhere in the valley below is a good way to feel how deep the history goes here.

The riding on the way is the real bonus. Coming from Banja Luka, the day takes you through the Vrbas gorge country and over the pass toward Gornji Vakuf, on roads that curl through beech woods and small farming villages, with the surface varying from smooth tarmac to patched and potholed stretches. Take it easy on blind bends, as tractors, livestock and the odd overtaking truck are part of the scene. Spring and early autumn give the best colour, and the afternoon light on the slopes is gentle.

Novi Travnik, with about 10,000 people just 13 km off, is the sensible place for fuel, a meal and a bed, and Gornji Vakuf is another option on the same road. Bosnian coffee, served in a small copper pot with a lump of sugar and a glass of water, is the right way to pause, and a plate of ćevapi in a bread pocket with raw onion is the unavoidable lunch. Carry some cash in convertible marks, as card acceptance in small places is not guaranteed, and keep an eye on local advice about off-road tracks, since parts of Bosnia still have unmarked mine areas away from main routes. Stick to paved or clearly used roads and you will have no trouble.
t.pavari sfilzi@41.8,16.0:
The Gargano is the spur of the Italian boot, a limestone mass pushing out into the Adriatic, and if you ask a rider to name Italy's best coast road, someone will name the one here. Pavari and Sfilzi are names I cannot pin to a particular monument, so I will tell you instead about the country around them, which lies between Vico del Gargano and Peschici on the northern side of the promontory. Vico, with seven thousand people, is a white town of narrow lanes on a ridge, surrounded by orange and lemon groves, with an old quarter that has a famous narrow alley, the Strada del Bacio. Peschici, three and a half thousand strong, clings to a cliff above the sea, with white houses and a castle.

The coast has its own character. Fishing platforms called trabucchi, large wooden structures with long arms and nets, stand on rocky points, and some are now restaurants where you can eat very fresh fish. The sea is clear and green, and the cliffs fall straight into it. Inland the Foresta Umbra, a huge forest of beech, oak and pine, covers the high ground, with deer, wild cats and a number of rare orchids.

The riding is superb. The coast road between Peschici and Vieste has a long series of bends above the sea, with views that change round every corner. The surface is mostly good, but the road is narrow, and in summer it is busy with cars and campers. Early morning is best, and October offers warm days without the crowds. Inland, the road across the forest is cooler, shaded and quieter. Watch for gravel, and for tractors on the minor roads.

Vico del Gargano is the place to expect fuel and a proper meal, and Peschici should have a pump too. The local pasta, orecchiette with turnip tops, and a plate of grilled sardines are excellent.

The ride goes on to Castel del Monte, the strange octagonal castle that the emperor Frederick II built on a hill in Apulia in the thirteenth century, with eight towers and a mystery of purpose that has never been settled.
t.falascone@41.8,16.0:
The Gargano is the spur on the heel of Italy's boot, a block of limestone pushed out into the Adriatic, and in its heart lies the Foresta Umbra, the shady forest. Falascone is a locality in that high country, and I cannot offer a monument to go with the name, only the landscape, which deserves more attention than it gets. The forest holds ancient beech, along with oak, hornbeam, maple and yew, and parts of it are protected as primeval beech forest in the UNESCO listing that links the beechwoods of the Carpathians and Europe. The canopy is so dense that even in July the air under the trees is cool, and the ground is carpeted with ferns and cyclamen.

There is wildlife here. Roe deer slip between the trunks at dawn, and there are wild boar, wildcats and a lot of birds, including woodpeckers and, if you are lucky, the rare white-backed woodpecker. In spring, orchids bloom in the clearings, dozens of species of them. Beyond the forest the Gargano plunges to a coast of white cliffs, sea caves and pine-backed beaches, but the interior is a quieter, older world.

The roads over the Gargano are some of the most enjoyable in southern Italy. They wind through the beechwoods in long, shaded curves, with a surface that is good in places and patched in others, and a few steep sections where you will be in second gear. Traffic is light outside August, when the coast crowds up. In summer the forest is a refuge from the heat of the plain. Mist can sit in the trees in autumn, and winter brings occasional snow, which can close the higher roads.

Vico del Gargano, about ten kilometres away, has seven thousand people and fuel, with a beautiful old quarter of whitewashed alleys and a famous narrow street, Via Mancini, nicknamed the Kiss Street, while Carpino is smaller. Carpino is known for its folk music festival. Stock up on fuel before you climb, since the forest has few stations, and bring a picnic. Local specialities include caciocavallo cheese, orecchiette with turnip tops, and the bitter oranges and lemons that grow on the coastal slopes.
t.grcko groblje@43.1,19.1:
High in the mountains of northern Montenegro, in meadows below the peaks of Durmitor, stand some of the strangest gravestones in Europe. Grcko groblje, the Greek cemetery, is a field of stecci, huge carved limestone blocks that medieval communities across Bosnia, Herzegovina, Montenegro and Serbia raised over their dead between roughly the twelfth and sixteenth centuries. Some are shaped like coffins, some like gabled roofs, some are slabs. They carry carvings of crescents and suns, spirals, vines, hunting scenes, warriors on horseback and rows of people dancing hand in hand in the old kolo. This site is one of several in the region that were listed together by UNESCO in 2016.

The name Greek cemetery is a local folk label, a way of saying it belongs to people from before, whoever they were. Historians connect the stecci to the Vlach herding communities and the Bosnian Church, a medieval Christian tradition that outsiders found baffling. Whatever their makers believed, they left an extraordinary open-air gallery.

Setting is part of the pleasure. Durmitor is a national park and World Heritage site in its own right, a high limestone massif of sharp peaks, glacial lakes and canyons. The nearest settlement, Zabljak, sits at around 1,450 metres and calls itself the highest town in the Balkans, with enough fuel and food for the area and a lively climbing and skiing trade. The roads here are some of the best riding in the Balkans, among them the road over the Sedlo pass with its high-mountain views, the descent toward the Piva canyon and the bridge over the Tara gorge at Durdevica, built in 1940 and one of the great sights of the region.

Weather is changeable and cold at altitude. Snow lies late and can return early, so the riding season really runs from June to September; even then, take a warm layer. Roads can be rough at the edges, with sheep and cattle wandering onto the tarmac.

For food, ask for kacamak, a heavy cornmeal and cheese dish, and for the local smoked ham and cheese. A stop at one of the guesthouses in Zabljak is the best way to end the day.
t.kristofers@61.7,16.2:
In Hälsingland, the farmers got rich on flax, and then they spent the money on wallpaper. From the late eighteenth century through the nineteenth, prosperous families in the forested valleys of this part of central Sweden built huge timber farmhouses, each with a festive room reserved for weddings, funerals and holidays, and decorated it with painted murals, stencilled borders and trompe-l'oeil panels in extravagant colours. They are still standing, red-painted outside, ornate inside, and seven of them were listed by UNESCO in 2012 as the decorated farmhouses of Hälsingland. I cannot say whether the one labelled here is among those seven or one of the many others, but it belongs to the same tradition.

The setting is the Ljusnan valley, a broad, gentle landscape of rivers, meadows and spruce forest, with the little town of Järvsö at its heart. Järvsö is a resort with a ski hill and a zoo, with enough shops and fuel for the area, and Ljusdal, a little further north, is the bigger centre. The roads between are quiet and good, with smooth, undulating bends along the water and through the forest, with farms set in clearings and fields cut by old stone walls.

Riding here is a gentle pleasure in Swedish style: low traffic, long views, polite drivers and strict speed limits with cameras in the places you least expect. Watch for elk at dusk and in the early morning, especially in autumn, as an elk collision is a serious matter. Midsummer is bright and nearly endless, and the locals celebrate it around a maypole with herring, new potatoes and strawberries.

Some of the farms are open to visitors in summer, though many are private homes, so be respectful, and look at what you can see from the road. The painted rooms are not usually visible from outside, so a guided visit is the way to appreciate them. Local food includes fermented herring in some parts of the region, and crispbread and cheese everywhere.

The best months for riding are June to September. Autumn colours in the forest are splendid, though days are short, and winter is a landscape for snowmobiles and skis. Pull over by a red barn and listen, because Hälsingland's quiet is its main attraction.
t.the historic center of berat@40.7,19.9:
Berat is called the town of a thousand windows, and one look across the Osum river explains why. The Ottoman-era houses of the Mangalem quarter stack up the slope in white tiers, their upper floors set back so that each window seems to look over the next roof. On the opposite bank the Gorica quarter faces them, linked by a graceful stone bridge, and above them both the castle walls crown a rock, with the long, bare ridge of Mount Tomorr beyond.

What makes Berat special is that the castle is still a living neighbourhood, with families, small churches and narrow lanes inside the walls, rather than an empty ruin. The churches are Byzantine in origin, with a number of them decorated with frescoes. The Onufri Museum, in the former cathedral, is named after a sixteenth-century painter who developed a famous vivid red for his icons. Muslims, Orthodox Christians and, until the twentieth century, a Jewish community lived side by side in the town, and this religious mix helped make it a symbol of coexistence. UNESCO listed the historic centre in 2008.

The ride from Tirana or the coast crosses the flat plain of central Albania, then ascends through low hills with olive groves and vineyards. Roads are mostly good now, but expect trucks, horse carts and the occasional stray dog. Evenings are the best time to see the town, when lights come on in the windows and the river gleams. Summer is hot and dry, and spring and autumn are pleasant, with mist in the mornings. A nearby mountain road leads toward Tomorr, which is a sacred peak for Albanians, with a pilgrimage in August.

Berat is a proper town with fuel stations, restaurants, banks and a good range of guesthouses, and Ura Vajgurore is nearby. Park the bike near the river and walk, because the old streets are cobbled and steep. Try local wine, which has been produced here for centuries, along with raki, and a plate of lamb baked in a clay pot. Leave time to climb to the castle at sunset.
t.mostar@43.3,17.8:
The bridge defines Mostar, and the bridge was rebuilt. The Stari Most, the Old Bridge, was designed by the Ottoman architect Hayreddin and finished in 1566, a single high arch of pale stone crossing the green Neretva. The town takes its name from the bridge keepers, the mostari, who watched it. For more than four centuries it stood, until in November 1993, during the Bosnian war, it was destroyed by shelling and fell into the river. A faithful reconstruction opened in 2004, using local stone and traditional methods, and the old town around it is now listed by UNESCO.

Today, the cobbled lanes of Kujundžiluk lead from the bridge past coppersmiths and café tables, and young men from the local diving club leap from the span into the cold river below, collecting tips before they do. It is a spectacle, and a slightly nerve-racking one, and it is easy to feel more than a tourist here. Walls and apartment blocks outside the centre still carry bullet scars, and the city's division between Bosniak and Croat communities remains visible. Be curious and kind, and ask questions rather than assuming.

The route north to Sarajevo is among the great rides of the Balkans. The road follows the Neretva upstream through a deep canyon, past the turquoise reservoir at Jablanica and into the mountains, where tunnels, bridges and long bends carry you toward the Bosnian highlands. At Jablanica a ruined railway bridge recalls the Battle of the Neretva in 1943, a famous episode of the Second World War in Yugoslavia. The surface is generally good but patched, and trucks slow the way in places, so take care before overtaking. Summer afternoons are hot, and thunderstorms can roll through the canyon.

Mostar has fuel, repair shops and a long list of grill restaurants. Ćevapi in soft bread, burek and strong Bosnian coffee, served in a copper pot with sugar cubes, are the local fare. Hot weather is the rule from June to August, and spring and autumn are more comfortable. Park the bike outside the old town, and leave time to walk across the bridge twice.
t.budva@42.3,18.8:
Budva is one of the oldest towns on the Adriatic, and it carries the claim lightly, between nightclubs. The walled old town sits on a small rocky peninsula, a tight cluster of stone houses, churches and narrow lanes protected by a ring of Venetian walls, and tradition suggests that a settlement has stood here for about two and a half thousand years. In 1979 a strong earthquake damaged much of it, and the rebuilt streets have a slightly too-neat look. The citadel on the seaward side, with its small museum, gives a view along the coast.

Around the old town, modern Budva has grown into the main resort of Montenegro, with a long strip of beaches, hotels, bars and restaurants known as the Budva Riviera. Some of the beaches, such as Mogren, are small coves reached by a short path from the old town, and the water is clear and warm in summer. A short drive south, the former fishing village of Sveti Stefan, built on a tiny island linked to the mainland by a causeway, is one of the most photographed sights on the coast. Behind the shore, steep mountains rise toward the highlands of the Lovćen national park.

The road along the coast is a classic. From Budva you can head north through the Sozina tunnel or along the coast toward Kotor, with sections that climb above the sea and give views over the bay and islands, with sharp bends and drops. Roads inland, climbing to the old royal capital of Cetinje and the mountain of Lovćen, with its famous serpentine road of many hairpins, are steeper and more demanding. Surfaces are generally acceptable, but traffic in July and August is dense, with tourist buses, scooters and cars crowding the road, and the heat can be fierce.

Budva has fuel stations and workshops, and an enormous number of restaurants serving grilled fish, octopus salad and cheese-filled pastries. It is a late-night town in summer, so noise can be a problem in hotels near the centre. The best months for riding are May, June and September, when the sea is warm enough for a swim, the air is mild and the road is easier. Evening walks around the old town walls give the best light on the stone.
t.makarska@43.3,17.0:
Makarska sits under a wall of grey limestone, with the Biokovo mountains rising almost straight out of the sea behind the town. The highest peak, Sveti Jure, stands at about 1,762 metres, and the ridge runs for thirty kilometres along the coast, so the town and its neighbours, Tučepi and Baška Voda, are squeezed into a narrow strip between mountain and water. This is the Makarska Riviera, one of the most scenic stretches of the Dalmatian coast, and the old Adriatic Highway runs right along it, with views over the sea to the islands of Brač and Hvar.

The town is built around a horseshoe harbour, with a wide pedestrian waterfront lined with cafés and restaurants and a baroque square beside the cathedral. The Franciscan monastery on the western edge has an unusual museum of shells, collected over generations by monks, and the Biokovo Nature Park above has hairpin roads that climb to a viewpoint, on a clear day, as far as Italy. The coast has long been a crossing place between the Venetian and Ottoman worlds, and the old defence towers and walls remind you of the centuries of conflict.

The riding is superb but busy. The coast road is a ribbon of curves, with the sea on one side and limestone cliffs on the other, and the traffic in summer is heavy, with tour buses, camper vans and cars heading for the beaches. Overtaking is difficult, and speed limits are strictly enforced. The best time is early morning or late afternoon, or the shoulder seasons of May, June and September, when the sea is warm and the roads are quieter. The bora wind can blow hard and unexpectedly down the mountain slopes, so be ready for sudden gusts.

Makarska has about thirteen thousand people, so fuel, supermarkets, cash machines and plenty of places to eat are easy, and the seafood is excellent. The beaches are pebbly, so bring sandals for the water, and the sea is clear and clean, with good swimming from the rocks.

This is a place to slow down. After the long drive from Split, take a walk along the harbour, have a coffee and an ice cream, and look up at the mountains. The ride to Dubrovnik continues south along the same road, with the Pelješac peninsula appearing across the water and the Neretva delta spreading out before you.
t.zabljak@43.2,19.1:
Žabljak claims to be the highest town in the Balkans, at about 1,450 metres, and it sits on a plateau among the peaks of Durmitor, a national park and UNESCO World Heritage site in northern Montenegro. The town is small, a place of low houses and mountain lodges, and it exists mostly for hikers, skiers and the occasional motorcyclist who has made the effort to come this far. Pines and spruce close in around it, the nights are cool even in summer, and the snow comes early.

The riding here is the reason to come. The roads around Durmitor are some of the best in the country, twisting through canyons, over passes and past glacial lakes. The Black Lake, Crno Jezero, lies a short walk from the centre of town, reflecting the peaks in calm weather. The Tara River canyon, nearby, is one of the deepest in Europe, and the bridge over it at Đurđevića Tara, finished just before the Second World War, is a well-known sight. The Sedlo pass road, which climbs to the east of Durmitor, is rough in places but gives vast views over the park. The surface of some mountain roads is patchy and broken by frost, and rockfalls are possible, so keep your speed under control.

Culture here is mountain and pastoral. Shepherds still graze flocks on the high pastures in summer, and the food reflects it, with cheese, smoked ham, kajmak, a rich clotted cream, and lamb cooked slowly under a metal lid, the peka. Local brandy, rakija, is offered generously. In winter the town turns into a modest ski resort, and the roads can be closed or icy from November to April.

Fuel is an important detail. Žabljak is a small town with a petrol station, but the villages nearby are tiny and stations are scarce on the mountain roads, so fill up whenever you pass one. The nearest larger town is Pljevlja, about thirty kilometres to the north, and Plužine and Šavnik, to the south and southwest, are small places with limited services. Mobile signal fades in the canyons.

Weather changes quickly at this height, and an afternoon storm can arrive from a blue sky, so carry waterproofs even in summer. The reward is a landscape that feels truly wild, and an evening on a pine-scented terrace when the air turns crisp.
t.bari@41.1,16.9:
Bari is a working port city on the Adriatic, and a lot more rewarding than most riders expect. With nearly three hundred thousand people it is the capital of Puglia, with all the traffic that implies: loud, quick, a little chaotic, and entirely good-natured once you accept the rhythm. Use it as a place to start, to eat, to arrive. The ride proper begins when you leave town and the olive groves open up.

Bari Vecchia, the old town on its little peninsula, is the part to see. It is a maze of narrow lanes and whitewashed courtyards, where women still make orecchiette pasta by hand on tables outside their doors, and washing hangs overhead. The Basilica of San Nicola, begun in the late eleventh century, holds the relics of Saint Nicholas, brought from Myra in Turkey by Bari sailors in 1087, and it is a pilgrimage site for both Catholic and Orthodox Christians. The castle, the Norman-Swabian Castello Svevo, stands at the edge of the old town.

Riding in the city needs care. Streets are narrow, scooters weave everywhere, and cobbled lanes get slick in rain. Leave the bike in a secure car park outside the old quarter rather than inside it. Outside the centre, the coastal road north toward Trani and south toward Polignano a Mare is flat and fast, with sea views and the heat shimmering. The inland roads through the Murgia plateau are quiet, with dry-stone walls and stunning light in the late afternoon.

Fuel is plentiful, particularly along the ring road, and eating is the joy: focaccia barese with tomatoes and olives, raw seafood from the harbour, panzerotti fried to order, and a glass of Primitivo. In summer the heat is fierce in the early afternoon, so follow local habit and rest between one and four. Winter is mild but can be wet and windy. A morning on the coast and an afternoon among the olives is a very good day out.
t.rocky mountain national park trail@39.4,:
Out on the Palmer Divide, southeast of Denver, the pin lands in rolling grass-and-pine country far from the high peaks its ride name implies. This is the broad ridge that separates the South Platte drainage from the Arkansas, a plateau of ponderosa pine, scrub oak and hay meadows at roughly two thousand metres, with the Front Range a blue wall away to the west. On a clear day, Pikes Peak stands out to the south as a great pale dome.

The nearest towns are the suburban sprawl of Parker and the smaller settlements of Ponderosa Park, Franktown and Elizabeth. It is ranch country that is rapidly turning into commuter country, with new houses spreading across what were once grazing fields. Highway 83, the Parker Road to the locals, runs south along the divide toward Colorado Springs, a good road with gentle rises and sweeping views, although it fills with commuter traffic at rush hours. Franktown has an old-time feel, with a historic schoolhouse and the Castlewood Canyon State Park nearby, where a collapsed dam and red sandstone cliffs make a good short stop.

For riding, this is the quiet plains approach to the Rockies. Back roads of gravel and tarmac lace the area, with long straights and rolling hills, and the sky is huge. Weather swings quickly: thunderstorms build on summer afternoons and can drop hail without warning, and in winter the divide catches snow when Denver sees rain. Wind blows steadily from the west, sometimes hard.

Practicalities are easy, because Parker and Castle Rock have fuel, supermarkets and cafés in plenty. Treat this as the start of the day, a place to top up and warm up before the mountains. A morning leaving here with the sun low behind you and the peaks lit pink ahead is as good a start as the Front Range offers. Pronghorn and deer graze the fields at dawn, and hawks hunt from fence posts.
t.rocky mountain national park trail@39.5,:
Parker is one of the fast-growing suburbs on the south-east side of Denver, a town of many thousands of people that used to be little more than a stagecoach stop. The pin sits at its edge, close to The Pinery, a leafy neighbourhood named for the ponderosa pines that grow on this stretch of the Palmer Divide. Despite the label, nothing here is a pass; the land is gently rolling and the nearest high peaks are thirty miles west, a blue-grey line of the Front Range along the horizon.

For a rider, Parker is a launch pad. You get fuel, breakfast and a few kilometres of warm-up on suburban roads before you point yourself toward the mountains. Parker Road, E-470 and the interstates all converge here, which makes it easy to head north to Rocky Mountain National Park or west to the passes. Traffic is the one real drawback: Denver's southern suburbs jam hard at rush hour, and weekend ski traffic adds to it in winter. Leave before seven and you will be through the worst.

The surrounding country has a quiet appeal. Open space trails and parks thread through the pines, and Cherry Creek State Park lies north with a reservoir, a prairie dog town and some good birding. Dawn light on the plains here is warm and golden, and in autumn the oaks turn a dull copper. Hail is a regular threat in summer, big enough to dent cars, and storms can blow up within an hour, so keep an eye on the western sky.

If you are ending a day here, you will roll in from the west on a long, slow descent from the mountains, tired and sun-burnt, with city lights ahead. There is no shortage of places to eat, from Tex-Mex to pizza to breakfast joints with big portions. Pick a hotel near the highway if you want an early start. The altitude, around 1,800 metres, takes a day to get used to for visitors from sea level, so drink plenty of water.
t.sangha trinational@2.6,16.6:
The Sangha is the river that gives this place its name, and the forest around it is divided among three countries: the Central African Republic, Cameroon and the Republic of Congo. In 2012 UNESCO recognised the three adjoining parks, Dzanga-Ndoki, Lobéké and Nouabalé-Ndoki, as a single World Heritage site, a block of lowland rainforest that is one of the best preserved in the Congo basin. The pin falls near the junction of the borders, in thick, humid forest that rises over the water.

What brings people here is wildlife on a scale that can feel overwhelming. At Dzanga Bai, a forest clearing in the Central African Republic, dozens of forest elephants gather to dig for minerals in the mud, and a visitor on a platform can watch them for hours. Western lowland gorillas are followed by trackers who have spent years winning their trust, and chimpanzees, buffalo, bongo antelope and giant forest hogs also live here. The forest is also home to the BaAka, a people who have lived by hunting and gathering for countless generations, and who know the forest in remarkable detail.

Motorcycle travel here is for the seasoned and the well supported. The nearest village, Bayanga, lies at the end of long and rough tracks from the capital, Bangui, and the roads between the forest settlements are laterite or mud, passable in the dry season, from December to February, and often impassable in the rains. Security in the region has been unstable at times, and travellers should check official advice and local conditions before making any plans. Park access is organised through conservation groups, with guides and permits.

There are no reliable fuel supplies, so everything must be carried. Heat and humidity are constant, and insects, including tsetse flies and sweat bees, are a trial. Medical help is far away, so a good first aid kit and good insurance are vital. If you manage to get here, the reward is a forest that feels untouched, with the thunderous calls of birds at dawn and the soft padding of elephants in the dark.
t.llogara pass@40.2,19.6:
At 1,027 metres, the Llogara Pass is the high point of the Albanian Riviera road, the SH8, and it is a place where the mountain suddenly lets go of the coast. From Vlorë the road climbs through the Ceraunian range, which the ancients called the thunder mountains, through forest of black pine and fir, and then at the saddle the whole Ionian Sea opens out below, with Corfu a smudge on the horizon on a clear day. The first time is hard to forget.

The pass sits inside Llogara National Park, one of the oldest protected areas in Albania, and the forest is a surprise for anyone who thinks of the Mediterranean as dry scrub. Pines grow tall and twisted, and one in particular, bent by wind into the shape of a flag, is a local landmark. The air at the top is cool and smells of resin, and in the evening mist can drift up from the sea. Goats and sheep wander the verges, and a few restaurants near the summit serve grilled lamb and local cheese to riders and truck drivers alike.

The road itself is the main event. The northern approach is a steady climb, and then comes the descent toward Dhërmi, a series of hairpins and long sweepers hanging over the sea, with sheer drops on the outer edge and little in the way of crash barrier in places. The surface has improved greatly in recent years, though patches of broken asphalt and loose gravel remain, and rockfall after heavy rain is possible. Take it slowly, stay in your lane on blind bends, and watch for oncoming drivers who cut the corners.

History touches the pass. Julius Caesar landed his army near here in 48 BC during the civil war against Pompey, at a place the sources call Palaeste, and marched inland. A road has been used across these hills for twenty centuries.

Fuel is the practical issue. There are no pumps at the pass, and the nearest big town is Vlorë, about thirty kilometres away, with stations on the approach. The smaller coastal towns of Himarë and Orikum have a few, but fill the tank at Vlorë and carry cash in leke or euros. Come early in the morning to avoid the tourist buses, and bring a jacket, since the top can be ten degrees cooler than the beach.
t.dhermi@40.2,19.6:
Below the pass, the road drops to the sea at Dhërmi, a village that spreads down a green slope from a ridge of old stone houses to a long, pale beach. The village was historically mostly Greek-speaking and Orthodox, part of the Himara region where Greek communities have lived for centuries, and its churches, notably the one called Panagia and a monastery up the hill, have fine old frescoes. The old quarter, with its steep lanes and walled gardens, is worth a walk before the day gets hot.

The beach is the great attraction, a long arc of fine shingle and pebbles with startlingly clear, bright blue water. In July and August it is lined with bars and sunbeds, with music in the evening, and the summer crowds from Tirana and abroad can make the road and car park slow. In June or September, the place is calmer, the water still warm, and the beach has space. Wear sandals for the pebbles, and take care if swimming near the rocks, where currents can be sharp.

For a rider, Dhërmi is the reward for the descent from Llogara. The road above and below the village is an excellent mix of fast bends and short straights with the sea always on one side, olive groves and wild fig trees on the other, and a limestone wall of mountain behind. The surface is better than it once was, but traffic can be dense in summer, with tourists in hired cars who stop without warning to take photographs. Be patient, and use the early morning for the best of the road.

The coast is part of the Ceraunian range, a steep mass of limestone that plunges directly into the sea, which is why the beaches are narrow and the water deepens quickly. The olive terraces on the hillside were planted over centuries, and the village keeps a tradition of olive oil, honey and fresh seafood. Lunch on a terrace with grilled fish, a Greek-style salad and a cold local beer is the thing to do.

Himarë, a town of nearly five thousand people about ten kilometres south, has petrol stations and shops. Fill up there, and keep some small bills for parking and beach fees. Evenings are lovely, with the light turning gold over the water.
t.konjic@43.7,18.0:
Konjic sits in a bend of the Neretva, a river that arrives out of the Herzegovinian mountains the colour of jade and stays that colour all the way to the Adriatic. The town of about sixteen thousand lies halfway between Mostar and Sarajevo, with the great bulk of Prenj rising behind it, and the road that links the two cities follows the river through a canyon where the walls climb straight out of the water. It is one of the best roads in the Balkans, and its best place to stop is here.

In the middle of town the old stone bridge crosses the river in a series of elegant arches. It was built by the Ottomans in the seventeenth century, and legend says it was one of the finest in the empire. It was destroyed in 1945, at the end of the Second World War, and rebuilt in the 1950s, which gives it the look of an old thing that has been through a lot. Konjic is also known for woodcarving, an old craft that still produces furniture and ornaments, and you can find workshops in town. In the hills beside the town is a secret that was kept for decades: a huge nuclear bunker built for Yugoslav leader Tito, hidden in the mountain and finished in the 1970s, now open as a museum and an art space.

The road in from Mostar goes past Jablanica, where a lake has been formed by a dam, and where the bridge over the Neretva was the scene of a famous battle of 1943 between Tito's partisans and Axis forces. The ride is quick and smooth, with long curves, tunnels and long views over water, though trucks and lorries are common, and road works are not unusual. North of Konjic, the road climbs toward the Ivan pass and then drops to Sarajevo, a route of pine forest, hairpins and clean mountain air.

Konjic has fuel stations, cafes serving strong coffee and burek, and grill restaurants where cevapi in a flat bread with onions is the standard meal. Rafting on the Neretva is a popular activity, and in summer the river can be cold enough to be bracing. Spring floods can swell it, and in autumn the hillsides turn gold. In winter the passes can be snowy, so check conditions.
t.bihac@44.8,15.9:
Bihać sits on a bend of the Una River in the far north-west corner of Bosnia and Herzegovina, hemmed in by Croatia on three sides, and the river is the reason to come. The Una is a famously clear, turquoise-green water that tumbles over travertine steps and small waterfalls, and rafters and kayakers come from across Europe to run it. The town itself is a modest, friendly place with a pleasant promenade along the water, a handful of cafés, and a few relics of its long and complicated history.

That history is layered. In the Middle Ages Bihać was a seat of Croatian and Hungarian kings, and later it became an Ottoman frontier town. The Fethija mosque in the old town was originally a Gothic church of St Anthony, converted when the Ottomans took the city in 1592, and it still has a Gothic doorway beneath its minaret. A little tower, the Captain's Tower, stands nearby. More recently, Bihać was besieged during the Bosnian war in the early 1990s, cut off from the rest of the country for years, and the scars of that time can still be seen in the occasional shell-pocked building. Locals are warm and open, though, and a visitor with curiosity is usually welcome.

The riding in the Una valley is the real draw. Roads follow the river through steep wooded gorges and open meadows, passing small villages, old mills and some of the most beautiful water in the Balkans. The Una National Park, the largest in Bosnia, protects the upper valley and its waterfalls, including the Štrbački buk, which is a short detour from the road. Surfaces are variable, with some potholes and gravel patches, so keep the pace sensible, especially after rain or in the shade, and watch for livestock on the road.

Practical matters are simple. Bihać has more than seventy thousand people, so fuel, supermarkets and repair shops are plentiful. The currency is the convertible mark, and card payments are widely accepted in town but not in villages, so carry some cash. Check that your insurance includes Bosnia, because the green card is required.

Eat grilled trout by the river, or ćevapi with bread and raw onion, and take your time over the coffee.
t.banja luka@44.8,17.2:
Banja Luka is the largest city in the northern half of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the capital of the Republika Srpska entity, set on the Vrbas River where the mountains of central Bosnia open onto the Pannonian plain. It is a spacious, leafy place with wide boulevards, plane trees and a riverfront that is busy with walkers, anglers and café-goers, and it has long had the reputation of being one of the greenest cities in the Balkans.

The city's story is a heavy one. A Roman fort stood where the Kastel fortress now looms over the river, and the city became an important Ottoman provincial centre. In 1969 a powerful earthquake destroyed much of the old town, and it was rebuilt in a hurry in modernist style. The Ferhadija mosque, a sixteenth-century masterpiece of Ottoman architecture, was blown up in 1993 during the Bosnian war, and it was painstakingly rebuilt, with original stones recovered from the rubble, and reopened in 2016. The experience of seeing a rebuilt mosque in a city that is now mostly Serbian Orthodox is a quiet lesson in the complexity of the country.

The Vrbas itself is the best reason to ride here. South of the city, the river runs through a deep, narrow canyon with limestone walls, and the road beside it climbs and winds through tunnels and past rafting stations toward Jajce, where an old walled town stands over a waterfall. The gorge ride the day is built around, through Ravanjska vrata, has steep rock and good curves, and it is best on a weekday morning when traffic is light. Surfaces are generally acceptable but patchy, with some rough patches and the occasional local driver overtaking on blind bends, so keep alert.

For practicalities, Banja Luka has over two hundred thousand people, so every service is available. Petrol stations are on all the main roads, and the city centre has plenty of cafés. Do not miss the local ćevapi, which are small grilled sausages served in a flat bread with onions and kajmak, a creamy dairy spread, and the local variant, the banjalučki ćevap, is a little different in shape.

Cross-border formalities are simple but check your documents and green card insurance before travelling.
t.engelsberg ironworks@60.0,16.0:
Central Sweden's Bergslagen district is a country of lakes, spruce forest and old iron, and the Engelsberg Ironworks stands in the middle of it, a few kilometres from Fagersta. It is one of the best-kept examples in Europe of a pre-industrial iron foundry, with its blast furnace, the forge buildings, the workers' houses and the manor all grouped around a pond where the water that once drove the machinery still flows. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 1993 as a place where the whole system of an old Swedish works, from smelting to community, can still be seen at once.

The reason works like this existed lies in the ground. Bergslagen has mined iron and copper since the Middle Ages, and Swedish iron, which was exceptionally pure, supplied half of Europe in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Furnaces needed water for power and charcoal from the surrounding forest, so they sat beside streams and rivers, with a whole village growing around each. Engelsberg became a showpiece, and the buildings that remain mostly date from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Guided tours in summer take you inside the furnace hall and explain how the process worked, which is far better than reading about it.

The ride from Stockholm is long, around two hours or more each way, mostly on good roads that cross the Mälaren lowlands before dipping into hillier forest. Once you leave the main route, the country roads wind through dark spruce, past red-painted farms and small lakes, with surfaces that are generally smooth and traffic that is light. It is gentle, rhythmic riding, rather than a dramatic run. Look out for elk at dusk, and respect speed limits, as cameras are common and Swedish police are not forgiving.

Fagersta, around thirteen kilometres away with nearly twelve thousand inhabitants, has fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and Norberg to the south has a mining museum at its old open-pit mine, which is worth a stop on the way back. Summer from June to August brings the guided tours and the warmest weather, while September has good light and the first autumn colours in the birches.
t.pikes@39.4,-104.7:
The Palmer Divide is a broad ridge that runs east from the Front Range between Denver and Colorado Springs, and the coordinates here lie on it, near The Pinery and Parker. It is easy to miss, because it looks like gently rolling ranchland, but it is a real watershed, sending creeks north toward the South Platte and south toward the Arkansas. The elevation is around 6,000 feet and above, the soil is sandy, and the ponderosa pine forest that covers part of it is called Black Forest, a name that comes from the dark colour of the trees from a distance.

This is quiet riding country, with undulating roads through open grassland, pine woods and large-lot homes with horses. The surfaces are generally good, traffic is moderate, and the views stretch to the long white line of the Rockies, with Pikes Peak rising above the rest on clear days, a good thirty miles or more to the south-west. The wind is often strong, thunderstorms build over the divide in summer, and the weather can change from warm to cold in minutes, so layers are useful.

Local history has a certain rough charm. Ranchers settled the divide in the late nineteenth century, and the old stagecoach roads and railroad grades still shape the lanes. In 2013 a wildfire burned part of the Black Forest, and the scars and the regrowth are visible in places, a reminder of how dry the ground can be. Deer, coyotes and wild turkeys are common, and the evenings can bring a sunset that colours the whole sky.

The Pinery is a community of about ten thousand people, with fuel and shops in the neighbouring towns of Parker and Castle Rock. Pikes Peak, the real destination of the ride, lies further south, and its toll highway climbs to over fourteen thousand feet. Riders usually pass through here on the way, filling up before the mountains, and a pause for coffee at a small cafe in Parker or Elizabeth is a good habit. April through October is the main season, with September especially pleasant.
t.shamrock texas@35.2,-100.2:
Shamrock, Texas, is a town named by an Irishman, and it has never been shy about the fact. A homesteader called George Nickel, so the story goes, gave it its name in 1890, and the town now holds an annual St Patrick's Day festival with a parade, a Blarney Stone and a great deal of green. It sits on the old Route 66, in the Texas Panhandle, a country of flat horizons, grain elevators, cattle and wind. The population is under two thousand, and the nearest other town of any size, Wheeler, is a good half-hour away.

The pride of Shamrock is the U-Drop Inn, a gas station and cafe built in 1936 in the Art Deco style, with a green tower and curving glass, which was a roadside landmark on Route 66 for decades. It was restored in the 2000s and now serves as a visitor centre. It is said to have been the inspiration for Ramone's House of Body Art in the animated film Cars. Beside it, the old Tower Station and its neighbours keep the period flavour, and the whole block feels like a film set that people still use.

The ride along Route 66 in this part of the country is long and straight, with slow rises and gentle bends. There is a wide sky, a lot of wind, and not much shade. Headwinds and crosswinds can be strong enough to tire you out, and summer heat in the Panhandle can pass a hundred degrees. Cattle trucks and wheat trucks share the road. Storms can build up quickly, with hail and, in spring, tornadoes, so keep an eye on the sky. West of Shamrock, McLean has the Devil's Rope Museum, devoted to barbed wire, which is a lot more entertaining than it sounds.

Fuel is available on the main roads, and the old cafe is a fine place for a chicken-fried steak and a slice of pie. Shamrock is a place to fill the tank, take a photograph of the U-Drop in the light of late afternoon, and think about the people who drove here in the Depression, looking for a better life. Drink plenty of water, and wear sunscreen.
t.million@39.3,-104.9:
Castle Rock takes its name from a flat-topped butte of rhyolite that rises above the town, with a crown of stone that looks like a battlement, and the rock has been used as a landmark since the days of the wagon road. It stands in the middle of town, with a little star lit on it at Christmas, and in a few minutes you can see why settlers reached for the word castle. The town, with about fifty-five thousand people, sits between Denver and Colorado Springs on the Interstate 25 corridor, and has grown fast from a small ranching and quarrying centre into a busy suburb.

South-west of town, the landscape becomes more interesting, with red sandstone formations around Perry Park, near the village of Larkspur. The towers and fins of rock there rise out of the pine and scrub oak in a way that reminds many visitors of the Garden of the Gods, near Colorado Springs, though they are quieter and less crowded. The little community of Perry Park has fewer than two thousand residents, and the roads around it are winding and shaded. Every summer weekend from June, Larkspur hosts a Renaissance festival that draws large crowds in costume, a part of local life that is fun to witness if you are passing by.

The label on this stop mentions the Million Dollar Highway, which is a long way south-west, but the roads in this corner of Douglas County make a good warm-up. The back roads between Castle Rock, Larkspur and Sedalia roll across ranch land and forest, with long views of the Front Range and decent surfaces. Traffic is light away from the interstate, though weekend cyclists on the narrow lanes deserve space. Hail can come with little warning in the summer, so keep an eye on the sky.

Fuel, groceries and restaurants are easy to find in Castle Rock, with the outlet mall and plenty of local cafes and bakeries along the main street. In autumn the scrub oak turns red and gold, and in winter the roads are often clear after storms but icy in the shade. April to October is the best riding season.
t.starigrad@44.3,15.4:
Starigrad lies on the Adriatic shore beneath the grey wall of the Velebit mountains, a long strip of pebble beach, pine trees and low stone houses squeezed between the sea and the rock. Locals know it as Starigrad-Paklenica, after the national park that begins at its back door, where two gorges, Velika and Mala Paklenica, cut deep into the limestone. Sheer cliffs rising hundreds of metres make it a magnet for climbers, and the sound of ropes and carabiners at the foot of the walls is part of the village soundtrack in spring.

The road that runs through is the Adriatic Highway, the old coastal route that links Rijeka with Dubrovnik, and for a rider it is one of the great drives of the Mediterranean. North of Starigrad it follows the Velebit Channel, with the island of Pag stretched across the water like a bare, pale whale. Towards Zadar it crosses the Maslenica bridge and drops into the Dalmatian hinterland. The road is generally smooth, with long open bends, and views at every turn. The challenge is the wind, the bura, a cold, violent gust from the mountains that can knock a bike sideways and sometimes forces the closure of the road to light vehicles, so look at the warnings before you go.

In summer the beaches are packed, restaurants serve grilled fish and local lamb, and the temperature climbs high, so early and late rides are better. May, June and September are the sweet months, with warm sea and calmer traffic. Winter brings the bura and sometimes ice higher up.

Starigrad is a village, so fuel is not guaranteed; the reliable choice is Zadar, about twenty-six kilometres away, or the stations along the Highway. Fill your tank before the emptier stretches, and carry water if you plan to hike into the gorge, as the walk is warm and shade is scarce.
t.otocac@44.9,15.2:
Otočac lies in the Gacka valley, a green strip of meadow in the middle of Lika, the sparsely populated highland behind the Velebit mountains. The river Gacka is the town's treasure. It rises from limestone springs, runs cold and so clear that every stone shows on the bottom, and holds trout and grayling that draw fly fishermen from across Europe. In the town itself, the river passes between old stone houses and mills, with willows and ducks along the banks.

Otočac was a frontier town for centuries. In the sixteenth century the Habsburgs set up the Military Frontier here, settling soldier-farmers along the border with the Ottoman Empire, and the little fortified towns and watch towers of the area belong to that era. The cathedral and the old centre give it a quiet dignity, though the 1990s war left scars that you can still see in the surrounding villages.

On the bike the area is a pleasure because it is so empty. From Senj on the coast, the road climbs over the Vratnik pass, at roughly seven hundred metres, in a series of well-engineered bends, and drops onto the Lika plateau, where the air is cooler and the landscape opens into meadows, beech woods and scattered farmsteads. It is a natural route toward Plitvice Lakes, about an hour inland. The surface is mostly good, and traffic is light outside July and August. Beware of the bura wind on the pass, which can be violent in winter, and of black ice and snow in the cold months, since Lika is one of the coldest regions in Croatia.

Otočac is small, only a few thousand residents, but it has shops and a fuel station, with Senj and Gospić the nearest larger places if you need more choice. Local cooking is hearty: lamb, cheese, smoked ham and, of course, trout from the river, which many restaurants grill simply with olive oil. The best seasons are late spring and early autumn.
t.pag@44.4,15.1:
Pag is a strange, beautiful island, a long strip of bare grey limestone that looks like the surface of the moon, swept by the bura wind and stripped of most of its trees centuries ago. The town of Pag sits in the sheltered bay at the southern end, a neat grid of stone houses around a small harbour and a church square. It was planned in the fifteenth century by Juraj Dalmatinac, the master builder who also worked on Šibenik cathedral, and the regular streets show his ordered mind.

The island is famous for what it produces despite the harsh ground. The sheep graze on salt-sprayed herbs and sage, and their milk makes the hard, sharp cheese called paški sir, one of the most prized in Croatia. The meat of the lamb is just as good. Fine lace is another local craft, and women still sit in doorways making it. Salt has been harvested from the shallow pans next to the town since the Middle Ages, and the white heaps glittering in the sun are part of the view.

For a rider, the road across Pag is a lesson in wind and space. A bridge now ties the island to the mainland at its southern end, and the road runs north in broad curves with the sea on both sides and not a tree to hold off the gusts. The bura can be dangerous, and the bridge is sometimes closed to motorcycles and high-sided vehicles in strong winds, so look out for the warnings. The surface is good, the traffic heavy in summer, particularly when holidaymakers head for Novalja and its beach clubs on the north-west coast.

Fuel is available on the island, but Gospić and Zadar are the larger towns, so if you are low, fill up at the stations before the bridge. In town, order a plate of cheese with local olive oil and a glass of white wine. The best seasons are May, June and September, since high summer is hot and crowded, and the bare landscape offers no shade.
t.gospic@44.5,15.4:
Gospić is the small capital of Lika, a high, cold plateau tucked behind the Velebit mountains, and the town sits at about five hundred and sixty metres above the sea in a broad valley of meadows and pine woods. Winters here are famously harsh, with deep snow and temperatures that can drop far below freezing, and people sometimes call the region Croatia's Siberia. The summers are mild and fresh, and the long evenings are good for sitting outside.

It is the nearest town to the village of Smiljan, where Nikola Tesla was born in 1856, the son of a Serbian Orthodox priest. A memorial centre there, which is easy to reach, preserves the house and church and tells the story of the inventor of the alternating-current system, with some demonstrations of electricity that delight children and adults alike. In Gospić itself, a statue of Tesla stands in the centre, and a few old public buildings recall the time when it was part of the Austro-Hungarian Military Frontier.

The riding in Lika is characterised by emptiness. Roads run through forest and meadow, with few villages and little traffic, and the surface is mostly good. To the west, the road climbs over the Velebit via the old route to Karlobag, a series of dramatic hairpins with a view over the islands of the Adriatic that is among the finest in the country, although it can be closed in winter. To the north lie the Plitvice Lakes, a UNESCO site of terraced waterfalls, about an hour's ride away, though the roads around the park fill with coaches in summer.

Fuel is easy at Gospić, which has several stations, and it is wise to fill up here before heading into the mountains, since services can be distant. Local cuisine centres on Lika potatoes, lamb roasted under a metal bell, smoked meats and cheese. Choose the months between May and October for the best weather, and carry a warm layer, because the nights can be chilly even in midsummer.
t.korcula@43.0,17.1:
Korčula old town stands on a small peninsula that sticks out into the channel between the island and the mainland's Pelješac, and from the sea it looks like a fortress made of honey-coloured stone: a ring of walls, towers and a cathedral with a belltower on the top of a rise. The streets inside are laid out in a herringbone pattern, with the main street along the ridge and the side lanes angled to break the force of the wind and let in the breeze, a clever piece of medieval planning that is still obvious on a map.

The town claims to be the birthplace of Marco Polo, and a house said to be his stands near the cathedral, though historians disagree and Venice has its own claims. Whatever the truth, the story brings a steady flow of visitors. Another local tradition is the Moreška, a sword dance depicting a battle between Moors and Christians, which is performed in summer in the town and has a long history on the island. The island was also a centre of shipbuilding and stonecutting, and the quality of the stone shows in every doorway.

For riders, Korčula is reached by ferry, either from Orebić on the Pelješac peninsula, a short crossing, or on longer routes from Split. The island is long and narrow, about forty-six kilometres, with a spine of low hills covered in pine and scrub, and the roads along it are gentle, well-surfaced and quiet outside July and August. The views over the channel and the vineyards are very fine, and the island's white wines, Pošip and Grk, are worth tasting at the small cellars along the way.

Fuel on the island is limited, so fill up on the mainland before boarding. In summer ferries to the island can have long queues, so arrive early or book. The old town itself is largely pedestrian, with steps and polished stone that can be slippery, so it is best to leave the bike outside the walls.

May, June and September are the best months, with warm sea and calm roads.
t.sarajevo@43.8,18.4:
Sarajevo lies in a steep, narrow valley along the Miljacka river, with mountains close on every side, and the first thing you notice is how much of the city is stacked up the hillsides. Minarets and church towers stand within a short walk of each other, and the old bazaar quarter, the Baščaršija, has copper workshops, cafes serving thick Bosnian coffee from small copper pots, and stalls grilling ćevapi, little skinless sausages served in flatbread with chopped onion. It is a place where East and West meet, and where Ottoman, Habsburg and Yugoslav layers sit side by side.

The city carries a heavy history. In June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand was shot beside the Latin Bridge, which set in motion the First World War. In 1984 it hosted the Winter Olympics, and then, from 1992 to 1996, it endured the longest siege of a capital city in modern times. You can still see scars on the buildings, and the Tunnel of Hope museum near the airport tells the story of the lifeline dug under the runway. Rebuilding has been impressive, and the city is lively now, with cafes open late.

For riders, Sarajevo is a place to arrive, rest and then leave for the mountains. South of the city rise Bjelašnica and Igman, Olympic ski mountains with winding roads and wide views, and the road through the Neretva canyon to Mostar is among the finest in the Balkans, a long sequence of bends past lakes and rock faces. Traffic in the city is heavy and drivers are quick, so ride attentively and watch for tram lines and cobbles that can be slick in rain.

Fuel is plentiful. Foreign riders usually need a Green Card for insurance in Bosnia, so check your documents before the border. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, as summer can be hot in the valley and winter brings cold air and smog. Do not leave without sampling burek and a slice of baklava.
t.livno@43.8,17.0:
Livno sits on the edge of a huge karst plain, the Livanjsko polje, the largest of its kind in the Dinaric mountains, ringed by bare limestone ridges. In winter the plain floods and becomes a shallow lake, in spring it turns green, and in summer it is a patchwork of hay meadows with the dark mass of Cincar mountain rising behind. The town is about twelve thousand people and has an unhurried, provincial air, with a small old quarter, a mosque and Catholic and Orthodox churches standing within a short walk of each other.

Livno is famous for cheese. Livanjski sir, a hard, sheep-and-cow cheese cured for months and rich in flavour, is one of the best in Bosnia, and every household has a favourite supplier. Wild horses roam free on the slopes of Cincar and on the plain, descendants of animals abandoned long ago, and you may see herds from the road, which makes night riding a hazard because the horses are not always easy to see.

From a rider's point of view, Livno is a stopping point on a route between the Adriatic and the interior. The road over the pass from Split climbs through the Dinara mountains in sweeping bends and drops onto the plain, where long straights and distant peaks make for easy, open riding. To the north-east, the road crosses the Kupres plateau, a high, treeless landscape that can be bleak in winter and glorious in summer. Surfaces are generally acceptable but patchy in places, and winter ice and fog can make the high passes treacherous.

Fuel is easy in Livno, which has several stations, and it is a sensible place to top up before crossing the mountains. Try a plate of the local cheese with smoked ham and fresh bread, and a glass of homemade rakija if you are not riding on. The best months are May to September, with warm days and cool evenings. Remember that you will need a Green Card for insurance in Bosnia, and keep documents handy at the border.
t.jajce@44.3,17.3:
Jajce is a town built around a waterfall. The river Pliva joins the Vrbas right in the middle of town and drops about twenty metres over a lip of tufa into a green pool, with houses and a medieval fortress stacked above. It is one of the few towns in Europe where you can eat lunch within sight and sound of a waterfall that is part of the main street. The old walls climb the hill behind, with a citadel, gate towers and narrow lanes within.

Jajce was the last capital of the medieval Bosnian kingdom. After the Ottoman conquest of Bosnia in 1463, the last king, Stjepan Tomašević, was captured and executed, and Jajce fell in 1528 after a long resistance. In the Second World War the town hosted a decisive moment: in November 1943 the anti-fascist council of Yugoslav partisans met here and laid the foundations for the post-war federation, and the building where they met is now a museum. Under the town you can find catacombs and a small Mithraic temple, a reminder of how old the settlement is.

For riders, Jajce offers lovely roads in several directions. The Vrbas canyon road north to Banja Luka winds beside a green river between steep wooded walls, a popular route for rafting and for riders who love long flowing bends. South, the Pliva lakes and the little wooden watermills at Janj, a few kilometres out, make a good detour. Roads are generally decent but can be patched, and trucks and local drivers move fast.

Jajce has about ten thousand people and several fuel stations, so refuelling is easy, and the town has plenty of cafes and small restaurants serving grilled trout, cevapi and sweet pastry. The nights can be cool even in summer, and rain brings quick fog to the valleys, so carry a light waterproof.

Late spring and early autumn are the best periods, when the water is full and the forests are fresh or turning gold. Foreign riders should carry a Green Card for Bosnia.
t.plav@42.6,19.9:
Plav lies in the far east of Montenegro, in a high green basin beside a glacial lake, with the jagged limestone peaks of the Prokletije, the Accursed Mountains, rising to the south and west. The lake is calm and cold, edged with willows and reed, and the mountains behind seem to hang above it, their summits often streaked with snow until early summer. Zla Kolata, near the Albanian border, is the highest peak in Montenegro, at over twenty-five hundred metres, and the whole range is a wilderness of cirques, screes and deep valleys.

The town is small, only a few thousand people, and the culture is a blend of Bosniak, Albanian and Montenegrin traditions. Old Ottoman stone towers stand beside mosques with slim minarets, and in neighbouring Gusinje the springs of Ali Pasha, which pour out of the rock in a cold clear stream, make a favourite place to cool down. A visit to the Grebaje valley, with its pastures and shepherds' huts, shows how mountain life continues here at an old pace.

Riders come for the roads and the remoteness. From Berane, the road winds up toward Plav through a gorge and forest, then continues to the border crossing with Albania at Vermosh, from where the highway drops to Shkodër through the Kelmend region. Surfaces vary: parts are freshly laid, others are broken, and landslides and rockfall can happen after storms. Traffic is thin, but you may meet sheep, cows and horses on the road, so keep your speed down on blind corners.

Fuel is the main question. Plav is small, and while there is usually a pump in town, Berane, about twenty-eight kilometres away, is the larger place to rely on. Cash is useful in the mountain villages. Weather swings quickly, with cold nights even in July and thunderstorms in the afternoon. The best months are June to September, and snow can close the high roads from late autumn.

The food is excellent and simple: grilled trout from the lake, fresh cheese, and fruit from local orchards.
t.porto palermo@40.1,19.8:
Porto Palermo is a bay on the Albanian Riviera that looks like a film set, with a small castle on a rocky peninsula that pokes into clear blue water. The castle, a compact triangular fortress, was built in the early nineteenth century by Ali Pasha of Tepelena, the Ottoman governor who ruled much of southern Albania and northern Greece with his own mix of ambition and cruelty. The walls are thick, and the stone is the colour of honey, and from the causeway the fortress seems to float in the sea. Inside, the courtyard is bare but atmospheric.

The bay has a darker twentieth-century past. During the communist era, the harbour was a closed military zone, and a secret submarine base was built in tunnels in the hillside, first for the Soviet Union and later for China. The remains of the base are still visible on the shore, and a trace of that secretive time lingers in the empty buildings. Today, the peninsula is quiet, and the beach just beyond the castle is a place for a swim or a coffee.

The ride along the coast is the reason to come. The SH8 road runs south from Vlorë over the Llogara Pass, which is a steep climb through pine forest, then drops down the coast toward Himarë, with big views of the Ionian Sea and the Greek island of Corfu on a clear day. It is a spectacular road, with bends, drops and views at every turn, and the surface is usually good, though patchy in places. Traffic can be heavy in summer, with buses, minivans and some drivers who overtake in unlikely places, so keep your distance and ride defensively. Livestock sometimes wander onto the road, and rockfall is not unknown.

The villages along the coast have a strongly Greek feel, as this is a region where many ethnic Greeks live, and the food is a mixture of Albanian and Greek, with grilled fish, olives, goat's cheese and good local wine. Himarë, six kilometres to the north, has the nearest proper services, with fuel, restaurants and a long beach. Sarandë, further south, is larger, with a port and a wide choice of restaurants.

Summer is hot and busy, with the coast crowded in July and August. May, June and September are better, with warm seas and less traffic.
t.shkoder@42.1,19.5:
Shkodër is one of the oldest towns in Albania and the cultural capital of the north, a place where Catholic bell towers, mosques and Orthodox domes sit within a short walk of each other and bicycles outnumber cars in the old streets. It lies on a flat plain between the huge Lake Skadar, the largest lake in southern Europe, and the first foothills of the Albanian Alps, and the Buna river, a short, powerful stream, carries the lake's water to the Adriatic. Above the town stands Rozafa Castle on its rock, with views over both rivers and the lake. Legend says the walls kept collapsing until the builders agreed to wall up a woman alive, and the mother of a baby in the family agreed on the condition that one breast, one eye and one hand be left free to nurse the child.

Shkodër was a centre of trade, scholarship and photography. The Marubi studio, founded by an Italian immigrant in the mid-nineteenth century, produced a collection of portraits and street scenes that is one of the treasures of Albanian history, and a museum shows them. The old Ottoman bridge at Mes, a few kilometres out, spans a gorge with several graceful arches and is worth a visit.

For riders, Shkodër is the beginning of the road into the mountains. The SH20 heads north across the plain toward Koplik, then turns east into the Kelmend region and climbs toward the Montenegrin border at Vermosh, going deeper into the Accursed Mountains, with limestone walls, narrow valleys and stone villages. The road is a mix of fresh and rough sections, with potholes and landslides in places, and trucks and cows share the carriageway, so ride defensively. Traffic in the town itself is chaotic and drivers are unpredictable.

Fuel is easy in Shkodër, which is a city of nearly ninety thousand with many stations, and it is wise to fill up before the climb, as services in the mountains are few. Eat fish from the lake, grilled carp and bleak, and try the local sweets.
t.leqet e hotit@42.4,19.6:
Past the border village of Hani i Hotit, the landscape of the Hoti region opens into a dry, stony country of low hills, olive trees and rocky ground, with the great wall of the Prokletije, the Accursed Mountains, rising to the north. This is Hoti land, the home of one of the old Albanian mountain tribes, whose people lived on both sides of what became the Albanian-Montenegrin frontier. The area is thinly populated, with scattered houses, stone walls and small plots of vines, and the name Leqet e Hotit, the Lakes of Hoti, belongs to the region as a whole more than to any single shore, and the wet months bring water to every hollow.

The old tribal society of northern Albania was governed by a code of customary law known as the Kanun, which regulated everything from hospitality to blood feuds. Its traditions survived long after the rest of Europe had moved on, and guests, by the rules of the Kanun, were sacred. You will still find the habit of hospitality alive in the villages, in the offer of coffee, raki and something to eat.

The riding here is a different matter from the high Alps. The roads are generally flat to rolling, and the corners are gentle, but the surface can be worn, with potholes and patched asphalt. Traffic is a mixture of cars, vans, tractors and the odd horse cart, and livestock use the road with confidence. Border queues can build at the nearby crossing in summer, so allow time, and carry all your documents, including vehicle papers and insurance. In the distance, the peaks of the Prokletije, snow-capped well into spring, form a dramatic backdrop to the day.

The nature of this area is rugged. The limestone hills are covered with scrub oak, juniper and wild pomegranate, and the air smells of dust, thyme and sage on hot days. Birds of prey circle above the ridges, and the nearby Skadar Lake, one of the largest lakes in southern Europe, is a haven for pelicans and herons. Summers are very hot, often above thirty-five degrees, and winters are mild but wet.

Services here are limited. Tuzi and Koplik, each about eighteen kilometres away, have fuel and shops, and Podgorica, the Montenegrin capital, is about twenty-five kilometres off and has everything. Fill up before heading north into the mountains, and carry water on hot days.
t.tamare@42.5,19.6:
Tamarë, or Tamara, is a village in the Hoti region on the Montenegrin side of the border with Albania, set in a landscape of dry limestone hills, vineyards and scrub, a short distance north of Skadar Lake. The people here are mostly ethnic Albanians, and the place feels like the northern Albanian country on the other side of the line, with the same stone houses, the same language and the same hospitality. The border has shaped life here for a century, and it is closer than it looks.

Skadar Lake lies to the south and is the biggest lake in the Balkans, shared between Montenegro and Albania. It is shallow, warm and full of life, with pelicans, cormorants, herons and several hundred kinds of bird, including the rare Dalmatian pelican. The marshes and waterlily meadows are a nature reserve, and the old fortress of Žabljak Crnojevića stands on a small island near the northern end. The wine of the region, particularly Vranac, a dark and powerful red, is grown on the hills near Podgorica and has a name in the Balkans.

The ride is quiet, with gentle bends, slow villages and a good deal of local traffic. The roads linking Tuzi, Tamarë and the border at Božaj are generally in fair shape but can be uneven, and the wind from the mountains can be strong. Animals cross the road without warning, and in the evening, farmers move cattle and sheep home. In summer, the heat bounces off the stone, and a gentle early start is best. The mountains of the Prokletije rise ahead, and the road toward the border climbs into a more dramatic landscape.

Crossing the border into Albania is straightforward for most nationalities, but you need your passport, vehicle registration and a valid green card for insurance.
