At busy times, queues can be long, and the formalities are slow. Many riders choose to cross early in the morning, when the traffic is light, and to carry some local currency for small purchases.

Podgorica, about twenty-five kilometres away, is the nearest large town, and has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, as well as a pleasant old district. Tuzi, closer to the border, has some shops and stations. Food in the area is simple and hearty, with grilled meat, cheese, fresh bread and local honey, and a coffee in a village cafe is a good way to pause.
t.vermosh@42.6,19.7:
Vermosh is where the road runs out of Albania. The last village in the Kelmend valley sits in a green bowl of meadows at around a thousand metres, ringed by steep limestone peaks of the Accursed Mountains, and the border with Montenegro is only a short distance away. The people here are Catholic highlanders, the Kelmendi, who have a reputation for fierce independence, and their stone houses, with small windows and thick walls, were built for defence as much as for shelter. Some old kulla towers still stand, a reminder of the days when blood feuds were governed by the Kanun, the ancient code of the mountains.

The pleasure of the place is its silence. Streams run clear from the hills, cattle graze on the slopes, and hay is dried in cones in the summer. Guesthouses serve food made from the farm: fresh cheese, yoghurt, grilled lamb, and raki, the local brandy, which is offered more freely than you may want. A few trails lead to higher pastures and lakes, and in summer the mountains bloom with gentian and orchids.

For a rider, the road to Vermosh is the point. From Koplik, the SH20 climbs into the valley, passing waterfalls and deep gorges, and the tarmac becomes patchy as it approaches the village, with narrow stretches and sections that can be damaged by landslides. Take it slowly, and watch for livestock and children on the road. The scenery is large and wild, and you will meet few other vehicles. The border crossing leads to Gusinje and Plav in Montenegro, but opening hours and rules for foreign vehicles can change, so check before you plan a loop.

There is no reliable fuel in Vermosh, and the nearest sizeable stations are down the valley, so fill up before you go. In Montenegro, Berane is the larger town. Carry some cash, water and a warm layer, because weather in the mountains changes fast, and nights are cool even in summer. Snow can close the road from late autumn to spring.
t.trsa@43.2,18.9:
Trsa is a name on a map more than a place with a centre, a scatter of houses above the long green reservoir that drowned the Piva canyon. Plužine is the nearest village of any size, a few kilometres up the water, and Žabljak sits on the Durmitor plateau beyond that. What you are really riding here is the shoreline road, and it is one of the odd ones in the Balkans: it clings to the canyon wall, ducks through short rough tunnels that look as if they were cut by people in a hurry, and opens out every few hundred metres onto water the colour of bottle glass.

The lake exists because of the Mratinje dam, finished in the 1970s, and it is a reminder of how much was given up for it. The Piva Monastery, a Serbian Orthodox house with a famous painted church, would have gone under, so the whole building was taken apart and rebuilt higher up near Plužine, with its frescoes cut from the walls and put back. If you have an hour, that is worth more than any viewpoint. The canyon itself is deep and narrow, limestone with pines and beech hanging on wherever they find a ledge, and in the early morning the water is still enough to double every cliff.

Ride it slowly. The surface is patchy, tunnels are unlit in places, and a rental bus coming the other way will not give you much room. Take the sunglasses off before the tunnels and put them back on after, which sounds trivial until you have done it badly once. Wind off the plateau can be sharp even in July, and in late autumn the shaded stretches hold ice well after the sun is up.

Do not count on fuel here. Plužine is a small place and Žabljak is only a bit larger, so treat the pump in Žabljak as the sure one and arrive with some in hand. Food is simple and good in this part of Montenegro: grilled meat, kajmak, bread still warm, and cheese from the mountain farms. Mobile signal comes and goes with the walls of the canyon, so sort out your route before you drop in.
t.tara canyon@43.2,19.3:
Everyone who talks about the Tara canyon quotes the same number, and it holds up: up to about 1,300 metres from rim to river, which makes it among the deepest gorges in Europe and the deepest in this part of the world. The Tara runs for roughly eighty kilometres, cuts through the north of Montenegro on its way to join the Piva and become the Drina, and the whole thing sits inside a protected biosphere reserve. From the road you see the green end of it, black pine forest dropping into a thin turquoise line a very long way down.

The place most riders stop is the Đurđevića Tara Bridge, a concrete arch of five spans that carries the road about 170 metres above the water. It was finished in 1940, and its story is a sad one: during the Second World War its designer was made to take part in blowing up one of its arches to slow an Italian advance, and the bridge was patched up afterwards. Today it is a viewpoint, a photograph and a zip line, in that order of seriousness. Park off the carriageway, walk onto the bridge, and look down the canyon in both directions. In summer there are rafting trips below, and the little rafts look like confetti.

The roads on either side are what you came for, wide, fast bends through forest and open hayfields, with Durmitor's grey teeth rising to the south. Žabljak, fourteen kilometres away, is the base for the mountains, and Pljevlja to the north is the nearest proper town with services, so if the tank is low that is where the choice is larger. Traffic is light apart from tour coaches and the occasional herd on the tarmac.

Weather changes fast at this height. A morning of hard blue sky can turn to rain by afternoon, and the temperature at the bridge in June can be a long way below what you left in Podgorica. Take a layer, take water, and give the hairpins on the canyon road their full attention. The best light for riding is the first two hours after sunrise, before the shadows fill the gorge.
t.kotor serpentine@42.4,18.8:
The old road out of Kotor does not waste time. It begins almost at the town walls and starts climbing at once, and the famous count is twenty-five hairpins, numbered on small signs, with the bay shrinking below you at each turn until the cruise ships in the harbour look like toys in a bath. The Austrians built it in the nineteenth century, when this coast belonged to the Habsburgs and they wanted a way up the mountain wall to the Montenegrin capital at Cetinje. The gradient is steady, the corners are tight and well engineered, and the retaining walls are old dry stone that still do their job.

You should know that this is a busy road for what it is. Tour coaches and delivery vans share it with the two-wheelers, and the hairpins are narrow enough that a coach has to swing wide across the whole carriageway. Take it early, before the ten o'clock wave, and the rhythm is lovely: lean in, wait, lean out, a second of gravel under the tyre at a bend, a car park with a view, and then the next. The tarmac is mostly decent. In wet weather the painted lines and the polished stone edges are slick.

The bay beneath you is not a true fjord but a drowned river canyon, one of the deepest inlets on this side of the Adriatic, and the mountains on its far side rise straight out of the water with no beach to speak of. Kotor itself, three kilometres down, sits in the hollow of this wall with a fortress zigzagging up the slope behind the old town. That wall climbs to a chapel on the hill, and legend says the pilgrims made the ascent on their knees.

For fuel, Kotor and Dobrota, in the bay, are your options, and both are a few minutes from the foot of the climb. Fill up before you go, because the top is a pass in a national park, not a services area. Allow time for a coffee in the old town at the end; the lanes get hot and loud by noon, but the squares are a good place to sit, and the grilled fish on the waterfront is dependable.
t.krstac pass@42.4,18.8:
Krstac sits at 926 metres, and it is where the serpentine finally lets go of you. The last of the hairpins from Kotor swing out onto a shoulder of limestone, the bay disappears behind you, and what lies ahead is a different Montenegro: a high plateau of stone, thin pasture and beech, with Mount Lovćen rising on your right. The name Montenegro, black mountain, makes sense up here. The slopes look dark under the forest, and in cloud they look black indeed.

This is the junction where most riders choose. One way runs east into the village of Njeguši, ancestral home of the Petrović-Njegoš dynasty that ruled Montenegro for two centuries, and now better known for its smoked ham and cheese. Stalls and small restaurants sell both, with bread and a glass of the local rakija if you insist, and it is a very reasonable place to eat at midday. The other way climbs into Lovćen National Park toward the mausoleum of Petar II Petrović-Njegoš, the poet-prince who is the nearest thing Montenegro has to a national saint, on the summit at around 1,650 metres. That road is narrower and slower, but the view from the top is huge: on a clear day, sea, bay, lake and mountains in one frame.

The road from Krstac to Cetinje is a pleasant ribbon through karst fields, quicker than the climb, with long open corners and little traffic once the coaches have turned off. Weather up here is worth respecting. A hot, still morning in Kotor can be fifteen degrees cooler and cloud-wrapped at the pass, and fog on the plateau comes in quickly. Wind is common.

Kotor is five kilometres down, and Cetinje, the old royal capital with its embassies in wedding-cake villas, is about eight kilometres away on the other side and has everything. Water and a toilet are easier to find at Njeguši than at the pass itself, so stop there when you can. In winter snow can close or chain the upper sections, and a rider on the wrong tyres should check before committing.
t.cetinje@42.4,18.9:
Cetinje is a small town with a big past, the old royal capital of Montenegro. It lies in a high karst basin at about 650 metres, behind the mountain wall of Lovćen, and for centuries it was the seat of the prince-bishops who ruled this stubbornly independent land. The Cetinje Monastery, founded in 1484, still holds the right hand of St John the Baptist and a fragment of the True Cross, according to tradition. The streets are lined with former embassies from the days when European powers kept legations here, and the whole town has the air of a capital that has shrunk but kept its dignity. About fifteen thousand people live here.

The ride in is part of the story. The famous serpentine road from the Bay of Kotor climbs the steep face of Lovćen with some twenty-five hairpins, giving views over the bay that are among the finest in the Adriatic. The road is narrow and old, with tight bends and stone walls, and it can be crowded with tour buses and hire cars, so go early in the morning. Kotor lies about twelve kilometres away, and Budva a little farther. At the top, the road levels into the high plateau, with beech woods, stone walls and a cold, clean air that contrasts with the heat of the coast.

Nearby Lovćen National Park holds the mausoleum of Petar II Petrović-Njegoš, the poet-bishop and ruler who is the national hero, on a summit at about 1,660 metres, reached by a long stairway. The name Montenegro, black mountain, comes from the dark forests of this range. Winter brings snow, and the weather can change quickly, with fog and cold wind, so carry layers.

Cetinje has fuel stations and shops, and there are cafes in the centre where you can have a strong coffee. The local cured ham, njeguški pršut, and the cheese from the area are famous and worth trying. The best season is late spring to early autumn, with September especially pleasant, with fewer crowds and clear air. The town is quiet, even on a busy day, and it is a good place to rest after the hairpins.
t.terney@45.1,136.6:
Terney is the end of the line for most travellers on this coast, a small settlement of nearly four thousand people at the head of a bay in the far north of Primorsky Krai. The bay was named in the eighteenth century by the French navigator La Pérouse, who honoured a French admiral, and the settlement has been a base for exploration, fishing and forestry ever since. The Sikhote-Alin Nature Reserve has its administrative centre here, and the surrounding hills are the homeland of the Udege people, who have lived by hunting and fishing in these forests for centuries.

The name Terney also belongs to literature. The explorer and writer Vladimir Arsenyev travelled through this country in the early twentieth century, and his account of his guide Dersu Uzala, a hunter of the Nanai people, became a classic, later turned into the film by Akira Kurosawa. If you have read or seen it, the forest around Terney will look familiar, thick and dark, with a feeling of watching eyes. The settlement has a small museum that recalls the history of the area and its people, and it is worth a visit if it is open.

The road from Plastun is a long ride through wild country, with moderate bends, patchy asphalt and gravel sections, and views of forested ridges and distant sea. Traffic is almost non-existent, and wildlife is a real hazard, especially at dusk. Weather changes quickly: fog and rain can come in from the coast, and cold nights are common even in summer. The best time to ride is late August to early October, when rain is less frequent and the forest colours begin to deepen.

Terney has shops, a few cafes and a fuel station, though supplies can be limited, so arrive with a sensible reserve. There is nowhere larger nearby, so you will be self-reliant. Take a moment to walk to the shore, where the wide bay opens to the sea and the hills close in behind, and think about how few people have ever seen this place. It is remote, a little windswept, and very satisfying to reach after a long day in the saddle.
t.sikachi alyan@48.8,135.7:
Sikachi-Alyan is a Nanai village on the right bank of the Amur, a long way downstream from Khabarovsk, and it is famous for something that makes the journey worth it: the rock carvings. On basalt boulders on the river shore, ancient people pecked and scratched faces, animals, boats and spirals that archaeologists estimate to be thousands of years old, perhaps among the oldest art in this part of Asia. The images are strange and compelling, round faces with wide eyes, some staring up from the stone like masks. The Nanai, who still live here and in neighbouring villages, treat the site with respect, and so should visitors.

The road to the village follows the Amur through flat, open land of river meadows, willows and marsh, with Knyaze-Volkonskoye, a town of about nine thousand people, the nearest sizeable place some thirty-five kilometres away. That is where you should fill the tank, buy food and water and use a proper toilet, because the village is small and its services thin. Expect asphalt that varies from good to rough, wide, easy bends and plenty of space to look at the river. Traffic is light, mostly local, and in summer the air carries the smell of wet grass and woodsmoke. Mosquitoes can be a trial, so bring repellent.

The Amur is the dominant presence. It is one of the longest rivers in the world, and here it spreads out to a vast width, with sandbars, channels and islands. Floods in late summer can cover the lowlands and make some tracks impassable, so ask locally before heading toward the shore. The best months for riding are June to September, with warm days and long light, though the rains of July and August can be heavy. Autumn is clear, quiet and colourful.

If you are curious about the culture, take time to meet the people. The Nanai, who also live across the border in China, have a rich tradition of fishing, shamanism and storytelling, and their art and crafts, including fish-skin clothing, are known far beyond the region. A small museum or cultural centre may be open in the area, but opening hours are not guaranteed. Whatever you find, go slowly and be respectful, and take a moment at the boulders to imagine the hands that made them.
t.borak in the village of burati@43.8,18.9:
Scattered across the meadows and forest edges of Bosnia and Herzegovina are thousands of carved medieval tombstones called stećci, great blocks of limestone shaped like chests, slabs or little gabled houses, some plain and some carved with spirals, vines, crescent moons, hunting scenes, dancers and raised hands. They date mostly from the twelfth to the sixteenth centuries, and together with sites in Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia they were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2016 as the Stećci Medieval Tombstone Graveyards. Borak, near the village of Burati in the hills above Rogatica, is one of these graveyards, a cluster of stones lying among the grass where they have stood for six hundred years or more.

Nobody fully agrees on who carved them or what all the symbols mean, and that mystery is part of their power. Some have inscriptions in Bosnian Cyrillic, speaking in a plain, direct voice about the dead man who lies beneath. Visit quietly, do not climb on the stones, and take time to look at the carving in slanting light, when the reliefs come alive.

The country around is high and rolling, the edge of the Romanija plateau, with pine and beech forest, open pasture, haystacks and small villages of steep-roofed houses. Sokolac, thirteen kilometres away, and Rogatica, a little closer, are the local towns, with fuel, shops and simple cafés where you will be offered strong Bosnian coffee in a copper džezva. The war of the 1990s left deep scars in eastern Bosnia, and they are still visible in abandoned houses and memorials; in remote areas, stick to roads and marked paths, as some ground was mined and not all of it has been cleared.

For riding, the roads between Sarajevo, Sokolac, Rogatica and Goražde are a pleasure: winding, often freshly surfaced, with forest and long views, and light traffic away from the main routes. The descent toward the Drina at Goražde is particularly good. Winters are cold and snowy up here, so the season runs from late spring to autumn. Try ćevapi, burek or a slow-cooked lamb from a roadside grill.
t.the appia traiana at canusium and the of:
In AD 109, the emperor Trajan opened a new road from Benevento to Brindisi, shorter and easier than the old Via Appia, and it crossed the plain of northern Puglia, past the ancient city of Canusium, today's Canosa di Puglia. Near Canosa, the road crossed the Ofanto river on a bridge whose Roman foundations still support a later structure. The Appia Traiana at Canusium and the Ofanto crossing are part of the UNESCO listing of Via Appia, Regina Viarum, inscribed in 2024, and the plain around them is open, flat and fertile, a landscape of olive groves, vineyards and fields of wheat and artichokes.

The Ofanto valley has a famous battlefield. In 216 BC, at Cannae, a few kilometres upstream, Hannibal's army encircled and destroyed a much larger Roman army in one of the most studied battles in history. The site of Cannae has a small museum and an archaeological area on a hill above the river.

Canosa itself was an important Daunian and Roman city, with tombs, a basilica and a cathedral with Byzantine and Norman influences. On the coast, Margherita di Savoia has some of the largest salt pans in Europe, where flamingos feed in the shallow water and the salt is still harvested. Trinitapoli and San Ferdinando di Puglia are farming towns, known for artichokes and wine.

For riders, the plain of northern Puglia is not dramatic, but it is relaxing, with straight roads, little traffic, and big skies. The Gargano peninsula, to the north, offers twisting coastal roads and forests, and the Murge plateau, to the south, has rolling hills and castles, including Castel del Monte, Frederick II's octagonal fortress. Fuel is easy to find in the towns. Summer is hot and dry, so ride early. Try the local orecchiette with turnip tops, burrata, and the wines of the area, such as Nero di Troia.
t.gvozno@43.6,18.4:
Out on the high karst plateau around Kalinovik, south of Sarajevo, the land opens into wide pastures and rocky hills at well over a thousand metres, ringed by the mountains of Treskavica, Lelija and Zelengora. Here and there, half-hidden in the grass, lie stećci, the carved medieval tombstones that are unique to this corner of the Balkans. The necropolis at Gvozno is one of the sites included in the UNESCO listing of stećci, which spans Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia.

The stones date mostly from the twelfth to the sixteenth centuries. Some are simple slabs, others great blocks shaped like houses or sarcophagi, decorated with spirals, crescents, vines, hunting scenes, dancers and figures with raised hands, and a few carry inscriptions in old Cyrillic. Nobody is quite sure what all the symbols meant, which only adds to their mystery. Out here, with the wind moving through the grass and a hawk circling, they feel like the work of people who looked at the same hard landscape and decided to leave their mark.

Life on the plateau is tough. Winters are long and snowy, summers short and bright, and much of the area was badly affected by the war of the 1990s. Villages are small and scattered, many of them partly abandoned, and sheep and cattle graze freely. The roads across the plateau are a mix of good asphalt and rough gravel, with long straights broken by sudden curves where they drop into valleys. The descent towards Foča and the Drina canyon to the southeast is spectacular, as is the route through Sutjeska National Park with its primeval Perućica forest.

Fuel is scarce on the plateau, so fill up in Sarajevo or Foča, the nearest town of any size. Landmines remain a real hazard in parts of Bosnia, so stay on roads and well-used paths and heed any warning signs. Village cafés may offer a simple meal of grilled meat, cheese and bread, and the region is known for its excellent lamb. Bring warm clothes even in summer, as the weather can turn sharply on the high ground.
t.luburica polje@44.0,18.8:
The Romanija plateau east of Sarajevo is a strange and beautiful upland: rolling meadows and dark pine forests at around a thousand metres, under a sky that seems bigger than it should. Luburića polje, a field near the town of Sokolac, holds one of the necropolises of stećci, the medieval tombstones of the Balkans listed by UNESCO, and the surrounding countryside has been a place of burial for thousands of years.

Long before the stećci, the people of the Iron Age raised hundreds of burial mounds across the Glasinac field nearby, giving their name to a whole archaeological culture. Finds from these tumuli, including bronze jewellery, weapons and horse gear, are now in museums in Sarajevo and Vienna. The medieval tombstones continue that tradition in their own way, some carved with crosses, swords and shields, others with moons and stars. Standing among them on a misty morning, with cows grazing between the stones and the forest edge a dark line on the horizon, you feel the continuity of the place.

The roads over Romanija are generally in decent shape, with long flowing stretches across the plateau and twistier sections as they climb from Sarajevo or descend towards Rogatica and the Drina valley. The main road from Sarajevo to Sokolac carries trucks and buses, while smaller routes offer quiet riding through forest and pasture. Winters are long and cold here, with heavy snow, and even in summer, nights can be chilly. Fog and sudden rain are common, and logging traffic can leave mud on corners.

Sokolac, with nearly nine thousand people, has fuel, shops and cafés. As elsewhere in Bosnia, landmines from the war of the 1990s are still present in some areas, so stick to paved roads and established paths. Local food is hearty: ćevapi, grilled minced meat served in flatbread with onions, burek filled with meat or cheese, and strong Bosnian coffee served in a small copper pot. The Romanija mountains are also known in legend as the home of hajduks, outlaw rebels of Ottoman times, and locals may have stories to tell if you linger.
t.bijaca@43.1,17.6:
In western Herzegovina, near the town of Ljubuški and close to the Croatian border, the land is a mix of karst hills, fertile valleys and vineyards, baked by the sun and scented with sage and fig. Near the village of Bijača, the necropolis of stećci, the medieval tombstones that are unique to this region, is one of the sites included in the UNESCO listing of stećci, spread across Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia. The tombstones, carved with crosses, spirals, figures and inscriptions, stand among the grass and stones, a silent reminder of the people who lived here centuries ago.

Herzegovina is a land of contrasts, from the green valley of the Neretva river, which flows past Mostar to the sea, to the stark, rocky hills around it. Nearby, the Kravica waterfalls, a series of cascades on the Trebižat river, are a popular spot for swimming and picnics in summer, and the wetlands of Hutovo Blato, south of Čapljina, are a haven for birds. The pilgrimage town of Međugorje, a short ride away, attracts millions of visitors who come to the site of reported apparitions of the Virgin Mary since 1981. The region is known for its wines, especially the white Žilavka and red Blatina.

Riding in Herzegovina is a pleasure, with roads winding through hills, valleys and gorges, and little traffic outside the towns. The main road between Mostar and the coast follows the Neretva, with views of the river and the mountains, and smaller roads lead to villages, monasteries and viewpoints. Surfaces are generally good on main routes but can be rough on smaller roads. Summers are hot, often over thirty-five degrees, so ride early or late and carry water. The border with Croatia is close, and crossings can be busy in summer.

Čapljina and Ljubuški have fuel, shops and restaurants. Bosnian and Herzegovinian cuisine is hearty: try ćevapi, grilled minced meat with flatbread and onions, and Herzegovinian prosciutto with local cheese. Wash it down with a glass of Žilavka or Blatina, and finish with a strong Bosnian coffee. Stay on roads and established paths, as landmines from the war of the 1990s remain in some areas.
t.dugo polje at blidinje@43.7,17.5:
High on a karst plateau in Herzegovina, between the massive mountains of Čvrsnica and Vran, lies Blidinje, a wide upland valley of meadows, limestone outcrops and black pine forests at around twelve hundred metres. At Dugo polje, the long field, a cluster of medieval tombstones stands in the grass, carved with crosses, spirals, rosettes, hunting scenes and human figures. These are stećci, the distinctive gravestones of the medieval Balkans, made between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries, and Dugo polje is one of the most impressive groups, part of the collection of stećci sites listed by UNESCO in 2016 across Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia.

The stones are large, heavy blocks of limestone, some shaped like houses, others like sarcophagi or slabs, and many are beautifully decorated. Their meaning has been debated for centuries, with theories linking them to the Bosnian church, to local nobility or simply to the communities who lived here. Standing among them on a quiet afternoon, with the mountains all around and the wind in the grass, is an experience that stays with you.

Blidinje is a nature park, with a shallow lake, Blidinjsko jezero, at its centre, wild horses grazing on the meadows, and a small ski resort at Risovac. The roads across the plateau are good, with long, open sections and wide views, while the roads up to it, from Jablanica in the Neretva valley or from Posušje and Tomislavgrad to the south and west, are steep and twisting, with hairpins, tunnels and steep drops. The surface can be rough in places, and snow closes the high roads for much of the winter.

Services on the plateau are limited, with a few mountain huts, guesthouses and restaurants offering simple food, often lamb and other grilled meats, cheese and bread. Jablanica, about eighteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel, known for its lamb roasted on the spit and for the ruined railway bridge over the Neretva, a famous episode of the Second World War. The weather can be harsh and changeable, with strong winds, sudden storms and cold nights, even in summer, so bring warm clothing and fill the tank before climbing onto the plateau.
t.st barbara@42.5,18.4:
Konavle is the long, fertile valley that runs south east of Dubrovnik towards the Montenegrin border, and St. Barbara is a small church at Dubravka, near its upper edge, surrounded by a field of medieval tombstones. These stećci, heavy carved blocks of limestone dating from the late Middle Ages, are part of the cross-border UNESCO listing of stećci cemeteries shared by Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Serbia. The Dubravka group is one of the most accessible in Croatia, and the setting, with the church, the old stones and the view over the valley, is quietly beautiful.

Konavle has always been a borderland. For centuries it belonged to the Republic of Ragusa, the merchant state of Dubrovnik, which bought it in the fifteenth century from Bosnian nobles. The valley supplied the city with wine, olive oil and food, and its villages kept a strong folk culture, with embroidered costumes, songs and dances that are still performed at festivals and on Sundays in Čilipi. High on a crag above the valley stands Sokol Grad, a fortress built into the rock that guarded the routes from the hinterland and has been restored and opened to visitors.

The riding here has two faces. The main coastal road from Dubrovnik to the border at Debeli Brijeg is busy, especially in summer, with tourist traffic and trucks, and the airport at Čilipi adds to the congestion. The smaller roads through the valley and up into the hills are another matter: narrow, winding, quiet, passing through vineyards, olive groves and stone villages, with views over the sea. The road up towards the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina climbs steeply into bare karst, and the view back over the valley and the coast is superb.

Cavtat, about seventeen kilometres away, is a pretty harbour town with restaurants, cafes and hotels, and it makes a good base. Herceg Novi, just across the Montenegrin border, is the nearest larger town on that side, with fuel and all the services you might need. Remember that crossing between Croatia and Montenegro means an external Schengen border, so allow time for checks in summer. The local wine, especially the indigenous malvasija of Dubrovnik, deserves a glass at the end of the day.
t.cengica bara@43.4,18.4:
Čengića Bara is a high pasture on the plateau around Kalinovik, in the mountainous heart of eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is one of the most remote of the stećci sites listed by UNESCO in 2016. A group of medieval tombstones stands in the open grassland, carved with simple decorations, weathered by centuries of wind, snow and sun. Few visitors make it here, and that is part of the appeal. The stones seem to belong to the landscape itself, as much as the rocks and the grass around them.

The area between Kalinovik, Nevesinje, Gacko and Foča is a land of high plateaus, deep valleys and forested mountains, including Treskavica, Visočica and the wild ranges of Zelengora further east. Shepherds still bring their flocks up to the summer pastures, and the villages are small, scattered and often half empty, a legacy of war and emigration. The light is clear and the air is cool, even in summer, and the silence is broken only by the wind and the bells of the sheep.

Riding here needs preparation. The roads to Kalinovik from Sarajevo, Foča or Nevesinje are mostly paved, but they are narrow, winding and sometimes potholed, and the side roads to the pastures may be gravel or dirt. Distances are longer than they look on the map, and services are very limited. Snow can block the high roads from late autumn to spring, and storms can build quickly on summer afternoons.

There is also a serious practical point. Parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina still have areas contaminated by landmines from the war of the 1990s, especially in remote mountain regions. Stay on paved roads and well-used tracks, do not wander into abandoned fields or ruined buildings, and respect any warning signs, usually red with a skull. Local people can advise on safe routes.

The nearest towns with fuel and supplies are Nevesinje, Gacko and Foča, all around thirty kilometres away, so fill the tank before heading into the mountains. The reward is a landscape that few outsiders ever see, with wide horizons, wildflowers in early summer, and evenings of extraordinary stillness. A simple meal of local cheese, bread and grilled meat in a village kafana tastes better here than almost anywhere else.
t.grcko groblje@43.3,18.9:
Greek cemetery is what the name means, and you will find the same name attached to old graveyards across the mountains of Bosnia and Montenegro. For generations, local people attributed the mysterious carved tombstones of the medieval period to the Greeks, a vague term for ancient or foreign peoples, because nobody remembered who had made them. In fact, these stećci were carved by the medieval communities of the region between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries, and the groups that bear the name Grčko groblje are among the many sites included in the UNESCO listing.

This particular site lies in rugged country near the meeting point of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro, close to Šćepan Polje, where the rivers Tara and Piva join to form the Drina. The landscape is extraordinary: deep canyons, rushing rivers, steep forested slopes and high limestone mountains. Just to the north lies the Sutjeska National Park, with the Perućica forest, one of the last primeval forests in Europe, and Maglić, the highest peak in Bosnia and Herzegovina, right on the border.

For riders, the road through the Piva canyon is the star of the region. Running from Plužine towards Šćepan Polje along the shores of the Piva reservoir, it passes through a long series of rough-hewn tunnels cut into the rock, many of them unlit and narrow, with dramatic views over the turquoise water between them. It is an unforgettable ride, but it demands caution: the tunnels are dark, the surface can be wet and uneven, and oncoming vehicles appear suddenly. Use your lights and take your time.

The Tara and the Drina are famous for whitewater rafting, and there are several rafting camps around Šćepan Polje and Foča, offering food, accommodation and trips down the river in summer. Foča, about nineteen kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, with fuel and services, while Plužine, on the Montenegrin side, has a few shops, restaurants and a petrol station. The border crossing at Šćepan Polje is small and can be slow. Bring your documents, check insurance cover for both countries, and allow time. The weather is mountain weather, with hot days, cold nights and sudden storms.
t.paestum@40.3,15.5:
The name on the ride says Paestum, but the coordinates sit well inland, among the high mountains of the Cilento near Sanza, Rofrano and Monte San Giacomo, and that is worth knowing before you arrive expecting Greek temples. Paestum itself, with its three magnificent Doric temples built by Greek colonists, lies down on the coastal plain south of Salerno, and it is part of a single UNESCO listing that covers the whole Cilento and Vallo di Diano National Park, together with the ancient city of Velia and the Certosa di Padula. This point is in the wild interior of that park, close to Monte Cervati, the highest mountain in Campania.

The Cilento interior is one of the least visited corners of southern Italy, and it is a fine place to ride. The mountains are covered in beech and chestnut forests, with high pastures, limestone cliffs and deep gorges, and the villages cling to hillsides with views over the valleys. The roads are narrow, winding and often empty, with endless bends, steep climbs and descents. The surfaces can be rough, with potholes and loose gravel, and landslides sometimes close roads after heavy rain. Allow plenty of time, because distances are deceptive.

To the north east lies the Vallo di Diano, a wide, flat valley with the great Certosa di Padula, one of the largest monasteries in Italy, with a vast cloister. Sala Consilina, about sixteen kilometres away, is the main town of the valley, with fuel, shops and services. To the south west, the mountains drop towards the coast at Palinuro and Marina di Camerota, with beaches, caves and clear water.

The Cilento is also famous as the place where the American scientist Ancel Keys studied the Mediterranean diet, living for many years in the coastal village of Pioppi. The local food is simple and delicious, based on olive oil, vegetables, legumes, cheese and fresh pasta, with the buffalo mozzarella of the plain around Paestum as a highlight. The villages of the interior are small, with limited services, so carry water and fill your tank in the valley towns before heading into the mountains.
t.mramor in musici@44.1,18.5:
In a meadow near the village of Musići, in the hills around Olovo in central Bosnia, stands a group of stećci, the great carved medieval tombstones that are unique to this part of the Balkans. They date roughly from the twelfth to the sixteenth centuries, and the people who raised them were Bosnian Christians, Catholics and Orthodox alike. The Musići necropolis is part of the group of stećci cemeteries inscribed by UNESCO in 2016, and its stones are among the finest: big slabs and house-shaped blocks decorated with spirals, crosses, vines, hunting scenes and strange, almost abstract human figures.

The setting is pure Bosnian upland. Wooded ridges of beech and pine roll away in every direction, small fields and hay meadows open up around scattered villages, and minarets and church towers appear in the same valleys. Olovo takes its name from the Slavic word for lead, which was mined here from medieval times, and the town is also known for a Marian shrine that draws Catholic pilgrims every summer. The Krivaja river, which cuts a deep green gorge nearby, is beloved of anglers and rafters.

The main road between Sarajevo and Tuzla passes through Olovo and is the logical way in. It is a proper mountain highway, two lanes with long climbs, tight bends in the gorges and plenty of heavy trucks, and surfaces range from good to rough. Overtaking needs patience and good judgement, especially on blind bends. The side roads up towards the villages are narrower and steeper, sometimes with broken tarmac and gravel patches, and in places sheep or cattle claim the road. Autumn is spectacular, when the beech woods turn and the air smells of woodsmoke.

Olovo has petrol stations and a few cafés serving strong Bosnian coffee in little copper pots, and grilled ćevapi are easy to find. Vareš and Kladanj, a bit further out, also have services. Respect the stones: people still regard these fields as burial grounds, and the carved surfaces are fragile. One practical note for the whole region: some hills in Bosnia still carry the risk of landmines from the war of the 1990s, so stick to roads, paths and obviously used ground.
t.historical complex of split with the pal:
Few cities have grown inside a palace, but Split did exactly that. Around the year 300 the Roman emperor Diocletian, born in nearby Salona, built himself a vast fortified retirement residence on the shore of the Adriatic, a rectangle of walls, towers and gates. When Salona was sacked in the seventh century, refugees moved into the palace, and over the following centuries they turned its halls and corridors into streets and houses. The result is a living old town where medieval and Renaissance homes lean on Roman walls and washing hangs between ancient columns.

The heart of it is the Peristyle, a colonnaded courtyard in front of Diocletian's mausoleum, which became the cathedral of St Domnius, named, rather pointedly, after a bishop martyred under the emperor's persecutions. Its bell tower gives a wonderful view over the roofs and harbour. The cellars beneath the palace, used for centuries as a rubbish dump and therefore beautifully preserved, show the plan of the imperial rooms above. Outside the walls, the Riva promenade is the city's living room, and the wooded Marjan peninsula offers shade and swimming coves.

Riding into Split is a test of patience. The approach roads from the motorway and along the coast are busy, with heavy traffic, tight junctions and scooters everywhere, and the old town itself is pedestrian. Park outside the walls and walk. The pay-off comes when you leave: the Jadranska magistrala, the coast road, runs both ways along cliffs and coves, north towards Trogir and Šibenik and south towards Omiš and Makarska, with the islands floating offshore. Ride it early before the summer traffic builds, or in May and October when the light is golden and the heat bearable.

Fuel, mechanics and supplies are everywhere around the city. Food is a joy: grilled fish, black risotto coloured with cuttlefish ink, pašticada stew and the local Plavac Mali wines. Ferries to Brač, Hvar and Vis leave from the harbour, and a bike on an island ferry is a fine way to stretch a ride. In July and August the heat can be brutal in the middle of the day, so carry water and plan the riding around it.
t.cilento and vallo di diano national park:
South of Salerno, past the temples of Paestum, the coast bends out into a great knuckle of mountains, and inland from the beaches the Cilento national park climbs into wooded massifs that most visitors never see. The coordinates sit high in the interior near the villages of Stio, Campora and Moio della Civitella, on the flanks of Monte Gelbison, whose summit sanctuary of the Madonna del Sacro Monte has drawn pilgrims for centuries. The park, together with Paestum, ancient Velia and the Certosa di Padula, is a World Heritage Site, recognised as a cultural landscape shaped by Greek colonists, Lucanian tribes and long monastic tradition.

Velia, on the coast below, was the Greek city of Elea, home to the philosophers Parmenides and Zeno, and it is a strange thrill to walk its stone streets knowing some of Western thought was hammered out here. The interior is a world away: chestnut and beech forests, karst gorges, villages perched on spurs, and terraces of olives and figs. The Cilento's white figs, buffalo mozzarella from the plain near Paestum and simple cooking based on beans, vegetables and olive oil gave rise to a famous study of the Mediterranean diet by the American scientist Ancel Keys, who lived for years at Pioppi on this coast.

The roads are a rider's dream if you like corners. Narrow provincial roads twist up from the coast, stringing together hairpins and switchbacks with drops into deep valleys and views across to the sea. Surfaces vary wildly, from smooth new tarmac to potholes and gravel spilled from landslides, and in places rockfall is a real hazard after storms. Traffic is light outside August, and spring, with wildflowers everywhere, and early autumn are ideal. Mornings bring clear air and sharp mountain views before the afternoon haze.

Down in Vallo della Lucania, six kilometres away, you will find pumps, a pharmacy and a few trattorias. Higher villages may have a bar and not much else, so do not count on fuel in the hills. Stop for a plate of fusilli with ragù or some local cheese, and if you head down to the coast, the beaches around Palinuro and Marina di Camerota offer clear water for a swim after a hot ride.
t.decorated farmhouses of halsingland@61.7:
Farmers in nineteenth-century Hälsingland had money, thanks to flax, timber and good land, and they spent it on houses. Their large wooden farmhouses, many of them painted red with Falun copper-mine pigment, often contained rooms reserved for festivities, decorated by itinerant painters with flowers, biblical scenes and allegories in bright colours. Seven of these farms, including Pallars in Järvsö, Gästgivars in Vallsta and Bommars in Letsbo, were inscribed together by UNESCO in 2012, and stepping into their painted rooms is like entering a folk tale.

The coordinates sit just outside Järvsö, a village in the valley of the Ljusnan river, surrounded by forested hills. It is a popular summer destination, with a ski slope that becomes a mountain biking centre in the warmer months, and the valley is dotted with old farms, meadows and lakes. Moose are common, especially at dawn and dusk, and the forests are full of berries and mushrooms in late summer. In June the nights are short and light, and the long, soft evenings are a joy.

The roads are a mix of smooth tarmac and gravel, with many quiet byways leading to remote farms and lakes. Traffic is light, but watch out for moose and deer, especially at dawn and dusk, and for timber trucks on the gravel roads. The landscape is gently rolling, with forests, fields and lakes, and the views across the Ljusnan valley are lovely. Summer is the season, from June to August, while winter brings snow and cold.

Järvsö itself has a filling station, a grocery and cafés, and Ljusdal, fifteen kilometres up the river, covers anything bigger. Try the local cheese and the cinnamon buns, and perhaps a fika in a café overlooking the river. The farmhouses are still privately owned, and some of them are open to visitors in summer, while others can be seen only from outside; check before visiting.
t.natural and culturo historical region of:
The Bay of Kotor is a drowned river canyon on the Montenegrin coast, a set of linked basins pushed deep into the limestone mountains, and here at its inner reaches, around Risan and Perast, it feels more like a Norwegian fjord than the Adriatic. The mountains drop almost straight into the water, the villages cling to a thin strip of shore, and the light changes the colour of the sea from green to steel to deep blue as the day goes on. The whole region is on the UNESCO list for its natural beauty and the cultural layering of its little towns.

Risan is the oldest settlement on the bay, and the remains of a Roman villa there have some lovely mosaic floors, including a sleeping Hypnos. Perast, a few kilometres on, was a prosperous Venetian sea captains' town in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, with palaces, campaniles and a maritime school that famously trained Russian naval officers for Peter the Great. Off its shore sit two small islands: Sveti Đorđe with its Benedictine monastery and cypresses, and Our Lady of the Rocks, an artificial island built up over centuries by sailors dropping stones and sinking old ships on a reef where an icon was said to have been found.

The road around the bay is narrow, winding and almost always within a metre of the water, which makes it beautiful and stressful in equal measure. In summer it fills with coaches, rental cars and cruise passengers heading for Kotor, and overtaking is pointless. Ride it early in the morning, or in spring or autumn, and it becomes one of the most magical bits of tarmac in the Balkans. Watch for polished surfaces on the bends and pedestrians stepping out of nowhere in the villages.

For something more dramatic, the old serpentine road from Kotor up to Lovćen and Njeguši climbs some twenty-five hairpins above the bay and gives the view everyone photographs. Fuel is available in Risan and Kotor, and Tivat, across the hill, has more choice and the airport. Grilled fish, Njeguši smoked ham and cheese, and a glass of local Vranac red make a fine reason to stop; the cafes along the shore are a pleasant place to watch the boats.
t.the sassi and the park of the rupestrian:
Matera is one of those places where the first view genuinely changes the mood of a day. You walk to the edge of the modern town, look down, and there are the Sassi: two hollows in the limestone filled with houses stacked on top of each other, their roofs serving as streets for the houses above, churches cut into the rock, staircases and alleys tumbling down to the edge of a deep ravine, the Gravina. Across the gorge, the Murgia plateau is riddled with caves and rock churches, some with Byzantine frescoes, used by monks and shepherds for over a thousand years. People have lived in these caves since prehistoric times, which makes Matera one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in the world.

The twentieth century nearly ended that. In 1945 Carlo Levi's book Christ Stopped at Eboli exposed the poverty of the region, and the Sassi, where families lived crowded in caves with their animals, without running water, became a national scandal. In the 1950s the government moved the inhabitants to new housing, and the Sassi were left empty for decades. Then came a long, slow revival: UNESCO listing in 1993, restoration, hotels and restaurants in the caves, and the title of European Capital of Culture in 2019. Film crews love it too; it stood in for Jerusalem in The Passion of the Christ and saw a famous car chase in No Time to Die.

For riders, Matera is a fine base for exploring Basilicata and Puglia, two regions with superb quiet roads. Inland, towards Montescaglioso, Craco's eerie ghost village and the clay badlands called calanchi, the roads twist through empty hills with almost no traffic, though surfaces can be rough and potholed. Towards Puglia, the Murgia plateau has long straight roads through stone walls, wheat fields and masserie, the fortified farmhouses of the south. Summer is hot and dry; spring and autumn are ideal.

Matera has fuel stations, shops and plenty of restaurants. The Sassi themselves are a pedestrian zone, steep and slippery, so park in the upper town. Try the famous bread of Matera, a tall loaf made with durum wheat, crapiata, a legume soup, and peperoni cruschi, crispy fried sweet peppers. In the evening, when the Sassi light up, it is one of the most magical sights in Italy.
t.olovci@44.3,18.6:
In a meadow above the Drinjača valley, a short way from the small town of Kladanj, a group of carved limestone blocks lies scattered among the grass and young trees. These are stećci, the medieval tombstones of Bosnia and the surrounding lands, and Olovci is one of the necropolises listed together by UNESCO as a single heritage site spread across four countries. The stones date roughly from the twelfth to the sixteenth centuries. Some are plain slabs or chests, others shaped like little houses with pitched roofs, and the best of them carry reliefs: spirals, crescent moons, vines, hunting scenes, a figure with a raised hand. Nobody is entirely sure who was buried under them, and the arguments about whether they belonged to Catholics, Orthodox or the Bosnian church have run for a century.

What strikes you on a quiet morning is the setting. The hills around Kladanj are densely wooded with beech and pine, and the air is cool and clean even in high summer. The town is known across Bosnia for its spring water, the Muška voda, which local legend credits with making men stronger, and you will see people filling bottles at the fountain. Beyond the hills, to the east, the land falls away towards the Drina.

The main road through here is the M18 between Sarajevo and Tuzla, which climbs over the hills via Olovo and Kladanj in long, flowing bends, with forest pressing in on both sides. Surface quality is variable: smooth new asphalt can switch suddenly to patches and ruts, and heavy trucks use the route, so overtakes need care. The side roads into the villages are narrow, sometimes gravel, and fun if you take them slowly. Rain makes the forest roads slick with leaves and mud.

One serious practical point: Bosnia still has areas contaminated by mines from the war of the 1990s, and although the main sites are cleared, you should never wander off into unmarked woods or abandoned fields. Stick to paths and tracks that are clearly used. Kladanj, a few kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés where a strong Bosnian coffee in a copper džezva costs very little, and Stupari is closer still for basics. Tuzla to the north is the nearest city if you need anything more serious, from tyres to a proper hotel.
t.capo palinuro@40.1,15.4:
The ride calls it Capo Palinuro, but the coordinates sit a little further east, above the harbour of Scario on the Gulf of Policastro, beneath the bulk of Monte Bulgheria. The cape itself, a rocky headland full of sea caves, lies some way west around the coast, past Marina di Camerota, and both belong to the same wild southern end of the Cilento. The name comes from Virgil: Palinurus was the helmsman of Aeneas, who fell asleep at the tiller, tumbled overboard and washed up on this shore, where he was killed by the locals. His ghost, in the Aeneid, asks for a proper burial, and the cape was named for him.

The Cilento and Vallo di Diano national park is one of the largest in Italy, and its southern coast is its most dramatic. Between Marina di Camerota and Scario lies the stretch called the Costa degli Infreschi, a protected marine area with coves and freshwater springs bubbling up into the sea; there is no road along it, only boats and a coastal footpath. The water is very clear, the rocks are pale limestone and the maquis smells of rosemary and myrtle in the heat. Inland, the Cilento was home to the Greek city of Elea, later Velia, where the philosopher Parmenides was born.

The roads are the reason to come. From Marina di Camerota the road climbs inland through Lentiscosa and over to San Giovanni a Piro, twisting through olive groves and terraces with views across the gulf to the mountains of Basilicata and Calabria. Then it drops in a series of hairpins to Scario. Surfaces can be patchy, and in August the coast fills with Italian holidaymakers, but outside summer you may have whole valleys to yourself. Watch for loose gravel washed onto the road after storms.

San Giovanni a Piro sits on the ridge above and Scario is its little harbour, with a promenade, cafés and seafood restaurants where the catch of the day is the only menu you need. For fuel, the coast road towards Policastro Bussentino and the town of Sapri at the head of the gulf are your best bets. Try the local fusilli, rolled around a knitting needle, and the white figs of the Cilento, dried and stuffed with almonds.
t.the via appia in the upper bradano valle:
The Via Appia, the queen of roads, ran from Rome to Brindisi, and in Basilicata it crossed the upland of the upper Bradano valley, a high, open country of wheat fields and rolling hills, near the towns of Venosa and Palazzo San Gervasio. In 2024 the Via Appia was listed as a World Heritage Site along its whole length, and here, in the empty farmland, the line of the road can be traced in field boundaries and tracks, with occasional fragments of paving and the ruins of way stations.

Venosa, eight kilometres away, was the Roman colony of Venusia, and the poet Horace was born here in 65 BC. The town has a castle, a cathedral and the remarkable Abbey of the Santissima Trinità, an unfinished Romanesque church built on Roman and early Christian foundations, whose open, roofless nave is one of the most atmospheric sites in southern Italy. A Jewish catacomb outside town is among the earliest evidence of Jewish life in the region.

The Vulture, an extinct volcano to the west, is the source of Aglianico del Vulture, one of the finest red wines of the south, and of mineral waters bottled at its foot. Melfi, on its slopes, has a mighty Norman castle where the emperor Frederick II issued his Constitutions of Melfi in 1231.

The riding in this part of Basilicata is a pleasure: empty roads across rolling hills, with long views and gentle bends, and more challenging roads climbing the Vulture and into the mountains to the south. Traffic is very light, surfaces are mostly decent though potholes appear, and the summer heat can be intense on the open plateau. Spring, when the wheat is green, and early autumn are the best times.

Venosa has pumps, cafés and shops, and Palazzo San Gervasio and Maschito are smaller towns with basic facilities. Maschito, interestingly, is one of the Arbëreshë villages of southern Italy, founded by Albanian refugees in the fifteenth century, where an old form of Albanian is still spoken. Local food includes pasta with peperoni cruschi, crisp dried peppers, and lamb.
t.prasuma janj@44.1,17.3:
Prašuma means primeval forest, and Janj is one of the few places in Europe where that word is literally true. In the hills above the Janj river, between Šipovo and Donji Vakuf in central Bosnia, a block of mixed beech, fir and spruce forest has survived without logging, its oldest trees reaching enormous heights and girths. Since 2021 it has been part of the World Heritage site of ancient beech forests of Europe, joining a chain of reserves from the Carpathians to the Pyrenees.

The forest itself is strictly protected and you cannot ride into it, but the surrounding country is wonderful riding territory. Roads climb from the valleys of the Vrbas and Pliva through farmland, meadows and forest onto high plateaus with long views over rolling green hills. The main routes between Jajce, Šipovo, Donji Vakuf and Bugojno are paved, with good curves and modest traffic, though surfaces can be rough and potholed in places. Smaller roads and forestry tracks turn to gravel quickly. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; winters are snowy at altitude, and summer can bring sudden thunderstorms.

The Janj river is a tributary of the Pliva, and both are known for their clarity and their trout. Downstream, the Pliva runs through a series of lakes and old wooden watermills before plunging over a waterfall into the Vrbas in the middle of Jajce, a town crowned by a medieval fortress where the last Bosnian king was crowned. The region carries the scars of the wars of the 1990s, and you may still see damaged buildings. Landmines remain in some remote areas, so stick to roads and marked paths.

The forest is home to brown bears, wolves, lynx and many bird species, including woodpeckers that thrive in the old trees. The dead wood left lying on the ground, which would be cleared in managed forests, supports a huge variety of insects and fungi. Visiting in the early morning, you may hear the forest waking up with a chorus of birdsong.

Donji Vakuf, about nine kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and basic services. Bugojno and Šipovo are larger, with more options for food and accommodation. Try local trout or a hearty Bosnian stew, and expect warm hospitality from people who are often curious about travellers on bikes.
t.stari grad plain@43.2,16.6:
Hvar's best farmland is not on a hillside but on a flat, fertile plain just inland from the town of Stari Grad, and it has been laid out in the same pattern for about twenty-four centuries. Greek settlers from Paros founded a colony called Pharos here in the fourth century BC, and they divided the plain into neat rectangular plots, marked out by dry-stone walls. The walls are still there, the plots still follow the old grid, and the people who farm them today are growing grapes and olives much as their predecessors did. UNESCO listed the plain as a World Heritage site in 2008, and for once the listing is tied to something you can actually walk across.

For a rider, the surprise is how gentle it feels. The island of Hvar is long, narrow and mostly limestone ridge, with its main road, the D116, running along the spine, and the plain is a broad pause in that ridge, with rows of vines, low stone huts and sometimes a farmer on a three-wheeler. The lanes through the fields are narrow, patchy and occasionally gravelly, so ride them slowly and watch for a tractor in the next bend. The big roads are better, with decent asphalt and a few lovely switchbacks as you climb out toward the hills.

Stari Grad itself is a quiet harbour town at the end of a long, narrow bay, and it is the ferry port from Split, which is how most riders arrive on the island with a bike. The bay is sheltered, and in the evening the town smells of grilled fish, wood smoke and cut grass. The nearby towns of Jelsa and Bol give you a few more options for food, and fuel is available in Stari Grad and Jelsa, though in summer the pumps can be busy and it is wise not to run low before a long day on the island.

Hvar is dry, bright and very hot from July to August, so start early, and carry water. The best months for riding are May, June and September, when the light is soft, the sea is warm, and the lavender and wine harvests give the plain its colours. A glass of the local plavac mali, from a vineyard just off the road, is a good way to end the day.
t.bommars@61.9,15.9:
In the forests of Hälsingland, in central Sweden, you find farms that look as though they belong in a fairy tale. Prosperous farmers of the nineteenth century, who made their money from flax and timber, built large, many-roomed farmhouses and decorated their best rooms with paintings, wallpaper and carved details, often in rich reds, blues and golds. Several of these farms, the Hälsingegårdar, were listed by UNESCO in 2012, and others are still in private hands and used as homes. The place named on our list lies in the countryside near Ljusdal, in this farming country.

What is surprising is the size. The farms have separate buildings for dwelling, storage, stables and festivities, arranged around a courtyard, and the best room, the festive hall, was kept for weddings and celebrations. The painted decoration borrows from town fashions and biblical scenes, and was often done by travelling artists. Flax, the crop that paid for all this, produced linen that was sold across Europe, and the wealth it brought is visible in the houses. I cannot tell you details of what is on show at each farm, so check opening times before you go, because many are open only in summer or on certain days.

For a rider the area is good, calm and scenic. The roads run along the Ljusnan river and across low, forested hills, with smooth surfaces, gentle bends and long views over lakes and fields. Traffic is light, and the main risk is wildlife, especially moose, which cross at dusk and dawn and can be lethal to a rider. Reduce your speed in the evening and watch the verges. June to August are the best months, with long light nights, while winter brings snow and ice and is not suitable for most riders.

Ljusdal, sixteen kilometres away, is a town of several thousand with fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes. A fika, a coffee and cinnamon bun, is a ritual you should try, and Swedish rules on open access mean you can usually walk through the forest and pick berries and mushrooms with respect. Fill the tank in Ljusdal before heading deeper into the countryside, because villages are small and distances long.
t.becani@44.3,18.8:
The hills above the Drinjača river in north-eastern Bosnia are covered with beech and oak, and in clearings on the slopes stand the stećci, large limestone tombstones, some shaped like chests and some like gabled roofs, carved with crescent moons, spirals, hands, swords and hunting scenes. Bečani is one of the places where they are found, on the outskirts of the little town of Šekovići, three kilometres away, in the eastern part of the country that is now Republika Srpska.

The stećci were made between about the twelfth and the sixteenth centuries across Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in parts of Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia, by communities of different faiths, and no one knows for certain exactly why the tradition arose here and nowhere else. They are standing memorials in stone, some with writing in Cyrillic describing the dead, and in 2016 a group of the necropolises was inscribed on the World Heritage list. Many are surrounded by long grass and moss, leaning at odd angles under the trees, so that you find them almost by accident. It is a quiet and moving place, and visitors should walk carefully and leave nothing disturbed.

The valley of the Drina and its tributaries carries a heavy memory from the war of the 1990s, and local people do not always speak of it easily. Ride and walk with respect, and ask before photographing people. The reward is a countryside of great beauty, with small farms, haystacks, plum orchards and long, wooded ridges.

As for the road, the minor routes between Šekovići, Vlasenica and Zvornik are narrow, hilly and sometimes in poor condition, with potholes, loose gravel and livestock on the corners. Traffic is light and drivers are used to bikes. Winter brings ice and fog, and the best time is from late April to October, with May and September especially pleasant. The plum orchards blossom white in spring and turn gold in autumn.

Šekovići, with around six thousand people, has fuel and shops, and Vlasenica and Zvornik are larger. Look for a roadside kafana for a strong Bosnian coffee served in a copper pot, grilled ćevapi with onion and soft flatbread, or a slice of burek, a flaky pastry filled with meat or cheese. If someone offers you a glass of rakija, a fiery plum brandy, a polite sip is expected.
t.velika and mala crljivica@43.5,16.9:
Behind the Makarska Riviera the land climbs abruptly into the grey limestone of Biokovo, and on the inland side of that range lies a high, stony plateau called the Dalmatian Zagora, a country of dry-stone walls, thin soil and scattered villages. Velika and Mala Crljivica, the Greater and Lesser Crljivica, sit in this landscape near the small town of Lovreć, about twenty-one kilometres from Omiš and a little further from Imotski, and the site is a field of old tombstones.

They are stećci, the monumental medieval gravestones found across the western Balkans, carved from local limestone between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries. Some are plain slabs and others take the shape of chests or gabled houses, and many bear carved figures of horsemen, deer hunts, rosettes and crescent moons. UNESCO inscribed a group of stećci sites, including some in Croatia, in 2016. They lie scattered in the grass among thorn bushes and rocks, and they feel remote and old. As a rule there is no staff, no ticket booth and often only a small sign, so take care and do not climb on them.

The landscape around is hard and beautiful. The Zagora is a karst country, where rain disappears underground and appears as springs and lakes, such as the famous Blue Lake near Imotski, a sinkhole of green water ringed by cliffs. Fields of grapes, figs and olives are marked out with stone walls, and tiny chapels stand on hilltops. The area makes its own strong wine, Plavac Mali, and prosciutto air-dried in the cold wind, the bora.

On a motorcycle the pleasure is in the descent to the coast. The road from the Zagora to Makarska or Brela crosses the Biokovo range through a long, winding series of hairpins with sweeping views of the islands of Brač and Hvar, and the old road over the mountain is narrow and steep. The new A1 motorway runs through tunnels, with tolls, and carries the heavy summer traffic. Wind can be fierce, with sudden gusts on exposed bends, and in winter ice and snow can close the higher roads. Early summer and September are the best seasons, when the coast is not too crowded.

Lovreć is small, with about nine hundred people, so fill up in Imotski, Omiš or on the coast. Zagvozd has a few cafes. Order a plate of pršut and local cheese in a konoba, and watch for the tourist crowds on the coast.
t.pallars@61.4,16.0:
Hälsingland, a province in central Sweden, is a country of long forested ridges and deep river valleys, and its farms are far from ordinary. Pallars, near the village of Alfta, is one of seven Hälsingland farmhouses inscribed by UNESCO in 2012 as the Decorated Farmhouses of Hälsingland, and it stands in open farmland about six kilometres from the village, with Edsbyn twelve kilometres away and Bollnäs, the main town, about nineteen.

In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the farmers of this region grew rich on flax, which was spun into linen and sold across Europe, and they spent their wealth on their houses. The farms are large and handsome, built in the usual red-painted wood, but inside is a different world. The best rooms, used only for festivals, weddings and visits by distinguished guests, are painted from floor to ceiling with flowers, biblical scenes, garlands and scrolls in bright colours, and hung with painted cloths. Many were decorated by travelling painters, and the style ranges from stiff to joyful. Several of the farms are open to visitors on a seasonal basis, usually in summer and sometimes only by guided tour, so check beforehand.

The scenery is the quiet, open farmland of the Ljusnan valley, with fields, lakes and spruce forest, and the riding is a pleasure, with long, flowing curves, smooth tarmac and almost no traffic. Sweden's speed limits are strictly enforced, with cameras often near villages. Moose and deer are a serious risk, especially at dawn and dusk, so slow down near woodland. Summer days are long and bright, and in June the sun barely sets. Autumn colours are glorious in September, and winters are cold and snowy, with ice on the roads.

Bollnäs has about fourteen thousand people and is the place for fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and Edsbyn, with four thousand, has a few shops. Alfta is smaller. Fika, the Swedish coffee break with a cinnamon bun, is a ritual that you should observe at least once a day, and local specialities include smoked fish, game and the crisp bread baked in this region. Midsummer, in late June, is the biggest festival, with dancing around a pole, and many places are closed.
t.fort of st nikola@43.7,15.9:
Šibenik has the odd distinction of being a Croatian city founded by Croats rather than by the Greeks or Romans who established most of the Adriatic coast, and its old town climbs a hillside above a natural harbour, a maze of stone lanes and stairs. The harbour is approached through a narrow channel from the sea, and the fort of St Nicholas guards the entrance, standing on a small rocky islet. The Venetians built it in the 1540s to protect the city from Ottoman galleys, and it is a remarkable piece of military design, with a triangular plan and walls shaped to deflect cannon fire. UNESCO has listed it among the Venetian Works of Defence of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, together with the defences of Zadar. The fort is reached by boat from the Šibenik waterfront.

The cathedral of St James in the old town is the other great sight. It was built from the 1430s over more than a century, entirely of stone, with no brick or wood, and its dome and vaults are made of carved stone slabs fitted together without mortar. A frieze of seventy-one carved faces runs round the outside of the apse, portraits of ordinary citizens, in expressions ranging from grumpy to cheerful. The architect Juraj Dalmatinac, and later Niccolò Fiorentino, shaped it, and it is among the finest Renaissance buildings on the Adriatic.

The coast road, the old Adriatic highway, runs through Šibenik, with views of islands and the blue water on one side and the grey limestone hills on the other. The riding here is pleasant rather than demanding, with long, easy bends and a mostly good surface. In summer the traffic is heavy, and the bura, a cold, gusty wind from the mountains, can blow in winter and spring with surprising force. Early morning is the best time.

Šibenik has fuel stations, supermarkets and many restaurants, and Vodice, a resort a few kilometres north, is a good place for a swim. The Krka National Park, with its waterfalls, is a short ride inland. Grilled fish and a glass of local white wine are the right lunch, and spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.the appia traiana from aecae to herdonia:
The coordinates drop you on the Tavoliere, the great wheat plain of northern Puglia, a few kilometres from Castelluccio dei Sauri and about fourteen from Foggia. There is nothing here that announces itself. What you have is a long, almost featureless landscape of grain, stubble and the odd masseria, and under it the line of a Roman road. The Via Traiana was commissioned by the emperor Trajan around 109 AD as a faster, drier alternative to the old Appia between Benevento and Brindisi, and the stretch from Aecae to Herdonia is one of the places where you can follow its logic: flat, direct, and aimed at the next town.

Aecae is modern Troia, whose Apulian-Romanesque cathedral and its lacy rose window are worth the detour if the ride allows it. Herdonia is now the archaeological park near Ordona, where the Romans and Hannibal fought more than once during the Second Punic War, and where the later Roman town grew up on the Traiana itself. Rome knew exactly what it was doing when it laid roads across this plain: grain went out, legions came in.

For a rider the Tavoliere is honest rather than thrilling. The roads are straight, the surface is a mixed bag of patched asphalt, and the wind can be genuinely tiresome, a steady crosswind that makes you lean for kilometres. Late spring is the pretty moment, when the wheat turns from green to gold and the poppies run along the verges. By July the land is scorched, the light is flat and white, and the best hours are early morning and the last hour before dusk. In winter, fog sits in the plain and the temperature feels colder than the thermometer says.

Practically, small places like Castelluccio dei Sauri and Ordona will have a bar and probably a pump, but for a reliable fill and a proper meal Foggia is the sensible choice. Foggia is not a pretty city, but it is the capital of the Capitanata and it eats well: look for orecchiette with turnip tops, and bread that has a real crust. The mountains of the Monti Dauni stand to the west like a blue wall, and they are the reason many people end up on this plain in the first place, either coming down from them or heading up.

Stop at the road itself if you can find a clear section. Nothing dramatic, a worn line of stones and a field boundary, but it is quietly a good place to think about the weight of two thousand years of traffic.
t.chincua campanario chivati huacal@19.6,-:
The mountains where Michoacán meets the State of Mexico are cold, high and thickly forested with oyamel fir, and every winter they host one of the great natural spectacles of the continent. The Chincua, Campanario, Chivatí and Huacal sanctuaries are part of the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, a UNESCO site, and they are where millions of monarchs arrive from Canada and the United States after a journey of thousands of kilometres. Nobody has ever fully explained how butterflies that have never seen the place find it, but they do, usually in early November, around the Day of the Dead, which locals link to the souls of the departed.

The butterflies cluster on the fir branches at about three thousand metres, so densely that the boughs bend, and in the cold they hang like dead leaves. When the sun warms the forest at midday they spill into the air in orange clouds, and the sound of their wings has been compared to light rain. The best time to see them is from late January to early March, between about eleven and three in the afternoon, on a sunny day. The final approach to some sanctuaries is on foot or by horse, and visitors must walk quietly and not touch the insects.

Angangueo, the small mining town below, was once a silver and gold producer and has steep narrow streets and old miners' houses. A flood in 2010 hit it badly, and the memory is still part of local life. The approach roads are winding mountain roads, partly paved and partly rough, with fog, potholes and sharp bends, so they are best ridden dry and in daylight. Nights are bitterly cold in winter, so bring serious layers, and rain can make the unpaved parts slippery.

Angangueo and Ocampo have simple accommodations and fuel is limited, so top up in a larger town such as Zitácuaro before climbing. Family kitchens near the sanctuary entrances serve quesadillas, trout and hot corn drinks, and the guides are usually local farmers who earn part of their income from tourism, which is why the butterflies are protected. Out of season, the forest is quiet, cool and fragrant with fir resin.
t.mramorje@44.0,19.4:
Standing stones in Serbia's western hills are not what most visitors expect, but the medieval necropolises called stećci are among the most remarkable monuments in the Balkans. They are big carved tombstones, shaped like chests, slabs or gabled roofs, made between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries across Bosnia, Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia, and decorated with spirals, crescents, hunting scenes and knights on horseback. UNESCO listed a selection of the sites in 2016, and Mramorje, in the municipality of Bajina Bašta, is the Serbian one. The word comes from the old Slavic for standing, and at Mramorje, among the grass and beech trees, the stones lean at slight angles, mossy and weathered.

The country around is spectacular. Bajina Bašta sits on the Drina river, which here has cut a deep green canyon through the mountains, and the long reservoir of Perućac fills part of it. A famous little house stands on a rock in the middle of the river, built by swimmers in the 1960s and rebuilt many times after floods, a wonderfully odd sight. The roads along the Drina twist and turn in tight bends, with sheer drops, tunnels and bridges, and the surface varies from smooth to patched. Traffic is light, apart from trucks and the occasional tractor.

Bajina Bašta, eleven kilometres from the site, is a town of about eight and a half thousand people, with fuel, food and a few small hotels. Ðurići, a village of a thousand people, is closer but has few services, so fill up in Bajina Bašta. Rača Monastery, a short ride away, is a thirteenth-century foundation and one of the most beautiful in Serbia, with a rich history of manuscript copying. Local food is hearty, with grilled meat, kajmak, a creamy dairy spread, and strong plum brandy, rakija.

Plan for mist in the early morning, and for cool nights even in summer. In autumn, the beech forests turn gold and copper, and the river valley fills with mist. Treat the stones with respect. They are graves, and some are very fragile, so do not climb on them. A quiet visit is the best way to honour the people who made them.
t.mramorje@43.9,19.4:
The high country behind the Drina is Tara, a wide, forested mountain that stretches for kilometres, and it holds one of Europe's best-known tree stories. The Serbian spruce, the omorika, is a tall, narrow conifer that once grew across much of Europe, before the ice ages squeezed it into a tiny range on the Drina's slopes. It survived here, and Tara National Park protects it, along with a rich forest of fir and beech, brown bears, chamois and wolves. A second Mramorje stands in this landscape, a village scatter of stećci near the settlement of Musići, a medieval graveyard with large carved stones leaning in the grass and half buried by moss.

The riding here is a joy for those who like quiet, winding mountain roads.
