The route climbs from the river in long bends through forest, with occasional hairpins and wide views over folded green ridges, and the surface is a mixture of good asphalt and patched sections. Weather in the mountains changes fast, and mist can drop in summer, so pack a waterproof. Autumn colours are glorious, and spring brings fresh green. Summer weekends are busy with visitors heading for the lakes and viewpoints, but on weekdays you may have the road almost to yourself.

Fuel needs a plan. Ðurići, a few kilometres away, has about a thousand people and probably little more than a small shop, and Bajina Bašta, seventeen kilometres off, is the proper town for stations, workshops and food. Fill up there before heading up the mountain, and carry some water and a snack. Along the way, village houses sell honey, jam and cheese, and the generous hospitality of western Serbia often means you will be offered coffee and a glass of something stronger.

Stop at one of the lookouts above the canyon, if the weather allows. The view across the Drina gorge is magnificent, with the river a green ribbon far below and the forest dark on the cliffs. Tara has its own kind of silence, deep and resinous, and it holds the sound of your engine for a long moment after you switch it off.
t.split@43.5,16.4:
Split began as a retirement home. The Roman emperor Diocletian, born nearby, built a vast fortified palace on this peninsula around the year 300 and retired here after abdicating, to grow cabbages, so the story goes. After the Roman world fell apart, refugees from the nearby city of Salona sheltered inside its walls, and over the centuries the palace turned into a town. Today you walk through the Golden Gate, the Peristyle and the old cellars, and find cafés, shops, apartments and washing lines inside what is, effectively, a Roman building, with the emperor's mausoleum converted into a cathedral. UNESCO lists the palace and the historic centre.

Split is the largest city on the Croatian coast, so it feels like a real place, with a working port, football crowds, a busy market and ferries to the islands of Brač, Hvar and Šolta. The seafront promenade, the Riva, is the place to take an evening coffee, and the wooded hill of Marjan to the west is a pleasant green lung with paths and views.

For riders the city is a base and a junction. The Adriatic Highway, the D8, runs south along the coast toward Omiš and the Makarska Riviera, with the Biokovo mountains behind, and north toward Trogir and Šibenik. It is a good road, with fine coastal views and a lot of curves, but in summer the traffic is heavy and slow, and a sudden burst of wind, the bura, can hit hard on exposed sections. Inland, the road up to Klis fortress and the mountain roads beyond give a different feel, with dry stone walls and karst.

Everything you need is here, from fuel stations to tyre fitters and big supermarkets. Parking in the centre is hard, and the old town is pedestrian only, so use a garage or the lots by the port. Summer is hot and crowded, and May, June and September are more comfortable. Eat grilled fish, black risotto, or a plate of pršut and cheese, and try the local sweet wines. Have your passport handy for the ferries and, if you cross into Bosnia on the coast near Neum, for the border checks.
t.dubrovnik@42.7,18.1:
Dubrovnik was once an independent republic, called Ragusa, and it lasted for centuries by being clever. It was a small city-state that paid tribute to bigger powers, traded with everyone, banned slavery early, and kept a splendid ring of walls that still surrounds the old town. Walking the walls, about two kilometres of stone with towers and bastions, takes an hour or two, and offers views over terracotta roofs and a glittering sea. In 1991 and 1992 the city was shelled during the Yugoslav war, and the damage has been repaired, though a few signs remain. UNESCO added it to its list in 1979.

The old town is closed to traffic, and it is lovely in the early morning and the evening, when the stone glows and the crowds thin out. In summer the cruise ships dock and the main street, the Stradun, is full, so go at dawn or after dark. Take the cable car to Srđ for the best view, and for a reminder of how steep the hills are behind the city.

The riding in the area is exceptional. The Adriatic Highway, which runs high above the old town, has views of the walls and islands, and the road south toward Cavtat and the Montenegrin border winds above the sea. North, the road follows the coast to Ston and the Pelješac peninsula, and since 2022 a bridge links the peninsula to the mainland, bypassing the short stretch of Bosnian coast at Neum so the border checks there no longer interrupt a ride. Traffic is slow in July and August, and the heat and glare are strong. Spring and autumn are the best times.

The city has fuel stations at the edge of town, parking garages near the old town, and a full range of food. Local specialities include black risotto, oysters from Ston, and rozata, a caramel custard. Prices are high in season, and rooms should be booked well ahead. Be careful on the polished stone of the old town in wet weather, and note that speed cameras and traffic police are active on the coastal road.
t.kotor@42.4,18.8:
The Bay of Kotor looks like a fjord but is really a drowned river canyon, a series of linked basins surrounded by limestone mountains that rise nearly straight from the water. Kotor itself sits at the innermost end, a walled town tucked under a steep cliff, with a fortress that climbs the slope behind it in a zigzag line of walls. It was a Venetian possession for centuries, and its narrow lanes, stone churches and small squares have kept their medieval layout. The Cathedral of St Tryphon, from the twelfth century, is the main landmark, and cats are everywhere, as the town's unofficial mascots.

The climb to the fortress takes about an hour on steps, past a small church halfway up, and rewards you with the best view of the bay. Go early or late, since midday is hot and cruise ship groups arrive in numbers. In the evening the lights come on across the water, and the town takes on a quiet, theatrical charm.

For riders, this is among the great roads of the Balkans. The Adriatic Highway comes down the coast from Dubrovnik and winds around the bay, passing through villages with stone houses, little harbours and old churches. A short ferry runs between Kamenari and Lepetane at the mouth of the bay, saving time. From Kotor, a famous mountain road climbs the Lovćen range in around twenty-five hairpins, to a pass with views of the bay below and then on to the old royal capital Cetinje. The tarmac is fair, the bends are tight and narrow, and large buses sometimes block the corners, so patience helps. The best months are May, June, September and October.

Kotor has a small population but good services, with fuel stations around the bay and nearby Tivat, restaurants serving seafood, and a market outside the walls. The old town is pedestrian only, with parking outside the gates. In summer, thunderstorms can roll over the mountains with little warning, and winter brings rain and fog. Keep passports and vehicle papers handy, and remember that Montenegro uses the euro. Try the local cured ham from Njeguši, the village along the Lovćen road, and a glass of Vranac red.
t.radimlja@43.1,17.9:
Above the Bregava river valley, a few kilometres from Stolac in Herzegovina, a hillside is covered with huge stone slabs that look like sarcophagi and tilting boxes. These are stećci, medieval tombstones that were carved in Bosnia, Herzegovina, Serbia, Croatia and Montenegro between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries, and Radimlja is the best known cemetery of them. Over a hundred of them stand here, and several carry reliefs of exceptional quality, showing hunting scenes, riders with spears, dancing in a circle, stylised crescent moons, spirals and vines. In 2016 UNESCO listed a group of these sites together.

Who made them is a question of much debate. People used to link them to the Bosnian Church, sometimes called Bogomil, but modern scholarship shows that Catholics and Orthodox Christians were buried under them too, and that they were a regional fashion among all communities. What is certain is that the carvers were skilled and that the hillside was a place the living chose to commemorate their dead. The weather has been kind in places and cruel in others, and some of the stones are covered in lichen.

The setting is classic Herzegovina, with dry limestone hills, vineyards, fig trees and pomegranates, the Bregava running clear and green. The roads from Mostar and from Čapljina to Stolac are decent and quiet, with gentle curves and good views, and in the cooler season they are a delight. Surfaces are generally paved, though patched, and there is some goat traffic. Summers are fiercely hot and dry, with a strong sun, so aim for spring or autumn, and go early or late in the day.

Stolac, about three kilometres away, is a small town of some seven thousand with fuel, cafés, and a little old quarter, and a good place for a coffee, grilled meat, or a slice of burek. Čapljina and Mostar offer more services, and Mostar is about forty kilometres to the north, with its famous reconstructed bridge. The area was badly damaged in the 1990s war, and some buildings still show scars. Entry to the necropolis is typically free, but facilities are minimal, so bring water and a hat. Carry vehicle papers and a green card for border crossings in the region.
t.zadar@44.1,15.2:
Alfred Hitchcock is supposed to have said that Zadar has the most beautiful sunset in the world, and the people of the town have taken him at his word. The city sits on a narrow peninsula on the Dalmatian coast, with the sea on three sides and the island of Ugljan across the channel, and the sun drops into the water in a long fire of orange and pink. The best place to watch is the waterfront promenade at the end of the old town, where a pair of modern works of art, the Sea Organ and the Greeting to the Sun, turn the shoreline into an instrument and a light show.

The Sea Organ, designed by the architect Nikola Bašić and opened in 2005, uses pipes under the marble steps that are played by the waves, producing a low, shifting chord that never quite repeats. People sit on the steps with their feet near the water and listen as the light goes. It is oddly moving, and it brings the whole town to the shore every evening.

Zadar is also an ancient place, with a Roman forum, a round pre-Romanesque church called Saint Donatus, built in the ninth century from stones taken from the forum, and a long, long tradition of making maraschino, a cherry liqueur that was once the town's great export. Everything is within a short walk, along marble-paved lanes closed to traffic.

For riders, Zadar is a stop on the Adriatic Highway, known to Croats as the Magistrala, which runs for hundreds of kilometres along the coast, with views of islands, limestone cliffs and a very blue sea. North of Zadar the road crosses the Maslenica bridge and runs under the Velebit mountains, where the bora wind can blow hard enough to close the road to motorcycles. Check conditions on windy days. Summer traffic can be heavy, with campervans and queues in the villages, so early starts are rewarded.

With seventy-one thousand people, Zadar has plenty of fuel and food, and fish restaurants near the harbour. Parking in the old town is limited, so use a car park outside the walls.
t.defensive system of zadar@44.1,15.2:
Zadar spent much of its life on the front line, and its walls prove it. Once the chief city of Venetian Dalmatia, it stood on the border between the Republic of Venice and the Ottoman Empire, and in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries the Venetians turned it into one of the strongest fortress towns in the Adriatic. The ramparts, bastions and gates that survive are part of the Venetian Works of Defence between the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, a group of sites across Italy, Croatia and Montenegro that UNESCO inscribed in 2017.

The best known gate is the Land Gate, designed by the Veronese architect Michele Sanmicheli and finished in the 1540s, a triumphal arch in stone with the winged lion of Venice above the central opening. Inside the walls, the old town is a maze of narrow lanes, and beyond the gate lies the Citadel and a huge moat that has been turned into a park. The Five Wells Square, near the walls, is named for the cistern that supplied the city during sieges and which still stands, its five stone wellheads in a row.

Walking the ramparts at dusk is a good way to feel the place. The stone is warm underfoot, the sea sparkles beyond the harbour, and the fishing boats come home. The walls have survived earthquakes, sieges, bombing in the Second World War and a good deal of neglect, and they still enclose a living town where people hang washing from the windows and drink coffee at pavement tables.

Zadar lies on the Adriatic Highway, and the roads in and out are busy in summer. The coast road north and south is a rewarding ride with sea views, but be aware of the bora wind in winter and spring, which can strike with little warning. Parking near the walls is tight, so park outside the old town and walk in.

With seventy-one thousand people, Zadar has plenty of fuel, shops and restaurants. Try the local fish and a plate of Pag cheese with olive oil, and finish with a small glass of maraschino.
t.the trulli of alberobello@40.8,17.2:
Alberobello is a town of grey stone cones, with some fifteen hundred of them, called trulli, packed into two hillside districts, Rione Monti and Aia Piccola. The roofs are built from flat limestone slabs laid dry, without mortar, in overlapping rings until the cone closes at the top, and many of them carry a whitewashed symbol painted on the roof, some Christian, some older and more mysterious. UNESCO listed the town in 1996.

The story told to visitors is that the trulli could be dismantled quickly to hide from the tax inspectors of the Kingdom of Naples, who taxed settled houses. It is a good tale, but historians doubt it. What is certain is that the district's peasants were using a very old technique of dry stone building that still crops up across the Itria valley, in field shelters and sheepfolds, and that Alberobello grew into a dense warren of them in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

You need to see it early or late. By eleven in the morning, tour coaches are arriving and the alleys are lined with souvenir stalls selling everything from lace to olive oil, and a cheap version of the town fills the main street. At dawn, or in the evening when the cones turn grey-gold, the place is quiet and genuinely strange, like a settlement for hobbits who had studied geometry.

The riding in the Itria valley is among the gentlest in Italy. The roads wander between whitewashed hill towns, Locorotondo, Martina Franca and Cisternino, past old olive trees, almond orchards and vineyards on red earth. The surface is generally good, the corners easy, and the traffic in the evening light is kind. Spring brings flowers and a fresh green on the dry-stone walls, and summer is hot, so start early. Locorotondo, a few kilometres away, makes a white wine of the same name that is a perfect companion to the local food.

Fuel is easy: Alberobello itself has pumps on its ring road, and Locorotondo and Martina Franca have more. For food, look for orecchiette with turnip tops, burrata from the nearby farms, and a plate of grilled lamb in the town's trattorias. Park outside the old districts and walk the lanes.
t.museo storico@40.8,17.2:
A museum in a trullo sounds like a joke, but the Museo Storico in this part of Apulia belongs to a landscape where almost everything is a stone cone, and it makes sense to treat it as the doorway to the countryside rather than a single building. The ride this point belongs to leads north-west to Castel del Monte, the strange octagonal castle that the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II raised on a hill in the thirteenth century, with eight towers and no moat, no drawbridge and no obvious military purpose.

The route crosses the Murge, the limestone upland that forms the heel of Italy's spine, where the soil is thin and red and the land is a patchwork of stone walls. This is a karst country: rain disappears underground, so there are few rivers and plenty of caves, and the farmers built the dry-stone walls from the stones they cleared from their fields. Olive trees, some of them centuries old, spread their silver crowns over the fields, and almond blossom in February turns the slopes white.

Riding here rewards a slow pace. The roads are mostly well maintained but narrow, and farm machinery can come around any bend. Villages such as Locorotondo, Cisternino and Martina Franca have steep, whitewashed lanes and baroque churches, and make good stops for coffee. The wind off the Adriatic can be strong, and the summer sun hits hard at midday, so plan the ride for morning and evening. Autumn brings the olive harvest and the first cool air, and is perhaps the best season.

Fuel is easy in this area, since Alberobello and Locorotondo are both towns of several thousand people with pumps along the main roads. Fill the tank before leaving the main valley if you are heading onto the Murge, where villages are further apart.

If you can, finish the day with a plate of orecchiette and a glass of Primitivo in the Itria valley. Frederick would have liked it, since he was a man who enjoyed hunting, falcons and a good table.
t.monarch butterfly biosphere reserve@19.6:
Between November and March, the fir forests on the mountains of central Mexico turn orange. Millions of monarch butterflies, which have flown some four thousand kilometres from Canada and the northern United States, cluster on the oyamel firs at about three thousand metres, hanging in dense clusters that bend the branches. In the warmth of the sun they open their wings and fly, and the air fills with soft movement, a sound like rain falling on leaves. Nobody knows exactly how they find the place, since the generation that arrives has never made the trip before, and the mystery adds to the wonder. The Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, on the border of Michoacan and the State of Mexico, protects the wintering grounds and was listed as a World Heritage site in 2008.

Cerro Pelon, one of the sanctuaries on the ride, is a steep walk or a horse ride from the village, and at that altitude the air is thin and cold, so take your time. The visit has to be on foot, and local guides lead groups to the colonies. The best time to see the butterflies in flight is on a sunny late morning between January and early March. Logging, a threat for years, has been restricted, but the forest remains under pressure, and local communities have found income in guiding.

The road in is half the day. From Aculco, you cross hills and valleys of farmland and then climb into the mountains, with narrow roads, hairpins, fog and sudden showers. Michoacan roads can be broken in places, and trucks carrying timber and produce share the narrow bends. Take warm clothing: it can be near freezing at the sanctuaries at dawn, and wet and windy in the afternoons. The old mining town of Angangueo, nearby, has colourful streets and small restaurants.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Small towns on the way, like San Nicolas Guadalupe, have little in the way of services, and the bigger town of Zitacuaro, on the main road, has stations and hotels. In the villages near the reserve, you will find simple lodgings and kitchens serving tortillas, beans, trout and fresh cheese. Keep your distance from the butterflies and avoid touching them: their wings are fragile, and a crowd makes it harder for them to rest.
t.sibenik@43.7,15.9:
Šibenik is one of the few Croatian Adriatic towns not founded by the Greeks or Romans but by Croats, first mentioned in the eleventh century, and it still has the feel of a place that grew from the hillside rather than from a plan. It climbs steeply from a natural harbour, protected by the long channel of St Anthony, with stone houses, steps and lanes arranged like a staircase up to the fortress of St Michael. At the foot of the slope stands the Cathedral of St James, a UNESCO-listed building constructed entirely of stone, without any binding material, between the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Its dome is a vaulted shell of carefully fitted slabs, and a frieze of seventy-one carved faces runs around the apses, said to be portraits of ordinary townspeople.

You reach Šibenik along the Adriatic Highway, the old D8, which runs down the coast from Zadar toward Split. The road is a ribbon of rocky hills on one side and blue water on the other, with views of islands, headlands and the Kornati archipelago in the distance. It is a good riding road but not an empty one, because in summer it is full of campervans, coaches and holiday cars, and overtaking requires patience. The surface is usually decent, curves are long and gentle, and the bura wind, a cold gust that comes down from the mountains, can be severe in winter and sometimes closes parts of the coast road to motorbikes.

The Pinery is a leafy suburb on the high plains south of Denver, in Douglas County, close to the town of Parker and the road known as Parker Road, Highway 83, which runs south toward Colorado Springs. At about 1,800 metres, the land here is already high, rolling and open, with ponderosa pines on the ridges and grass in the hollows, and the mountains of the Front Range stand on the western horizon like a long blue wall. It is a landscape that feels transitional, with the plains giving way to the foothills.

A few kilometres south, Castlewood Canyon State Park preserves a small canyon cut by Cherry Creek, with red-brown cliffs, pines and the broken remains of an old dam. The dam failed in 1933 after heavy rain, sending a wall of water down Cherry Creek into Denver and causing serious damage and loss of life, and the ruins stand as a reminder of the power of floods in this dry country. The park has hiking trails, rock climbing and a pleasant picnic area, and it is a good place for a short stop.

Highway 83 is the old road between Denver and Colorado Springs, a two-lane highway that climbs and falls across the Palmer Divide, a ridge that forms a watershed between the Platte and Arkansas rivers. It is a popular road with riders, with decent curves, long views and a fair amount of traffic, and the weather on the divide is changeable, with storms, hail and snow possible even in spring and autumn. Wind can be strong and gusty. Heading south on a weekend morning, you meet many cyclists, so share the road.

Fuel and food are plentiful, since The Pinery has about ten thousand people and Parker next door has many more, with stations, bakeries and diners along the main roads. Fill the tank and eat well here, because the next stretch, toward Pikes Peak and the canyon of the South Platte, has fewer options. In summer, thunderstorms start by early afternoon, so start early. The light on the mountains at dawn is a good reason to be on the road. Bring layers, because the temperature can vary by twenty degrees between the plains and the mountains.
t.sedlo pass@43.1,19.0:
Sedlo means saddle, and this one, at 1,907 metres, is the high point of the road that circles the Durmitor massif in the north of Montenegro. The road climbs through forest and then through bare limestone country, where the trees thin out and the ridges seem to catch the sky, and at the top, a pass opens to a view of Bobotov Kuk, the highest peak of the range at 2,523 metres, with its grey cliffs streaked with snow. The air is thin, clean and cold, and the silence is broken only by wind and the bells of sheep.

Durmitor National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1980, covers a wild mix of glacial lakes, pine forests and deep canyons, including the Tara, whose gorge is up to thirteen hundred metres deep, among the deepest in Europe. The town of Zabljak, ten kilometres from here, is the highest in the Balkans at about 1,450 metres, and a base for hikers in summer and skiers in winter. Close by, the Black Lake, a glacial pool ringed by pines, is a pleasant spot for a walk.

Shepherds have used the high pastures for centuries, moving their flocks up in summer and living in simple wooden huts called katuns, and you may see them by the road. Cheese, smoked ham and kajmak, a rich, salty cream, are the local foods, served with fresh bread and a glass of rakija, the plum brandy. A meal in a village inn here is simple and filling, and the hospitality is warm. Ask what is fresh, and be prepared for large portions.

The road over Sedlo is paved but narrow, with tight bends, steep sections and patches of broken tarmac. There are few barriers, and the drops are real. Sheep, cows and horses wander across, so slow down on blind corners. In winter and early spring, snow closes the pass, and even in June, patches of ice may linger in shaded gullies. Fuel is available in Zabljak, which has about two thousand people, but the larger town of Niksic, thirty-seven kilometres away, has more choice, so fill the tank beforehand. Weather changes quickly, with fog and sudden storms, so carry rain gear and layers. The best time to ride is from late June to September, with clear mornings and quiet roads.
t.ivan sedlo@43.7,18.0:
Ivan Sedlo is a mountain saddle at about 970 metres in the Dinaric Alps of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the old road between Sarajevo and Mostar, and it is also a divide. Water that falls on the southern slopes runs toward the Neretva and the Adriatic, and water on the northern side runs into the Bosna and eventually the Black Sea. The pass sits in beech and pine forest, with cool air and a clear view across the folded ridges, and in winter it is a place of heavy snow.

The pass has a notable railway history. When the Austro-Hungarian Empire took over Bosnia in 1878, it built a narrow-gauge line between Sarajevo and Mostar, an extraordinary piece of engineering that crossed the Ivan with a rack-and-pinion section, so that locomotives could haul trains up the steep slopes. The line closed in the 1960s, and a new motorway has since bypassed the pass with tunnels, but remains of the old line, along with tunnels and viaducts, can still be found in the forest. Railway enthusiasts come to trace them.

For a rider, the older road over the Ivan is a lovely, quiet alternative to the motorway, with long, fluid bends climbing through forest and a surface that is patchy but mostly rideable. The traffic is light, since most vehicles now use the tunnel, so you often have the pass to yourself. In summer the temperature is cool and fresh, while in late autumn and winter, ice and fog make it dangerous. Take care on the descent, where potholes and loose stones appear on the sharper bends.

Nearby, Konjic is a pleasant town on the Neretva, known for its old stone bridge and for a secret nuclear bunker that Yugoslavia built for Tito and his military leaders. It is now open to visitors, a vast underground complex carved into the mountain, and it is a striking piece of Cold War history. Just north, the area around Pazarić is rural and green, and the road is dotted with small farms selling honey, cheese and plums.

Fuel is available in Konjic, about twelve kilometres from the pass on the southern side, and in the larger towns around Sarajevo on the north. There is little on the pass itself, though roadside stands sometimes sell local products. Remember to carry cash in convertible marks, because small places do not always accept cards, and be prepared to share the road with cattle.
t.strbacki buk@44.7,16.0:
The Una River in western Bosnia is one of the clearest rivers in Europe, an extraordinary emerald-green stream that runs through limestone country in a succession of pools, rapids and waterfalls. Štrbački Buk is the most dramatic of these, a broad staircase of cascades where the river drops over a wide barrier of travertine, the mineral deposit built up over thousands of years by the water itself. The roar is audible long before you arrive, and the spray cools the air.

The falls lie within Una National Park, which Bosnia and Herzegovina established in 2008, close to the border with Croatia. The park protects the river, the canyon and the surrounding forest, with trails, viewing platforms and a small visitor centre. You can walk along the river for a few minutes from the car park to a platform just above the main drop, and in the warm months people swim in some of the pools. The water is cold and astonishingly clear, and the colour changes from turquoise to jade with the light.

The Una is also a rafting and canoeing river, and in summer there are organised trips on the calm stretches above and below the falls. An annual regatta of canoes and kayaks attracts paddlers from several countries. The valley has a wild, gentle character, with old watermills, orchards and small farms, and the people are famously hospitable. You may be offered coffee, plum brandy or a plate of grilled meat, and it is polite to accept at least the coffee.

The ride from Bihać is a pleasant country road, winding through villages and low hills, with a surface that is generally acceptable but patchy in places. Traffic is light, and animals, including dogs, cattle and the occasional horse, sometimes wander onto the road. It is worth remembering that this area saw heavy fighting in the war of the 1990s, and warnings about unexploded mines remain in some rural areas. Stay on marked roads and paths and do not wander into overgrown land.

For fuel, Bihać, about twenty-one kilometres away, is the nearest large town and has several stations, banks and supermarkets. Orašac, the nearest village, is smaller. At the falls there is a cafe and a restaurant serving fresh trout, and food is cheap by European standards. Early morning, before the day visitors arrive, is when the light is best and the river seems to belong to you.
t.martin brod@44.5,16.1:
Martin Brod is a quiet village at the upper end of the Una, close to where Bosnia meets Croatia, and it is the place where the river first shows what it can do. Here the Una flows through a short canyon, tumbles over a series of waterfalls and passes the remains of old watermills, built beside the water so that the stream could turn the stones. Some of the mills are still standing, with wooden wheels and moss-covered roofs, and a few are in use.

The village is small and rural, with a handful of houses, a monastery church and a bridge over the river. The Orthodox monastery of Martin Brod stands on the bank, a modest complex with a simple church that reflects the long Serbian Orthodox presence in the region. Its quiet cloister and garden are a gentle place to rest, and visitors are welcome if they are respectful and cover their shoulders and knees. The surrounding landscape is wooded karst, with limestone rocks, caves and sinkholes, and the river often disappears underground and re-emerges elsewhere.

The ride to Martin Brod is a long, quiet backroad from Bihać or from the south, and it is more of an exploration than a speed run. The surface varies, from reasonable asphalt to patches of broken tarmac, and sections of the road are narrow, with blind corners and livestock. The bends are open and sometimes rough, and the scenery is beautiful, with the river in the valley and the forested hills above. Traffic is almost non-existent, so you can take your time.

The region has a complicated history. During the war of 1992 to 1995, the upper Una valley was a front line, and the villages suffered heavily. Many people left, and the population is still low, so the sense of emptiness that you feel is a result of that history as well as the rural economy. Warnings about landmines are still posted in some areas, and it is essential to stay on roads and established paths.

Services are very limited. Orašac is about sixteen kilometres away and Bosansko Grahovo, a larger town about thirty-nine kilometres from here, is the practical place for fuel and supplies. Bihać is farther but offers much more. Carry cash and water, and plan your fuel carefully. A coffee in a village cafe, if one is open, will be strong, sweet and unhurried.
t.crystal reservoir@38.9,-105.0:
Not many reservoirs cost an entry fee for the road, but then not many are on the way up a fourteen-thousand-foot mountain. Crystal Reservoir sits in a granite bowl partway up the Pikes Peak Highway, a small, still lake edged with spruce, with the slopes of the peak rising behind. It is the first place on the climb where the world feels properly alpine, and a good moment to take a breath, check the weather, and look at what the sky is planning.

The road itself is a famous one, nineteen miles of switchbacks and sweeping granite country that runs from Cascade up to 14,115 feet. It has been fully paved only since the early 2010s, which cheers motorcyclists and disappoints people who liked the gravel. Below the reservoir the bends are tight and well banked, through aspen and pine; above, the trees thin and the road gets steeper and more exposed. The speed limit is modest, rangers watch, and they will check your brakes and temperature on the way down. It is a road to savour, not an apex hunt. Mornings are best: afternoon thunderstorms are routine and lightning on an exposed peak is no joke.

History runs deep here. Zebulon Pike never climbed the mountain that bears his name, but gold miners and tourists did, and a carriage road led to the summit in the nineteenth century. In 1893 the poet Katharine Lee Bates climbed up and found the view that inspired America the Beautiful. The Pikes Peak hill climb, the Race to the Clouds, has run since 1916, and every summer the road becomes a testing ground for fast cars and bikes. Cascade, at the foot, is a small place with a few shops, and the Pikes Peak toll gate sits just above it.

Woodland Park, about eight kilometres away, has petrol and cafes, and Colorado Springs is down the hill. Fill up before the toll gate. Pack a jacket, because the temperature at the top can be thirty degrees colder than at the bottom, and bring water. It is a calm place, even on a busy day.
t.parc national de dzanga ndoki car@2.9,16:
In the extreme south-west corner of the Central African Republic, where the forest runs on into Cameroon and Congo, the Sangha river sweeps past a national park that protects one of the last great blocks of Congo Basin rainforest. Dzanga-Ndoki is part of the Sangha Trinational, a World Heritage area shared by three countries, and it is one of the few places on Earth where you can sit in the forest and watch elephants and gorillas in the open.

That opportunity is Dzanga Bai, a big clearing in the forest, where mineral-rich water brings forest elephants, sometimes more than a hundred at once, together with buffalo, bongo antelope and a good deal of noise. Nearby, researchers and trackers have habituated western lowland gorillas to human visitors over many years, so that small groups can be approached with great care. The forest is thick, hot, humid and full of sound, and a walk in it, with the scent of leaf mould and the chirp of insects, is unlike any other.

Riding is another matter. The roads in this part of the country are laterite tracks, often poorly maintained, passing through logging concessions and small villages, with deep ruts in the wet season, from roughly May to October, and choking dust in the dry months. Bayanga, the village that serves the park, lies far from the capital Bangui, and the journey to it is long. The wider security situation in the Central African Republic is difficult, and many governments advise against travel to parts of the country, so anyone thinking of going must research current advice and arrange transport and permits with the park's management and local operators, not on impulse.

The forest has been home for many generations to the BaAka, hunter-gatherers who know the plants, animals and paths intimately and often work as trackers and guides. Their songs, particularly the polyphonic singing that weaves voices together without a leader, are among the most remarkable in the world. The logging industry has also shaped the area, and conservation in Dzanga-Ndoki is balanced against these economic realities.

As for fuel and supplies, the nearest dependable source is thin and distant, so everything has to be carried or arranged in advance. Take medical supplies, malaria protection, a water filter and cash in Central African francs. Follow your guides, and respect the animals' distance.
t.adelaide@-34.9,138.6:
Adelaide is one of the neatest cities in Australia, laid out in 1837 by Colonel William Light on a grid of wide streets, squares and a ring of parklands that still wraps the centre like a green belt. Unlike most Australian colonies, South Australia was settled by free emigrants rather than convicts, and the city has long had a reputation for being quietly civilised, with good food, many festivals, and a relaxed pace. The Torrens river runs through the centre, the Adelaide Hills rise to the east, and the Gulf St Vincent lies to the west.

For a motorcyclist, the city's best feature is how close the good roads are. Within twenty minutes of the centre you can be on the climbs of the Adelaide Hills, through bends shaded by gum trees, with views back over the plain to the sea. Gorge Road, following the Torrens Gorge, is a favourite, and the Chain of Ponds and the roads toward Birdwood have a good flow. The Barossa Valley, famous for its Shiraz, lies about an hour north-east, and the Clare Valley, with its Riesling and old stone villages, a bit further beyond. Spring, from September to November, and autumn, from March to May, are best. Summer can be fiercely hot, with bushfire risk in the hills, and total fire ban days can restrict activity, so check conditions.

Culture is easy to find. Hahndorf, in the hills, was settled by German Lutheran immigrants in 1839 and still has the look of a Prussian village, with bakeries and beer halls. The Barossa has the same heritage, with its Lutheran churches, sausages and rye bread. Back in the city, the Central Market, one of the largest undercover fresh produce markets in the southern hemisphere, is a great breakfast stop, where you can eat coffee, pastries, cheese and olives while the stallholders do their morning shouting. Adelaide is also well known for its pie floater, a meat pie floating in thick pea soup, a strange and loved local invention.

Practicalities are never a problem in a city of over a million. Fuel is available on every main road, including twenty-four-hour stations, and there are plenty of motorcycle shops and repair services. Kangaroos can be a hazard on country roads at dawn and dusk, so keep your speed down when the light fades. Carry water in summer, and remember that mobile coverage thins out in some of the more remote valleys.
t.zlatibor@43.7,19.7:
Zlatibor is a high, rounded upland in western Serbia, a plateau of meadows and pine forest that has been a holiday place for generations. The name means gold pine, and the old landscapes here were a mix of open pasture and clumps of fir and spruce, with a mild, sunny climate that made it popular with city people looking for fresh air. Today the main village has grown into a resort town, with new hotels, apartments and a long pedestrian centre, but the surrounding hills remain green and open.

The area has its own traditions. Kajmak, a clotted cream, and pršuta, dry-cured ham, are famous here, and the local roast lamb and pork are sold at roadside stalls by the side of the road. Užice ham is among the best known in the country. Zlatibor is also known for a type of woollen jersey, and for village houses with steep shingled roofs. Nearby, the old village of Sirogojno is an open-air museum of rural life, and the small farming settlements around it, Mramorje among them, sit in the same upland landscape.

The roads around are good for a relaxed ride. They roll over gentle hills, pass through forest and open meadows, and offer long views toward the Dinaric ranges, with the border of Bosnia not far to the west. Surfaces vary, and some small roads are patchy, but main routes are in decent shape. Traffic is heavy in summer and on weekends, particularly on the road from Belgrade, and lorries and slow tourist cars hold up traffic. Spring brings cool air and green slopes, autumn gold, and the winter season sees snow and some skiing.

Fuel is available in Zlatibor and at nearby Čajetina, and Užice, the largest town in the area, with a population of more than sixty thousand, lies about twenty kilometres away and offers everything. Cash is useful in smaller places, though cards work in larger shops. Serbian drivers can be impatient and overtake freely, so ride defensively.

Evenings are cool at this altitude even in summer, and the stars are bright. Pull on a jacket and sit outdoors with a plate of grilled meat and a glass of rakija, and you will understand why people keep coming back.
t.vlore@40.5,19.5:
Vlorë is where the Adriatic and the Ionian Sea are said to meet, and that is the first thing a local will tell you, with some pride, even if the geographers are a little vague about exactly where the line falls. The town sits at the head of a wide bay, closed off to the west by the long mountainous arm of the Karaburun peninsula and the island of Sazan, and behind it the Llogara range stands up to well over two thousand metres. It is a big, busy, slightly chaotic place of nearly ninety thousand people, with a long seafront promenade of palms and cafes.

History is thick here. Albania declared its independence in Vlorë in November 1912, and the town still keeps that date as the centre of its identity, with a monument and a museum dedicated to it. Under Ottoman rule it was a trading port, and the great architect Sinan is credited with a mosque still standing in the centre, which tells you the place mattered. In the twentieth century it was a Cold War outpost, and Sazan island was a closed military zone for decades; the bay carries the traces of that era in rusting installations and concrete bunkers dotted across the hills.

For a rider, Vlorë is the true start of the coastal road, the SH8, which heads south over the Llogara Pass and down the so-called Albanian Riviera towards Himarë and Sarandë. Getting out of town is the only slow part; once the roundabouts and the shared taxis are behind you, the road climbs steadily through pine and fir to the pass, with the sea falling away below you in a hundred shades of blue. The surface has improved enormously in recent years but still deserves respect: patches, loose gravel in the bends, the occasional goat, and drivers who treat overtaking as a negotiation.

Fuel and food are easy here, which is exactly why a ride starts and ends in this town. Fill the tank before you leave, because south of Orikum the stations thin out, and there is a nice habit of breakfast at one of the seafront bakeries before the climb. Fish is the thing to eat in the evening, grilled and plain, with a cold local beer. Go in late spring or September, when the water is warm, the light is soft and the road is not yet jammed with summer traffic, and do the pass in the morning when the haze lifts off the sea.
t.podgorica@42.4,19.3:
Podgorica is Montenegro's capital, and you could drive past it without knowing, because it has few of the old stones and picture-book bays that fill the coast. It lies in a broad plain where the Morača and Ribnica rivers meet, about thirty kilometres from the shore of Lake Skadar, with mountains circling it. About a hundred and forty thousand people live here, nearly a quarter of the country, and it is a young, busy place of cafes and traffic.

The city has been through several names and wars. Under the Ottomans it was a fortress town, and in the Second World War it was heavily bombed, so little of the old city remains apart from a clock tower and a few Ottoman remnants near the river. From 1946 to 1992 it was called Titograd, after Tito, and the Millennium Bridge, a cable-stayed span over the Morača opened in 2005, is its modern symbol. The Ribnica ruins and the confluence are a pleasant walk.

The real reason to use Podgorica is its position. Lake Skadar, the largest lake in the Balkans, is a short ride south, with marshes full of pelicans, herons and water lilies, and the old village of Rijeka Crnojevića. West lies the road to the coast, and north the dramatic Morača canyon, a gorge with cliff walls and a road clinging to the side, which leads toward the mountains and Durmitor. The Ostrog monastery, built into a cliff face, is a major pilgrimage site, about fifty kilometres away.

Fuel is available in the city and along every main road, and parking is not difficult. Summers are hot, with temperatures above thirty-five degrees, and winter brings rain and mountain snow. Eat grilled meats, cheese and kajmak, and the local Vranac red wine. Cafe life runs late into the evening, and a stroll along the river after a day of mountain roads is a quiet, comfortable ending.
t.guanella pass@39.6,-104.6:
Guanella Pass is up in the Front Range, between Georgetown and Grant, and it tops out at about 3,500 metres; these coordinates, though, are out on the high plains south-east of Denver, a hundred kilometres or so from the pass. Parker, a growing town of fifty thousand, lies twenty kilometres away, with Bennett and Stonegate also nearby. So treat this as the place where a day in the Rockies ends: rolling prairie at about 1,800 metres, shortgrass and scattered ponderosa, with the long wall of the Front Range lying on the western horizon.

The plains here are a surprise to people who think of Colorado as all mountains. Ranches and horse properties sit on gentle ridges cut by creeks, and the Palmer Divide, a low rise running east from the mountains, gives the area its rolling look and a surprisingly cool, snowy winter. Spring and early summer bring violent afternoon thunderstorms with hail the size of marbles, sometimes bigger, and every rider along the Front Range learns to read the towering clouds that build over the peaks by midday. On a clear evening you can see Pikes Peak far to the south, and the light on the grass is a pale gold.

The pass itself is a different story. The road, Colorado 381, climbs from Georgetown in a series of tight switchbacks, then crosses high alpine meadows with views of Mount Bierstadt and Mount Evans, among the fourteen-thousand-foot peaks of the range. The paved section is narrow and has few guardrails, and the southern side toward Grant becomes gravel, so check conditions, since heavy snow closes the upper part in winter and it usually opens by Memorial Day. Moose and elk are often seen in the willow marshes, and the aspens turn gold in late September.

Back here on the plains, fuel and food are easy, with stations and chain restaurants in Parker and along the main roads. Traffic on the highways into Denver can be heavy at rush hour. Afternoon weather is the main thing to watch: start early, be off the high roads before the storms build, and carry a rain layer.
t.sarajevo@43.9,18.4:
Sarajevo lies in a narrow valley along the Miljacka river, with steep green hills on all sides, and the old town at its heart is a bazaar quarter called Baščaršija, where copper-workers still hammer out coffee sets and the smell of grilled ćevapi drifts down every lane. The city has about seven hundred thousand people in its wider area, and its position between mountains means the air can be very still, with smoke in winter and the call to prayer echoing from the hills.

It has been a meeting point of faiths for centuries. Ottoman rule left mosques and a covered bazaar, the Austro-Hungarians added neo-Moorish buildings and the great City Hall, now the national library, and within a few minutes' walk you can find a mosque, a Catholic cathedral, an Orthodox church and a synagogue. In 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand was shot near the Latin Bridge, a spark that led to the First World War. Much more recently the city endured the longest siege of a capital in modern warfare, nearly four years from 1992 to 1996, and the marks are still there: shell scars on walls, the Sarajevo roses, memorials and the tunnel that kept the city supplied. The 1984 Winter Olympics left their own mark on the nearby mountains of Bjelašnica, Jahorina and Trebević.

For riders, the approach from Mostar is the highlight. The road follows the Neretva river through a deep canyon past Jablanica and Konjic, then climbs through forest and over the mountain shoulders toward the capital, with plenty of bends and long views. Traffic in the city itself is dense, trams share the main street, and parking a bike near the old town is possible but needs care. Surfaces are variable, and potholes and rough patches appear on side roads.

Fuel is plentiful in the city and along the main roads. Food is among the best in the Balkans, with burek, ćevapi, sweet baklava and thick bosanska kafa served in small copper pots. Evenings in the old town are lively and safe, and the light on the minarets at dusk is lovely.
t.drvar@44.4,16.4:
Drvar sits in a high green bowl of western Bosnia, circled by forested mountains and close to the Dinara range, which marks the border with Croatia. It is a small town, remote and quiet, and for a rider following the Una River route it is a place where the road runs out of towns for a while, so it makes sense to top up when you can. The larger centres are Bosansko Grahovo, about twenty kilometres away, and Sanica, though neither is large by European standards.

The area carries a heavy history. In May 1944 German paratroopers dropped on Drvar in an operation called Rösselsprung, aiming to capture or kill Josip Broz Tito, the Partisan leader, who had his headquarters in a cave on a hillside above the town. He escaped, and the cave remains as a historic site. The town was badly damaged in the wars of the twentieth century, including the conflict of the 1990s, and many of the people who live here came back after years of displacement. It is worth approaching with respect and curiosity rather than a camera in hand.

The landscape is a pleasure. The Unac, a tributary of the Una, runs through a narrow canyon of limestone and clear water south-east of the town, passing the village of Martin Brod where waterfalls tumble over travertine terraces. The forests of beech and spruce shelter bears and wolves, though you are far more likely to see sheep, cattle and the odd tractor. Roads are narrow, with variable surface, tight bends and occasional gravel, and in some places, there are no crash barriers and long drops.

Weather at this altitude can turn quickly. Summer afternoons bring storms, and winter brings deep snow and ice, which can close the minor roads. Spring and early autumn offer the most reliable conditions, with cool mornings and clear light.

Cafes and small shops are found in the town, usually serving strong coffee, cevapi and pita, and prices are very low by Western standards. Carry some cash in convertible marks, because card machines are not universal in the countryside.
t.peak@39.9,-104.8:
The Peak to Peak Highway belongs to the mountains, but this point is on the plains northeast of Denver, near Brighton and Todd Creek, where the land is flat enough to see the whole Front Range in a single glance. On a clear day the wall of the Rockies stretches across the western horizon for a hundred kilometres, with the snowy summits of Longs Peak and Mount Evans standing out, and the wide sky is the real feature of the place.

This is farm country, once a huge cattle range and then irrigated by ditches that brought snowmelt out of the mountains. Sugar beets, corn and vegetables grew here, and Brighton still holds a local festival around its strawberries in the summer. The South Platte River, a wide shallow stream with cottonwoods along its banks, curves through, and the old irrigation ditches still run beside the roads in places.

Nearby Barr Lake State Park is one of the best places in Colorado for birds. The big reservoir, ringed with cottonwoods, hosts great blue herons, pelicans and a good number of bald eagles, which nest there. A paved loop around it lets you walk or cycle, and the park's nature centre is in a barn at the edge. Not far to the southwest, the Rocky Mountain Arsenal National Wildlife Refuge occupies land once used to make chemical weapons and is now a wildlife sanctuary, with a herd of bison, prairie dogs and deer. It is a fascinating example of land that turned from military to wild use.

The riding is of the straight, open kind, on county roads laid out in a grid and running dead straight for miles, with the mountains in front. The wind can be strong and gusty, and thunderstorms in summer can build fast, with hail. There is almost no shade, and the sun is fierce at altitude, which is about 1,500 metres here. A grain elevator or a distant windmill is the only landmark.

Brighton has fuel, supermarkets and a range of Mexican restaurants and diners, and the airport is not far, which makes this a convenient place to start or finish a trip to the high country. Evening light is the best, when the mountains turn pink and purple and the plains glow gold.
t.khabarovsk@48.5,135.1:
Khabarovsk stands on high bluffs above the Amur, one of the great rivers of Asia, in the far east of Russia, and from its waterfront the view across the broad brown water to the far shore feels immense. Founded in 1858 as a military outpost, the city was named after Yerofey Khabarov, a seventeenth-century explorer who led Cossacks into the Amur region. Today around five hundred and eighty thousand people live here, making it the largest city of the Russian Far East after Vladivostok, and it has a settled, broad-streeted air.

The river is the heart of the place. The Amur forms the border with China for a large part of its length, and the city lies close to the point where the Ussuri river joins it. In the early twentieth century, a railway bridge of a couple of kilometres was built across the Amur, an enormous project for its time, completing the Trans-Siberian line, and it remains a landmark. In summer the riverfront is crowded with strollers, ice-cream sellers and boat tours, and in winter the river freezes into a vast white road, with fishermen cutting holes in the ice.

The city has several museums, a tidy cathedral and a lively market. t.ston@42.8,17.7:
Ston is a tiny town with a huge wall. Where the Pelješac peninsula narrows to a thread, the old Republic of Ragusa, Dubrovnik's city-state, built a line of fortifications that climbs a steep hill and runs for several kilometres, more than five by most accounts, joining Ston to its twin Mali Ston on the other side of the isthmus. Construction began in the fourteenth century, and the wall is often called the European Great Wall. Walk it if you have the legs, because from the top you see the salt pans, the oyster beds and the narrow channel of Mali Ston Bay opening on each side.

The salt pans are the reason for all that stone. Ston has produced salt for centuries, and the Republic guarded the income carefully. The pans are still worked, and the sight of white crystals and old stone sluices in the afternoon light is easy to love. The bay is also famous for oysters and mussels, and a plate of the former in Mali Ston, with a glass of local white, is the traditional treat. The earthquake of 1996 damaged the walls, and restoration has taken years.

For riders, Ston is a handy junction. The coast road from the north and Dubrovnik, the Adriatic Highway, passes close, and the peninsula road runs out west toward Orebić through vineyards that produce Plavac Mali, the grape behind the heavy red wines of Dingač and Postup. The road itself is quiet and bends along the ridge with sea views left and right, though the surface can be rough and gusts of bura wind can hit the exposed sections hard. Summer brings heat and tourist traffic, especially on the main coast route, so early starts help. Neum, about eleven kilometres away, is a Bosnian town on a short stretch of coast that interrupts the Croatian shoreline, with border checks that can mean queues in season. The new bridge to the peninsula now bypasses it for travellers who prefer to stay in Croatia.

Ston has only a few thousand people at most, so do not count on a large choice of services. Check the fuel level before arriving, because larger towns are on either side. There are restaurants and a bakery by the walls, and a short stop is easy to enjoy.
t.uzice@43.9,19.8:
Užice is built into a canyon. The Đetinja River has cut a narrow gorge through the hills of western Serbia, and the town spreads along it, with the ruins of its old fortress stuck onto a rocky spur above the water. People have defended this chokepoint for centuries, first the medieval Serbs, then the Ottomans, who rebuilt the fortress, and the town still feels hemmed in and a little defiant. With nearly sixty-four thousand people it is the main city of the Zlatibor region.

Its most notable moment came in 1941. After the German invasion, partisans led by Tito liberated Užice and the area around it, and for a couple of months in autumn it was a free territory, the Užice Republic, with a weapons factory that made rifles and ammunition, a radio and even a newspaper. German forces crushed it in late November, and the Kadinjača hill nearby is a memorial to the partisan stand. The history is worth knowing because it explains the solemn monuments you meet on the roads.

The riding around is good. South and west, the road climbs onto the Zlatibor plateau, a rolling highland of meadows and pine forest that Serbs treat as their mountain resort, with the village of Čajetina and the tourist centre of Zlatibor about eighteen kilometres away. The Zlatibor road is a wide, mostly well-surfaced affair with long bends and good views. Further west, the road to Mokra Gora and the narrow-gauge railway called the Šargan Eight winds through a landscape of steep green slopes, while the Tara and Drina canyons beyond are a major reward, with deep gorges and tight bends. Surface quality varies on minor roads, and trucks and tourist buses add to the mix in July and August. Fog in the valley can last into the morning.

Užice has all the services of a regional city, with fuel stations on the approach roads, bakeries, grill places and plenty of coffee. Zlatibor is famous for smoked ham and kajmak, a creamy dairy spread, and a plate of both with warm bread makes a good lunch. Autumn is clear and quiet, and the beech woods turn gold.
In the far north of the Republic of Congo, the forest is so big and so unbroken that it can feel like another planet. Nouabalé-Ndoki National Park covers more than four thousand square kilometers of lowland rainforest, swamp and river, and it is part of a conservation landscape that continues into Cameroon and the Central African Republic. Together with Lobéké and Dzanga-Sangha, it forms the Sangha Trinational, which UNESCO listed in 2012. This is one of the last large tracts of intact forest in the Congo Basin, and its remoteness has kept it largely free of the pressures found elsewhere.

The wildlife is outstanding. Forest elephants walk the paths, western lowland gorillas live in groups in the swampy clearings called bais, and chimpanzees here have been studied for their use of tools, such as sticks to fish for termites. One of the best-known sites in the park is Mbeli Bai, a clearing where researchers have watched gorillas for decades from a raised platform. Birds such as hornbills and grey parrots fill the canopy with noise, and the air is dense, warm and loud with insects.

There is no ordinary riding here. Access is from the town of Ouesso and the logging settlement of Pokola on the Sangha River, along dirt tracks cut by timber companies, and the park itself has no roads for tourists. These tracks can be impassable in the rainy seasons, and the dry months from December to February are the most practical. Travel is usually by four-wheel-drive vehicle, boat and on foot, with support from the conservation organizations that run the park and the camps nearby. A motorcycle can be used by experienced adventurers on the logging roads, but this is serious expedition territory.

Planning is crucial. Fuel and supplies must be arranged in advance, since the nearest reliable stations are in Ouesso and towns far to the south, and the camps near the park are basic. Permits, guides and health preparations, including malaria prevention and yellow fever vaccination, are essential. Mobile coverage is absent.

The reward for those who make the effort is a feeling of scale. At dawn, with mist rising from the swamp and the distant call of a gorilla, the forest seems endless.
t.cascade colorado@38.9,-105.0:
Cascade is a small settlement on the western edge of Colorado Springs, at the foot of Pikes Peak, and it is where the toll road begins. The village sits at the entrance to Ute Pass, an old Native American trail that climbs from the plains into the mountains, and the main road to the west still follows its route. At the gate, you pay the toll, check the weather, and begin a climb of nearly eight thousand feet in around nineteen miles.

Pikes Peak was known to the Ute people long before the first Europeans arrived, and it was named after Zebulon Pike, the army officer who saw it from a distance in 1806 and failed to climb it. The mountain was a landmark for the gold seekers heading west, who painted the slogan Pikes Peak or Bust on their wagons. In 1893 a teacher called Katharine Lee Bates stood on the summit and was so moved by the view that she wrote the poem that became America the Beautiful. The first carriage road to the top was built in the 1880s, and today a fully paved highway climbs the mountain, with a cog railway starting from Manitou Springs.

The ride is spectacular and demanding. From the gate, the road winds up through forest, with a steady stream of hairpins and switchbacks, passing alpine lakes and viewpoints before breaking out above the treeline. There are few guard rails in the upper sections, and drops are steep. Weather can change in an instant, with thunderstorms, hail and even snow in summer. Each June, drivers and riders race up the road in the Pikes Peak International Hill Climb, a famous test of nerve and speed.

Fuel is not available on the mountain, so fill the tank in Manitou Springs, about six kilometres from here, or Colorado Springs. The tollgate staff can tell you about conditions and any restrictions, and the road closes in bad weather. Dress in layers, carry water, and be prepared for much colder temperatures at the top. Start early, because afternoon storms are common, and, as altitude affects both rider and machine, be prepared for the engine to feel a little breathless.
t.pikes peak summit@38.8,-105.0:
At fourteen thousand one hundred and fifteen feet, or 4,302 metres, the summit of Pikes Peak is a cold, bright, windy platform at the eastern edge of the Rockies, and there is a feeling of having arrived somewhere that is not quite the planet you started on. The air holds about sixty percent of the oxygen you are used to, so walking from the bike to the summit house is enough to make you breathe hard, and a headache or dizziness is common. Take it slowly, drink water and do not rush.

The view makes the effort worthwhile. To the east, the high plains stretch out flat to the horizon, with Colorado Springs and its grid of streets laid out below. To the west, the ranks of the Sawatch and Mosquito ranges run into the distance, often with snow on the tops. A cog railway, completed in 1891, climbs from Manitou Springs, and some riders time their arrival to see the train come in. The summit house sells the famous high-altitude doughnuts, made with a special recipe to cope with the thin air, and they are hot, sweet and more than welcome.

Getting here is an adventure. The upper stretch of the highway is above the treeline, in barren granite rubble and tundra, with sharp switchbacks and big drops on one side. The wind can be fierce, and snow can fall in any month. There may be ice on the road even in July, so it is worth checking with the rangers about conditions. The descent is as important as the climb: long, steep gradients put a lot of heat into brakes, so use low gears and engine braking, and give your brakes time to rest.

Allow time for the descent, because the road is slow, and watch for marmots on the rocks. Dress warmly, with gloves and a windproof layer, and bring sunglasses, since the sun at this altitude is strong. The best weather is generally in the morning, and storms often arrive by early afternoon.
t.okaukuejo@-19.2,15.9:
Okaukuejo is the oldest of the rest camps in Etosha National Park, and its waterhole is the best reason to go there. The camp lies on the southern edge of the great Etosha Pan, a vast salt flat that glitters white in the dry season and holds shallow water in the wet, and the name of the park means great white place. A fort, built in 1901 by German troops, now serves as a museum and tower, and from the top, you can look across the plains and the pan, a view that is simply huge.

At dusk, the waterhole in front of the camp is floodlit, and animals come to drink in the dark. Black rhinos are a regular sight, appearing as grey shapes at the edge of the light, and elephants, lions, giraffes and hyenas arrive in turn, while jackals and owls slip around the edges. Visitors sit on benches in silence and watch the performance, which can last for hours, and the encounter has a quiet, primeval feel. It is among the most reliable places in Africa to see black rhino.

Think carefully about the practical side before planning a ride here. Etosha has strict rules, with speed limits, closing times for gates, no leaving vehicles in the open, and rules about motorcycles that are generally restrictive, so check with the park authorities whether a bike is admitted before you travel. Entry fees apply, and bookings for camps are usually essential well in advance. The roads on the approach are a mix of tarmac and gravel, with livestock and wildlife crossing, and heat is considerable for most of the year.

The camp has a fuel station, a shop, a restaurant and a swimming pool, which is a great relief after a dusty day, and it is the most convenient place to refuel in the western part of the park. Outside the park, the nearest towns are some distance away, so plan your supplies, and bring plenty of water. The best time for game viewing is the dry season, from about May to October, when animals gather at waterholes, while the green season brings birds and flowers but also heat and thunderstorms.
t.rundu@-17.9,19.8:
Rundu is where Namibia's long, dry north suddenly turns green. The town sits on the south bank of the Okavango River, and across the water, close enough to hear the roosters, is Angola. It is the capital of the Kavango East region and a proper working town of nearly sixty thousand people, which in this part of the country makes it a metropolis. After hundreds of kilometres of bush and cattle fences on the tar road from the south, the first sight of reed beds, dugout canoes and glittering river is a small shock.

For a rider, Rundu is a supply stop and a good one. There is fuel, there are supermarkets, banks that actually have cash, and a good choice of places to eat with the river in view. Treat it as the last dependable shop for a while before the long eastern run into the Caprivi, and top up everything that holds a fluid. The river road along the water is slower and more interesting than the main highway, with mud-brick homesteads, fields of mahangu millet and children waving from every gate.

The Kavango people have lived along this river for centuries, and their woodcarving is the thing most travellers take away. Along the roadside stalls, craftsmen sell animals, masks, bowls and chairs cut from local hardwood, and a good carver will happily explain which tree is which. You will not fit a giraffe on a motorcycle, but a small bowl wrapped in a jacket is entirely possible. Greeting people before you ask for anything is the local courtesy, and it works wonders.

Take the usual care with the riding around town. Pedestrians, goats, cattle and donkeys use the shoulder as their own, and after dark they use the tarmac too. Most locals will tell you not to ride the highway at night, and they are right. Mornings are the best light and the best temperature, and the dry season from roughly May to September keeps the days clear and the mosquitoes thinner. Sundowners by the water, with fish eagles calling and the Angolan bank turning orange, are the reward for a hot day in the saddle.
t.trsa@43.2,18.7:
Trsa lies in the high, rolling country of north-western Montenegro, close to the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina and not far from the long, narrow reservoir of Lake Piva. It is not a village that appears in many guidebooks, which is why it is pleasant to find: an upland hamlet of stone houses, hay meadows and pine woods, with the limestone summits of the Durmitor massif and the Volujak range somewhere beyond the horizon. The nearest town in Montenegro is Plužine, about ten kilometres away, and Foča in Bosnia is the closest sizeable place across the line.

The landscape here was shaped by water, ice and, more recently, concrete. The Piva river once ran through a deep canyon, until the Mratinje dam, one of the highest arch dams in Europe, was built in the 1970s, flooding the valley and creating the lake. Even the old Piva Monastery, a fine sixteenth-century church with remarkable frescoes, was taken apart and rebuilt on higher ground. The result is a long, glittering ribbon of green water in a gorge, with road tunnels cut through the cliffs above it.

Riding on the plateau is relaxed and bright. The roads wind through open farmland and forest, with moderate traffic, a decent surface and occasional potholes, and the occasional sheep or cow. Expect long, easy bends and the sight of limestone peaks on the skyline. The weather can change quickly in the mountains; summer afternoons bring storms, and winters are long and snowy, with some roads difficult. Spring and early autumn are lovely, with cool air and clear light.

For services, you should rely on the towns. Plužine has a small selection of shops, cafes and basic fuel, while Žabljak and Nikšić provide more choice, and Foča is the larger option on the Bosnian side. Carry your passport and bike papers, because the border is close and routes cross it. In villages you can often buy homemade cheese, kajmak, a rich cream, and rakija, the strong fruit brandy, though the sensible rider will decline the last. A short stop to listen to cowbells and look at the hills is reward enough.
t.tara canyon viewpoint@43.2,19.3:
The Tara river has cut one of the deepest canyons in Europe, a gorge that plunges as much as thirteen hundred metres below the rim at its greatest. It runs through the heart of Durmitor National Park in northern Montenegro, a UNESCO World Heritage area, with the clear green water of the Tara, known as the Tear of Europe, tumbling through rapids at the bottom. Standing at a viewpoint on the rim, you see the walls drop away through layers of pine and rock, with the river a bright thread far below and the sound arriving late.

Not far from the main viewpoints stands the Đurđevića Tara Bridge, a slender concrete arch more than 350 metres long and over 150 metres above the river, completed in 1940. Its story is part engineering, part war. In 1942, partisans, with an engineer's help, blew up the central arch to slow an Italian advance, and the bridge was rebuilt after the war. Today a zip line crosses beside it, and tour groups gather at a small cluster of stalls selling honey, cheese and brandy.

The road leading here is a classic of the Balkans. The route from Žabljak twists across the plateau through forest and meadow, with views of the Durmitor peaks, and then meets the canyon edge at a series of lookouts. Surface quality varies, with some excellent tarmac and some rough patches, and the road can be busy with coaches in high season. Early morning and late afternoon offer the best light, with fewer people and a golden glow on the rock. Mist can fill the canyon, which is magical if you are lucky.

For practical needs, Žabljak, around fourteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops, cafes and guesthouses, and is the best base for the area. Pljevlja, a larger town, lies to the north. At the viewpoint, a few stalls sell snacks and drinks, but not much else. Rafting trips run on the river in the spring and early summer, when snowmelt makes the water high and fast, and walking trails lead into the national park. Take a jacket, because the air at the rim is cooler than you expect, and keep a careful distance from the edge.
t.bosnia una river route point 3@44.5,16.1:
Martin Brod is a small village where the Una river, after rising in the Croatian karst, flows into Bosnia and begins a series of cascades, mills and green pools that continue for many kilometres. It is a quiet, remote place, with a handful of houses along the river and the old stone mills where grain was ground for centuries, and the sound of water over rocks is everywhere. The river here is wide and shallow, with clear water running over travertine steps.

The area is in the Una National Park, and the surroundings are a mix of forest, meadow and rock, with the wooded hills of the Dinaric mountains rising on either side. It was a battlefield in the 1990s, and parts of the region were mined, which is why you should follow marked paths and stay on roads. The people here are few, mostly farmers and herders, and hospitality is a matter of pride, so if you are offered a coffee or a glass of juice, accept with a smile.

On a bike, the roads here are quiet and sometimes rough, with narrow lanes, bends through forest and some patches that need attention, so go slowly and watch for gravel. There is little traffic, and this is a place where you are likely to meet more sheep than cars. Mobile signal can be patchy, so carry a map and tell someone your plan. The best time is late spring, when the river is high and the meadows are full of flowers, and early autumn, when the beech forests turn gold.

Services are scarce, and this is a place to arrive with fuel in the tank. Orašac to the north has the nearest shops, and Bihać is the sensible town for a proper fill, so plan carefully, and take food and water. A small guesthouse or two may offer a meal of trout or lamb. It is the kind of place where the quiet is the main attraction, and a morning walk along the water, with mist rising and the mills still, is a rare pleasure.

t.dubrovnik@42.6,18.1:
Dubrovnik was once an independent republic, called Ragusa, and it lasted for centuries by being clever. It was a small city-state that paid tribute to bigger powers, traded with everyone, banned slavery early, and kept a splendid ring of walls that still surrounds the old town. Walking the walls, about two kilometres of stone with towers and bastions, takes an hour or two, and offers views over terracotta roofs and a glittering sea. In 1991 and 1992 the city was shelled during the Yugoslav war, and the damage has been repaired, though a few signs remain. UNESCO added it to its list in 1979.

The old town is closed to traffic, and it is lovely in the early morning and the evening, when the stone glows and the crowds thin out. In summer the cruise ships dock and the main street, the Stradun, is full, so go at dawn or after dark. Take the cable car to Srđ for the best view, and for a reminder of how steep the hills are behind the city.

The riding in the area is exceptional. The Adriatic Highway, which runs high above the old town, has views of the walls and islands, and the road south toward Cavtat and the Montenegrin border winds above the sea. North, the road follows the coast to Ston and the Pelješac peninsula, and since 2022 a bridge links the peninsula to the mainland, bypassing the short stretch of Bosnian coast at Neum so the border checks there no longer interrupt a ride. Traffic is slow in July and August, and the heat and glare are strong. Spring and autumn are the best times.

The city has fuel stations at the edge of town, parking garages near the old town, and a full range of food. Local specialities include black risotto, oysters from Ston, and rozata, a caramel custard. Prices are high in season, and rooms should be booked well ahead. Be careful on the polished stone of the old town in wet weather, and note that speed cameras and traffic police are active on the coastal road.
